content:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway.

The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research.

Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses.

"The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service."

Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails.

The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top."

Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering.

However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026.

It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants.

What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface.

"The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said.

While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks.

"As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

content:
The Russia-linked threat actor known as APT29 is said to be behind a large-scale watering hole campaign targeting iOS and Android users through compromised websites, fake domains, and a supply chain attack involving a Ukrainian web analytics service called Plerdy SEO Tracker.

"The injected JavaScript code collects browser and device attributes," Sekoia researchers Amaury-Jacques Garçon and Félix Aime said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "Then, the delivery infrastructure delivers a platform-specific N-day exploit chain targeting either iOS or Android."

The end goal of the attacks is to serve payloads capable of stealing browser cookies, and in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords or full mobile device data. The activity, codenamed Poisoned Source, was discovered by the French cybersecurity company in mid-October 2026.

A defining aspect of the campaign is the use of three infection vectors -

  • Compromise of legitimate websites to inject malicious JavaScript
  • Lookalike sites masquerading as high-profile websites in the U.S. ("america250[.]holiday"), Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Bulgaria
  • Supply chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026, by injecting malicious code into "a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js"

Some of the compromised websites include a major industry trade association representing U.S. companies operating in the chemical industry, a far-right European political party, and a Bulgarian military-related website. It's suspected that the watering hole campaign may have been designed to target specific individuals rather than a broad effort.

"It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest," Sekoia said.

"However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war. This supply chain attack spread through high-value targets, such as army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) websites."

Regardless of the method employed, all roads lead to the same payload: a JavaScript loader that profiles the visitor's device and web browser, and then serves appropriate next-stage malware. For iOS users, it leads to an exploit kit called DarkSword to harvest cookies and full device data.

On Android, the malware is equipped to exfiltrate Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence. No less than three different exploits have been identified -

  • Class A, which targets iOS devices running iOS 16.7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft.
  • Class B, which targets iOS devices running iOS 18.5 and exploits the DarkSword exploit chain comprising CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 to deliver JavaScript malware for full device data exfiltration. This includes SMS messages and iMessages; Apple Mail Envelope Index and Protected Index SQLite databases; voicemail; WhatsApp and Telegram databases; iCloud Keychain, Wi-Fi passwords; contacts; call history; Safari browser history and cookies; photos; and data from Apple Health, Calendar, Notes, and iCloud Drive.
  • Class C, which targets Android devices running Chrome versions from 139 through 145 (but explicitly excluding version 143 for reasons that remain presently unknown) and exploits CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 to achieve remote code execution, sandbox escape, privilege escalation, and ultimately deliver AndroSnitch to collect Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords.

In all three cases, the exfiltrated data is sent to the "ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12" endpoint. The Android attack chain incorporates a check to determine whether the targeted device is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra by examining its model identifier (i.e., SM-S938B). If the device matches, the exploitation activity is terminated.

AndroSnitch derives its name from its similarities to ANDROSNATCH, a Chrome cookie-stealing payload that Google documented in August 2024 in connection with a suspected APT29 watering hole campaign, which targeted Android users visiting a Mongolian government website by leveraging a Chrome exploit chain involving CVE-2024-5274 and CVE-2024-4671.

"This operation also confirms the continued reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendors] mobile exploit frameworks, such as DarkSword, by state-sponsored intrusion sets," Sekoia said. "The adoption of packaged N-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation."

Coruna and DarkSword Kits Evolve

The development comes weeks after iVerify and Report URI detailed the P7 variant of DarkSword being delivered via half-click attacks that leverage ad-based infrastructure. In one case, the exploit is said to have been propagated through a malicious Instagram ad themed around the World Cup and served from "ad-track[.]live."

The other pathway is part of a criminal campaign dubbed DeadTag, in which attackers acquire expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that are still loaded by thousands of websites. The idea is to serve malicious JavaScript to iPhone visitors and silently do the attacker's bidding.

"It checks who's visiting," Report URI said. "Search engines, security scanners, automated browsers and anything else that looks like a bot gets nothing."

The script then interacts with the attacker's server, which then decides the destination to which each visitor has to be redirected. The iPhone exploit paths that take advantage of DeadTag lead to the Coruna exploit kit for older iPhones running iOS version 13 to 17.2.1 and DarkSword P7 for iOS devices running 18.4 to 18.7.

"These are not phishing pages or fake app downloads, both kits attack the browser itself," Report URI's Scott Helme said. "Simply opening the page is enough for your device to be compromised. There's nothing to tap, you don't need to click any link, nothing to install and no warning. If the iPhone is running a vulnerable version of iOS, the kit breaks out of the browser and installs spyware on the device."

Other schemes lead to decoy Google redirects, betting and casino scam sign-up pages, search advertisements for car deals and dentists, and fake surveys and "you've won" prize pages. More than 660 expired and re-registered domains are part of the DeadTag network.

According to an analysis published by Zimperium zLabs, campaigns distributing Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits have continued to evolve, with 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code as of October 2026.

Although Coruna was initially developed by a nation-state actor for highly targeted operations, its subsequent leak following initial disclosure has made the toolkit widely accessible to multiple threat actors for their own campaigns.

In many cases, the lure sites have been found to explicitly instruct visitors to exit their in-app browser or alternative iOS browser and open the link in Safari so as to trigger the exploit chain depending upon the device operating system.

"Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework (exhibiting byte-identical JavaScript payloads across multiple recovered configurations)," security researcher Santiago Rodriguez said. "Conversely, devices running later iOS builds receive a DarkSword-derived execution chain."

"The analyzed distribution footprint spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and – in several instances – compromised legitimate sites serving the kit via hidden iframes."

title: Critical Rails Flaw Lets Attackers Write Server Files via Crafted ImageMagick Uploads
author: The Hacker News
summary: A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails  could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads using ImageMagick . The Rails project disclosed the flaw in  an advisory  and fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.   The flaw is in Active Storage, the part of Rails that handles file uploads. Some apps store uploaded files using Active Storage's Disk service, which stores them on the server's disk. In those apps, an attacker could also read any file the app can read.   Those files typically include the app's secret_key_base and its credentials for other systems, according to Rails. Reading them may in turn allow remote code execution or lateral movement into those systems.   Rails rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. It is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and does not yet have a CVE identifier.   ImageMagick selects a format handler, which it calls a coder, based on the file's c...
content:
A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads using ImageMagick. The Rails project disclosed the flaw in an advisory and fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

The flaw is in Active Storage, the part of Rails that handles file uploads. Some apps store uploaded files using Active Storage's Disk service, which stores them on the server's disk. In those apps, an attacker could also read any file the app can read.

Those files typically include the app's secret_key_base and its credentials for other systems, according to Rails. Reading them may in turn allow remote code execution or lateral movement into those systems.

Rails rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. It is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and does not yet have a CVE identifier.

ImageMagick selects a format handler, which it calls a coder, based on the file's content. Some coders act on other files named inside the image, not on the image itself. Active Storage imposes no limits on which coders an upload can use, so the server's own ImageMagick policy was the only limit.

The ImageMagick analyzer in Active Storage runs when a file is attached. Attaching the upload is enough to reach the flaw. The app does not have to make a variant (a transformed copy of the image) or a preview, or call analyze.

An uploaded SVG file reached ImageMagick's MSL coder through that analyzer, according to the commit that fixed the flaw. MSL is a scripting coder that reads and writes files named by its script.

Rails said one attack chain was reported to it, but it does "not assume it is the only one that exists." The advisory does not say whether the flaw has been exploited.

The flaw was reported through HackerOne by RyotaK, a researcher at GMO Flatt Security.

Which Rails Apps Are Affected

An app is affected only if all three of these are true:

  • It uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. That is the setting config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick, the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier.
  • Its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the coders involved. Rails says the policies that Debian and Ubuntu ship do not.
  • It accepts file uploads from untrusted users.

To check the first condition, look at config.active_storage.variant_processor. If it is not set, the default depends on load_defaults: :mini_magick before 7.0, and :vips from 7.0 on. The same setting decides which library analyzes uploads, not only which one makes variants.

Every Active Storage version before 8.0.5.2 is affected, as are 8.1 versions before 8.1.4.1. Release series older than 8.0 are no longer supported, and Rails will not release fixed versions for them.

In July, Rails fixed a different critical Active Storage flaw, CVE-2026-66066, which affected apps that use libvips instead of ImageMagick. Apps using ImageMagick were not exposed to that flaw's attack path, but they can be exposed to this one.

The same releases fix a second Active Storage flaw, GHSA-v924-7rp8-4mxh, which Rails rates high with a CVSS score of 8.8. Active Storage passed uploads to ImageMagick and FFmpeg under temporary file names that kept the uploaded file's extension.

Those tools can pick a decoder from the extension when a file's content does not show its format. So an attacker who chose an upload's filename and declared its content type could choose the decoder that processes it.

What to Do

Rails strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. The two releases fix 21 security issues in total.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy. MiniMagick is the Ruby gem Active Storage uses to call ImageMagick. In its default setup, every ImageMagick command it runs applies the policy, not only commands from Active Storage.

The policy blocks the MSL coder; coders that read or delete files other than the image; coders that fetch remote or local references or display them on a screen; every coder backed by Ghostscript, along with the gs delegate; and @filename indirection.

  • Upgrade to Rails 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2. Apps on :mini_magick also need mini_magick 5.1 or later, or they raise an error at boot. Rails 8.0 gets security fixes only until November 7, 2026, under its maintenance policy.
  • Confirm that the app loads the new policy, as the Active Storage guide describes, by running bin/rails runner 'puts MiniMagick.identify { |i| i.list "policy" }'.
  • Check whether the shipped policy reaches the app at all. It does not reach an app that replaces MiniMagick.cli_env after boot, clears the environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix, or installs its own MiniMagick::Shell. Such an app must put the rules in ImageMagick's system policy.
  • Apps that use GraphicsMagick get no protection from the shipped policy, because GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies.
  • Check the server's own ImageMagick policy. The shipped policy adds to it rather than replacing it. A rule there that allows a coder, including a wildcard such as pattern="*", overrides the shipped policy's block on that coder.
  • If the app renders PDF or PostScript files through ImageMagick, re-allow the gs delegate and the coders it uses in the server's policy.xml.
  • If you cannot upgrade yet, copy the rules of the shipped policy, activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml, into ImageMagick's system policy, such as /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml. At a minimum, block the MSL coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the gs delegate. Rails also published the fix as patches for 8.1 and 8.0.
  • Apps on release series older than 8.0 can use that workaround or upgrade to 8.0 or later.
  • Rails' workarounds for the second flaw only change how FFmpeg is used. None of them covers ImageMagick.
  • If the app stores attachments with the Disk service, change secret_key_base and every other secret the app process can read. That includes the master key, everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not keep an exposed secret as a fallback.

The advisory does not explain how to check whether an app has already been targeted.

title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
author: The Hacker News
summary: Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.   Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an  advisory  on November 3. The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue. content:
Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

  • Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.
  • Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.
  • XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.
  • Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
author: The Hacker News
summary: Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one.   One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel.   No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external d...
content:
Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one.

One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel.

No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip.

The runtime is the application, not the pipe

The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model.

A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go.

Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing.

The inspection point is also a target

In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector.

None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure.

A millisecond verdict needs a memory

Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do.

Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist.

What real agent runtime looks like

Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block.

Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy.

Do not buy the end state

Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly.

What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime.

The first ninety days, in order

A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this.

Window The work How to know it is real
Weeks 1 to 2: get the number Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic. Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps.
Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first. A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?"
Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults. Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block.

The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance.

Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge.

Seven questions that sort vendors

Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists.

Ask What a good answer looks like
Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO? Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot.
For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain. A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score.
Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents? Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one.
When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain? Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one.
What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict? Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone.
What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised? A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly.
How long until I see my real agent inventory? Days. A quarter is a different product.

Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission and agent action into a single live view, so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days.

Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform.

The full ninety-day sequence, the four-level self-assessment and all fifteen vendor questions are in The Agent Security Checklist: Your First 90 Days.

Reco is the leader in Agent Security. The Reco Platform secures agents and their operating environments where applications, identities, permissions, and workflows intersect. It discovers an organization's entire third-party ecosystem, prioritizes real risk over alert volume and remediates with precision across every human identity, agent, app and permission in the environment. Built on the Reco Graph, with new integrations delivered in hours through the Reco Factory and pre-built agent and app intelligence from the Reco Library. With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat detection together in one place. title: China-Aligned Hackers Hijack Sogou Input Method DNS Requests to Deploy DarkVigil Backdoor
author: The Hacker News
summary: A China-aligned threat actor known as SlippyNunchucks  has been attributed to a Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking operation abusing insecure HTTP communications in Windows versions of Sogou Input Method as part of a surveillance campaign designed to deploy an implant called DarkVigil (aka FDMTP).   The campaign, observed starting July 1, 2026, is assessed to have targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka, according to ESET.   "DarkVigil implants are typically deployed through popular Chinese applications," ESET researcher Anh Ho said  in a report shared with The Hacker News. "By abusing these applications, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor has been able to reach Chinese-speaking users across Asia and Europe."   Some of the applications abused by the adversary include Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to.   Active since at least September 15, 2023, SlippyNunc...
content:
A China-aligned threat actor known as SlippyNunchucks has been attributed to a Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking operation abusing insecure HTTP communications in Windows versions of Sogou Input Method as part of a surveillance campaign designed to deploy an implant called DarkVigil (aka FDMTP).

The campaign, observed starting July 1, 2026, is assessed to have targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka, according to ESET.

"DarkVigil implants are typically deployed through popular Chinese applications," ESET researcher Anh Ho said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "By abusing these applications, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor has been able to reach Chinese-speaking users across Asia and Europe."

Some of the applications abused by the adversary include Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to.

Active since at least September 15, 2023, SlippyNunchucks is known for targeting organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals across South and East Asia. These attacks lead to the deployment of a modular .NET framework that includes DarkVigil and a set of over 20 plugins.

Although the use of the backdoor has been previously linked to Mustang Panda, ESET said it found no tactical overlaps between the threat actor and DarkVigil-related activity in its telemetry, prompting it to classify it as a distinct intrusion set.

Earlier this August, Fortinet's FortiGuard Incident Response Team detailed the threat actor's supply chain compromise of the QuickFox VPN and network acceleration tool to deliver DarkVigil.

According to the Slovakian cybersecurity company, the adversary shifted to exploiting Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language input method editor developed by Tencent, as a delivery vector three days after QuickFox released a clean version of its program.

Specifically, the attack involves hijacking the app's branded vocabulary promotion mechanism to serve a malicious configuration, which ultimately paves the way for the deployment of the malware via SGTool.exe, a legitimate Sogou Input Method component that functions as a multi-purpose task dispatcher.

In a clean environment, the executable sends an HTTP request to the "config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php" endpoint to fetch a configuration. But in the attack discovered by ESET, the DNS resolution of the domain is tampered with to resolve it to one of the two staging servers -

  • 47.239.250[.]102 (sogou-cdn[.]com)
  • 47.237.122[.]175 (dev.soft-png-cdn.com)

The consequence of this DNS hijacking was that HTTP requests to the "getBrandScd.php" endpoint were routed to one of the staging servers, which then responded with a malicious configuration. The configuration, for its part, instructs the binary to download two additional payloads from "sogou-cdn[.]com" and launch the malware via DLL sideloading -

  • A legitimate Adobe executable ("biz_helper.exe")
  • A rogue DLL ("libcef.dll") containing DarkVigil

DarkVigil is notable for its use of Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP) for command-and-control (C2), allowing the client to execute and orchestrate plugins received from an attacker-controlled server to facilitate persistence or data collection.

Following responsible disclosure, Tencent addressed the vulnerability (CVE-2026-120422) in version 16.10, released on October 29, 2026, by migrating the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS.

SlippyNunchucks is suspected to operate keeping the interests of the Chinese government in mind, with ESET describing it as a nation-state surveillance effort.

"Although SlippyNunchucks targets organizations and individuals across multiple sectors, we discovered significant surveillance activity against an organization operating Chinese-language online betting platforms in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, and the Philippines," ESET said.

"The targeting of this organization is notable given China's restrictions on gambling, including criminal penalties for operating gambling businesses and organizing Chinese citizens to gamble abroad."

This is not the first time China-nexus threat actors have weaponized the Sogou Input Method as an entry point for malware distribution. In September 2026, Gen Digital said a now-patched vulnerability in the input method editor (CVE-2026-51990) was exploited by UNC3569 to deliver a backdoor dubbed GRAYRABBIT by means of a crafted link.

"The vulnerability chains three separate weaknesses into a single, one-click exploit: unvalidated command-line argument injection in the sgbiz: custom protocol handler, unrestricted URL navigation in a CEF-based WebView, and a severely outdated, unsandboxed Chromium browser engine [susceptible to CVE-2021-38003]," Gen Digital said.

title: Microsoft spent two years telling you to buy 16GB of RAM, now it says...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Windows boss Pavan Davuluri says 8GB is enough for everyday work, backed by new memory optimizations. We trace Microsoft's shifting RAM advice from Copilot+ PCs and 32GB gaming guides to today's $429 ...
content:
With RAM prices pushing 16GB laptops out of reach, Microsoft now wants you to feel good about buying one with 8GB. “For many people, 8 GB is a great fit for the things they do every day,” Windows boss Pavan Davuluri wrote on November 3 in a blog that ends by recommending 8GB Windows 11 laptops from $429. Coming from the company that made 16GB the Copilot+ PC minimum and called 32GB the “no worries” upgrade for gamers, it’s quite a shift, and truth be told, I love it.

Also, Microsoft has numbers now. On 8GB PCs, Windows 11 is now up to 20% more responsive, and one heavy multitasking test finished up to 40% faster. Interestingly, before Microsoft (or anyone) shared any of their data, we had already tested Windows 11 26H2 on my dad’s 8GB laptop, and RAM usage after a restart dropped from 5GB to 3.3GB.

Microsoft says you can get faster performance from $429 Windows 11 laptops with 8GB RAM

 

The $429 deal in Microsoft’s blog recommends the Lenovo V15 G6 ARP at Walmart. It has a six-core AMD Ryzen 5 150, 8GB of DDR5 RAM, a 256GB SSD, and a 15.6-inch Full HD IPS display. Walmart’s listing also mentions two memory slots, which my laptop with soldered RAM sorely lacks.

Microsoft’s Surface Laptop 13-inch is a different story. When it launched in May 2025, it cost $899 with 16GB of RAM. Today, the base model with the identical Snapdragon X Plus costs $949.99 with 8GB, while 16GB will set you back $1,149.99. Thank the ever-so-powerful AI companies for that!

Funnily enough, Microsoft also promoted the $699 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB in June to hit back at Apple’s MacBook Neo, which also starts with 8GB. Either way, a $429 Lenovo makes a far better case for 8GB than a Surface that costs more than twice as much.

Microsoft spent years telling Windows users to buy more RAM

Windows 11’s official minimum is still 4GB, but Microsoft gladly steered us the other way. Copilot+ PCs launched in 2024 with 16GB as a hard requirement, and we found a recent Lenovo spec sheet labels anything below 16GB “Non-Copilot”.

Gamers got the hardest push. Microsoft’s gaming guide said “16GB RAM is the baseline; 32GB is the ‘no worries’ upgrade,” adding that “Moving to 32GB RAM helps if you run Discord, browsers, or streaming tools alongside your games.” We spotted it on May 1, and Microsoft deleted it a few days later after the outrage. In August, another guide that called 32GB “ideal for serious players” vanished as well.

The U-turn started in May, when Microsoft announced an 8GB Surface Laptop for Business at $1,299.99. By June, the Surface store called 8GB “great for everyday use like browsing, streaming, schoolwork, and productivity apps,” even as Microsoft’s AI store assistant called 16GB the “safer choice.”

Now the “great fit” line comes from the head of Windows, in a Windows blog, with seemingly hard engineering work behind it, which is always admirable. Tali Roth, Head of Product for Windows Shell, said: “The team has been laser focused here, should be something you notice for all PCs but especially 8 GB ones.”

Is 8GB of RAM enough for Windows 11 now?

For everyday work, Microsoft says yes, but with a caveat. “The workload still matters, and a PC with 16 GB or 32 GB can take on more,” Davuluri wrote, adding that 3D modeling, advanced video editing, and large-scale data processing benefit from 16GB or more. The $949.99 Surface page also says you need 16GB for “access to Copilot+ PC experiences.”

The “great fit” claim holds more weight because the work started months ago. On Microsoft’s April earnings call, Satya Nadella mentioned “performance improvements for lower-memory devices,” and in July, Davuluri made “memory optimization for 8GB and above“ an official priority. On Microsoft’s Inside Windows podcast, he said memory is top of mind “especially as we look at the rising cost of memory for computers across the board.”

Interestingly, IDC’s Jitesh Ubrani predicted in the beginning of June that the PC industry would answer the MacBook Neo with “new silicon, a more efficient OS from Microsoft, and aggressive promotional pricing.” Three months later, Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM, and Microsoft has cut committed-memory growth by up to 900MB in its tests. Neat prediction, I would say!

Microsoft’s own apps need a RAM diet too

Windows is getting leaner, but Microsoft’s own apps haven’t caught up. Windows 11’s Weather app uses over 1.2GB of RAM while idle because it’s a WebView2 web app, while macOS Weather uses 246.7MB. This might be the easiest app to be re-made into WinUI. C’mon Microsoft, you can do this.

Still, with PC shipments down about 20% last quarter as AI data centers eat the world’s RAM, making Windows 11 run better on cheaper hardware beats telling everyone to buy more memory. Would you buy an 8GB Windows laptop this holiday?

title: Xbox’s smallest controller is pocket-sized, rechargeable, and only $50
author: Jez Corden
summary: The Xbox Nano Controller drops on November 4, 2026 for the United States, UK, and other select markets. Here's some early impressions ahead of the full review.
content:
I managed to get my average-sized hands on a below-average sized controller this past week, as the Xbox Nano Controller prepares for lift off.

Microsoft revealed the Xbox Nano Controller a short while ago, but it had leaked a fair bit even before then via patents and regulatory filings. The pint-sized pad is a unique offering from team green, and it actually gives us a glimpse into how their thinking is evolving for their gaming operation in general.

The Xbox Nano Controller is CUTE, and hides a secret - YouTube
Watch On

The Xbox Nano Controller goes on sale on November 4, 2026 for the United States, United Kingdom, and other select markets, arriving right in time for Christmas. The Xbox Nano Controller is priced at $49.99 (via Amazon US here), comes with all the standard Xbox inputs, albeit without vibration motors or removable batteries.

We're still putting it through its paces before a full formal review, but initial impressions are positive. There's one feature here that isn't even activated yet ... though. Let's get into it.

Super cute, with super caveats

Yes, this controller is indeed Nano by name, and Nano by nature. It's roughly the same width as a standard Xbox controller, but it has a much shorter profile, with ergonomic palm grips that feel good in the hand even as an adult.

The thumbsticks, buttons, triggers, and bumpers are all slimmed down, but are positioned nicely making it easy to differentiate by feel alone. Actuating the triggers is easy because of the way they're lipped, and the bumpers are slightly raised rather than flush, which makes rolling your finger between them intuitive in motion.

As mentioned, there are no vibration motors this time around, however, as they naturally couldn't fit inside. The battery cell doesn't have a listed lifespan on the page, so we're still testing it out, but I've been abusing it a fair bit over the past week and still have 20% left which is impressive. I'm still working on a more in-depth analysis there.

Speaking of "a work in progress," for some reason, Microsoft has strangely tried to hide the fact this controller supports Wi-Fi direct capabilities for Xbox Cloud Gaming.

Indeed, as shared by The Verge and clarified by our own sourcing, Microsoft will soon reveal its Google Stadia-like capabilities for gamepad connections direct to your Wi-Fi, eliminating the latency of Bluetooth. By connecting directly to the servers over the internet, you eliminate some additional jumps your controller would otherwise have to do to reach the game. I'm told all future Xbox controllers will come with this tech as standard, including the Xbox Elite Controller Series 3, which is likely also imminent for reveal.

The Wi-Fi direct capabilities will only be available in the United States initially, and only in testing, before going global in the coming weeks and months ahead.

In any case, this is a really nice addition to the Xbox controller lineup. It's going to be ideal for travel due to its weight and size, and is easily pocketable. It might also be a better option for younger gamers with smaller hands. Microsoft has been marketing it against Minecraft Dungeons 2, which offers a glimpse at how they're thinking about positioning it.

I'll put together a full review in the coming days, but early impressions are very solid!

The Xbox Nano Controller is up now for preorder at major retailers, offering a portable way to access your games without the hassle of a bigger, beefier home controller.

title: Arkane Lyon may have found a lifeline as Ubisoft and others reportedly bid for the Xbox studio
author: Jennifer Young
summary: Ubisoft and at least two other gaming companies have reportedly submitted bids to acquire Arkane Lyon from Microsoft, potentially saving the acclaimed studio from closure and allowing work on Marvel’s...
content:
As Xbox tries to shed studios, there may a light at the end of the tunnel in store for Arkane Lyon. According to a new report from Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier, multiple companies, including French publisher Ubisoft, have submitted offers to acquire the acclaimed studio behind Dishonored, Deathloop, and the upcoming (at least we hope so) Marvel’s Blade.

Sources familiar with the negotiations revealed that at least two other gaming entities have made bids, while Microsoft has also considered management buyout options to spin the Lyon-based team out as an independent entity. Not unlike what has become of Undead Labs. While terms have not been finalized, a successful acquisition would reportedly allow Arkane Lyon to finish development on Marvel’s Blade, which was first unveiled at The Game Awards in 2023.

A critical deadline in Xbox's sweeping "reset" of studios under it's wing

The bidding comes after months of intense uncertainty for Arkane Lyon. Following the arrival of CEO Asha Sharma earlier this year, Xbox embarked on a sweeping "reset" across its studio portfolio aimed at reining in operational costs.

Latest Videos FromWindows Central

In July, Microsoft outlined plans to divest five internal studios. While teams like Double Fine and Compulsion Games transitioned toward independence and others secured new homes, Arkane Lyon was placed in an official consultation period under French labor laws to determine its fate.

Reports last month revealed that Arkane Lyon faced a strict mid-November deadline to secure a buyer or face complete closure, putting roughly 217 jobs and the future of Marvel’s Blade at risk.

You may like
  • id Software is finally opening up about its future under Xbox
  • Halo’s future moves to Activision while Obsidian folds into Bethesda
  • Bethesda promises Obsidian will keep its identity under ZeniMax

An Xbox spokesperson confirmed the company is actively exploring options ahead of a December deadline, though Microsoft declined to elaborate on specific negotiations.

Ubisoft actually makes sense

Ubisoft's bid has some geographic logic at least, they are headquartered in France and already have an extensive local infrastructure which would make it easy for them to absorb Arkane Lyon.

Interestingly, it won't be the first major asset Ubisoft has taken off Microsoft's hands. Back in 2023, Microsoft famously offloaded the cloud streaming rights for all current and future Activision Blizzard titles to Ubisoft for 15 years to appease regulators in the UK and close its merger. Securing Arkane Lyon would be the latest instance of Ubisoft swooping in to swipe up pieces of Microsoft's portfolio, if it happens!

title: Steam’s latest survey is a reality check for anyone who thinks PC gamers all have high-end rigs
author: Cale Hunt
summary: Steam's October hardware survey just arrived, and as I predicted, a lot of the major swings spotted in September have been corrected. The big news? Windows 11 continues to grow, but gamer hardware is ...
content:
Steam's October hardware survey has landed, and it basically performed a round trip compared to the previous month's results.

In September, I noted that the massive 4.77% jump in 32GB RAM systems was likely due to an influx of Chinese players, as it lined up with a 7.42% growth in the language on Valve's platform.

That appears to have been true. The 32GB tier took a massive 5.16% dive in October, falling back to 37.06%.

Latest Videos FromWindows Central

At the same time, the 16GB tier moved back into top position with a 3.60% increase to arrive at 41.42%. Users polled with Simplified Chinese as their main language dropped 9.41%.

The bigger news for many of our readers is the jump in Windows 11 adoption, which continues at a fairly steady pace.

You may like
  • 32GB of RAM takes over Steam's user base, but what's really going on?
  • Does Windows 11 26H2 actually use less RAM? I tested to find out.
  • Windows 11's October update adds more useful features than you might expect

Steam's share of Windows 11 users continues to rise

In October, Windows 11 users on Steam climbed by a respectable 1.17% to 72.51% overall. This caused Windows 10's share to drop 2.5%, hitting 21.11%.

About Steam's survey...

Steam's hardware survey is not mandatory, and results depend on who decides to opt in. This can skew results from month to month, as we saw in September 2026.

This is a better improvement than September, which saw just a 0.37% rise for Windows 11. In the same month, Windows 10 also rose by 0.71%.

Are gamers suddenly abandoning Windows 10 at a faster pace? Probably not. What's more likely is another correction to do with the polled sample. Windows 10 is still holding onto just more than a fifth of the overall OS share among Windows, Linux, and macOS.

NVIDIA's RTX 3060 reclaims the top spot

Another interesting tidbit from the October survey lands in the GPU section. Whereas last month the RTX 5070 took top place with a significant 5.86% share, it fell by 2.3% in October to land at 3.56%.

The GPU to replace it as the most common amongst polled Steam users? The legendary NVIDIA RTX 3060, jumping 0.08% to hit 3.62% overall.

What to read next
  • Windows 11 is getting these 9 useful improvements in October 2026
  • Microsoft details how it's made Windows 11 optimized for 8GB RAM PCs
  • Microsoft fixes 6 frustrating Windows 11 problems in October update

Looking at the overall results, 8GB GPUs (especially the RTX 3060) are back in top spots alongside 1920x1080 monitors, which now make up 50.23% (a 2.32% improvement since last month).


If RAM and storage prices were indeed driving users to upgrade, last month's 32GB RAM and RTX 5070 anomalies wouldn't have been crushed out so quickly or so drastically.

To me, as I mentioned, this seems to be more of a correction for September's skewed survey than large moves by consumers as they deal with the ongoing RAM and storage crisis.

Windows Central's take

It seems to me, based on Steam's October survey, that PC gamers are continuing to update their software while holding onto their hardware.

For example, Windows 10's end-of-life support that was extended until October 2027 is still looming over many heads. At the same time, PC component prices are obscene, forcing gamers to reconsider upgrades.

This could be bad news for game developers, as many rely increasingly on hardware that's priced out of the average gamer's reality.

For next month, I'm keeping an eye on whether or not Windows 11 keeps rising and if RTX 50-series GPUs get another boost in shares against older cards.

title: Microsoft admits Windows 11 was moving your open apps to slower storage on 8GB...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Microsoft has shared the test conditions behind every 8GB RAM claim, from a 900MB cut in memory growth to Widgets loading on demand. We put them next to our own 26H2 test, where an 8GB laptop's RAM us...
content:
On PCs with 8GB of RAM, Windows 11 is now up to 20% more responsive, and a heavy multitasking run finished up to 40% faster in one of Microsoft’s lab tests, according to Windows boss Pavan Davuluri. Better yet, Microsoft says you can get it today on Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, with updated Edge, Microsoft 365, and Teams apps.

We had a head start on this one. Two weeks ago, I updated my dad’s 8GB laptop to Windows 11 26H2 build 26300.9550 (which is the build with most of Microsoft’s new numbers), and RAM usage after a restart dropped from 5GB to 3.3GB. Microsoft’s new blog finally explains where the RAM went.

Windows 11 is up to 20% more responsive and 40% faster at multitasking on 8GB PCs

Microsoft made memory optimization for 8GB PCs an official priority in July, and today’s Windows Experience Blog post gives us a bunch of test results. So, Microsoft does put their money where their mouth is!

The 20% more responsiveness data come from telemetry on 8GB PCs, measuring how quickly Start, Search, right-click menus, Settings, Snipping Tool and File Explorer respond compared with the January 2026 update. Microsoft first quoted this 20% figure on October 15 without specifically mentioning 8GB PCs.

The 40% figure has a few caveats, though, but still impressive. On an 8GB HP OmniBook 3 with a Snapdragon X Plus, Microsoft opened 20 Edge tabs, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint and Excel files, Outlook and File Explorer one after another, keeping everything open. Automated UI checks confirmed each step before the next began, and the company says the result is scenario-specific and isn’t a benchmark.

Interestingly, both builds in that test are 25H2 builds from January and September, so those multitasking gains were shipping before 26H2 arrived.

Microsoft’s own apps open faster, too. When Edge is already running in the background, Windows now skips a pointless extra process and hands your click straight to it, making Edge 150 and later open up to 33% faster. The Edge team says most people will see about 15%, with 33% reserved for heavy multitasking.

Teams can now turn on Efficiency Mode by default on 8GB PCs, launching up to 20% faster, and lower your camera resolution in meetings to keep audio clear. Of course, it’s the least Microsoft could do for an app that eats RAM while doing nothing.

How Windows 11 keeps up to 2GB more of your work in RAM

Davuluri says Microsoft is “making better use of the memory in every Windows 11 PC, protecting the interactions that need to feel instant even under load, and ensuring key apps and Windows require less memory.”

For context, Task Manager showing most of your 8GB in use doesn’t mean your PC is struggling. Davuluri compares RAM to a desk and your drive to a drawer, where anything moved to the drawer takes longer to fetch. “The real test is whether your PC stays responsive, not how much memory remains unused,” he wrote.

Windows has compressed less-active data for years to keep it on the desk, and Microsoft has now returned how much it compresses, when it uses the drawer, and when it fetches data back on 8GB PCs. As a result, Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload.

Windows also briefly prioritizes whatever you ask for and backs off background tasks like search indexing while you’re active, a similar idea to Low Latency Profile, the CPU boost that made a 10-year-old 8GB PC feel snappier in our testing.

Microsoft cut memory growth by up to 900MB across Windows, Edge and Microsoft 365

In September tests on 8GB PCs running Edge, Office, Outlook and Teams, Windows and Microsoft’s apps reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900MB. Committed memory is what Windows has promised to back with RAM or the page file, and Microsoft measured its growth from the start of the workload to the end, so don’t expect Task Manager to show 900MB less.

Word, PowerPoint, Excel and Outlook contribute 360MB of savings through more efficient memory allocation. On PCs with 8GB or less, Widgets now loads only when you open it, cutting memory commitment by roughly 200MB while it’s closed. In my 26H2 testing, though, opening the Discover feed slowly pushed RAM usage back up. Edge also puts inactive tabs to sleep after 15 minutes by default now, down from two hours.

Microsoft says WhatsApp is already using this work to reduce memory use in its Windows app. Ironically, I uninstalled WhatsApp just yesterday after it crossed 2GB of RAM, so I’ll take that with a grain of salt.

Testing Windows 11 26H2 on a cluttered 8GB laptop

My dad’s laptop is far from a clean lab machine. It has 8GB of DDR4 RAM, a SATA SSD and a pile of software, from AutoCAD 2020 and SketchUp to PyCharm and VS Code. After a restart on 26H2, committed memory fell from 4.8GB to 2.9GB, and available memory rose from 2.9GB to 4.6GB.

Compressed memory dropped from 324MB to just 62.7MB, so Windows barely compressed anything after boot, which fits with Microsoft’s compression tuning, though I can’t prove the link. Switching between Chrome tabs also felt slightly quicker.

The laptop also went from build 26200.9550 to 26300.9550, which share one monthly patch level, so the drop most likely came from improvements Microsoft had been shipping gradually, which 26H2 switched on.

A fresh 8GB virtual machine also dropped from 4.1GB to between 2.8GB and 3.2GB, but it skipped a whole year of updates. To be clear, my numbers are readings after a restart, while Microsoft’s 900MB were during a workload.

Microsoft tested on over 20,000 PCs, but every number has its own conditions

Microsoft says it tests fixes on more than 20,000 PCs, including current 8GB models, with automated browsing, Microsoft 365, video call, and download workloads. It even uses high-speed cameras to time how long Start or an app takes to appear on screen, and rechecks real-world data after an update ships.

However, each claim comes from its own setup, according to Microsoft’s footnotes.

Microsoft claim Builds compared Conditions
Up to 20% more responsive 26300.9550 vs 26200.7628 Telemetry on 8GB PCs; Start, Search, right-click, Settings, Snipping Tool, File Explorer
Up to 40% faster multitasking 26200.7623 vs 26200.9445 One 8GB HP OmniBook 3 (Snapdragon X Plus); lab test, not a benchmark
Up to 2GB more active data in RAM 26300.9550 Varies by device and usage
Up to 900MB less committed-memory growth 26300.9550 vs 26200.7628 September 2026 tests; Edge, Office, Outlook, Teams
Up to 33% faster Edge launch 26300.9818 or later Edge 150+, already running; about 15% for most
Up to 94% faster multi-core CPU Not a Windows test 2026 vs 2021 8GB Dell XPS 13; Cinebench; commissioned

 

The 94% has nothing to do with Windows, as it compares a 2026 8GB Dell XPS 13 with a 2021 8GB model. In that testing by Principled Technologies, the new XPS 13 also performed about as well as a 2021 16GB configuration in CPU, browsing, AI web tasks and 4K video export tests. Funnily enough, a Microsoft-commissioned report called the MacBook Neo’s 8GB RAM a bottleneck six months ago.

Microsoft still recommends 16GB or more for 3D modeling, advanced video editing and large-scale data processing, and 8GB laptops can’t carry the Copilot+ badge either.

How to get Windows 11’s 8GB RAM improvements today

Build 26300.9818 came with KB5127936, the optional update from October 28.

  1. Open Settings > Windows Update.
  2. Turn on “Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available.”
  3. Click Check for updates, install KB5127936 if it’s listed, and restart your PC.
  4. Update Edge, Microsoft 365, and Teams, as some improvements come through app updates or the Microsoft Store.

Type winver in Start to confirm you’re on build 26300.9818 or higher. Rollout timing varies by device and region, and if you prefer to skip preview updates, these changes should reach everyone with the November 10 Patch Tuesday update.

 

Microsoft’s next 8GB fixes include WinUI 3 apps and shared web engines

Now, this is what I’m most excited about. Over the next few months, Microsoft plans to make memory compression smarter, while Search and Widgets will share one web engine, as will OneDrive and Photos. File Explorer, Notepad, Paint and the new Windows search, all built on WinUI 3, are being designed to open faster and use less memory. PC makers and chipmakers are also helping to cut the memory reserved for hardware.

Sharing a web engine is clever, but as someone who despises web apps on Windows, I’d much prefer native Widgets, especially after Davuluri admitted the rising cost of memory is why Microsoft is doing all this hard work.

Credit where it’s due, the software giant is finally showing its work. “Our goal is to make your 8 GB PC feel like it keeps getting better,” Davuluri wrote.

Unsurprisingly, the post ends by pitching 8GB Windows 11 PCs from $429 at Walmart this holiday, a few months after Microsoft started calling 8GB fine for everyday use. Well, at least now, Windows 11 is better prepared for them. Have you noticed any 8GB PC getting faster?

title: Microsoft made Windows 11 more responsive on these 8GB laptops
author: Cale Hunt
summary: Microsoft has revealed that it made Windows 11 about 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs, which makes recent sub-$1,000 laptop releases from Dell, HP, and Acer in particular a lot more attractive. If you'r...
content:
Microsoft has been busy at work reducing the amount of RAM that Windows 11 consumes, and it finally made an official statement today on the topic.

As it turns out, the company has already been quietly shipping performance improvements in the latest Windows 11 updates, focusing on making systems with 8GB of RAM feel a lot more responsive.

The result? Microsoft says Windows 11 is now about 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs compared to before this work started. The work also applies to systems with 4GB, 16GB, and beyond, with specific tuning for each amount.

This couldn't come at a better time. RAM and storage shortages (explained below) are driving up the cost of all PCs, and models with 8GB of RAM are being revived to lessen the burden on consumers.

Our favorite 8GB Windows laptops in November 2026

Why you can trust Windows Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Companies like Dell, Acer, and HP have all recently launched 8GB laptops that cost somewhere around $699, with student and regular discounts frequently dropping those numbers lower.

If you were hesitant to shop for an 8GB laptop before, the recent Windows 11 updates should have you reconsidering, especially when prices are this reasonable. Here are my three favorite 8GB laptops right now.

QHD+
Dell XPS 13: $699.99 at Dell


Dell's awesome XPS 13 starts at $699.99 (or $599.99 if you're a student) and includes an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 13.4-inch touch display with 2560x1600 resolution

👉 See at Dell.com

Dell's new XPS 13 for 2026 wowed both Zac Bowden and me at Computex earlier this year, and it's been available to buy since June.

It's a laptop with many premium features despite its price, including a higher-res 2560x1600 (QHD+) display with a 120Hz refresh rate, an IR camera for Windows Hello facial recognition, capable speakers, and a comfortable keyboard/touchpad combo.

👉 Does Acer's Swift Air 14 beat Dell's awesome XPS 13?

It does not, however, offer USB-A or 3.5mm audio ports. Its display does not use an OLED panel; it uses IPS instead. And the $599 price is only available for students.

Still, $699 for everyone else is not bad at all in this economy, and most users should have no issues with the XPS 13.

OLED
Save 14% ($100)
HP OmniBook 5 14: was $699.99 now $599.99 at HP US


HP's 14-inch OmniBook 5 is currently on sale for $599.99. It has an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 14-inch OLED touch display with 1920x1200 resolution.

👉 See at HP.com

HP's OmniBook 5 14 comes with the same Intel Core 5 320 CPU as the other laptops in this roundup, so don't expect any major performance changes.

The OmniBook 5 includes an OLED panel for deeper contrast and more vivid color than IPS. The tradeoff is a lower 1920x1200 resolution and lower 60Hz refresh rate compared to the XPS 13.

HP's laptop also includes HDMI and 3.5mm audio ports alongside dual USB-C at 10Gbps. It's nice to have native video, but the lack of Thunderbolt is a letdown.

This laptop is currently on sale for $599.99 for everyone, making it (temporarily) the best deal of the bunch.

512GB SSD
Acer Swift Air 14: $699.99 at Best Buy


Acer's Swift Air 14 costs $699.99 and comes with an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 512GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 14-inch non-touch display at 1920x1200.

👉 See at BestBuy.com

Acer's Swift Air 14 immediately makes an argument for itself with twice as much storage (512GB) as the Dell and HP laptops. For those who prefer to store locally, this could be the deciding factor. However, it does drop down to PCIe 3.0 speeds.

Performance is largely the same thanks to it having the Intel Core 5 320 chip inside, with 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM.

The display hits a 1920x1200 resolution; it doesn't have touch, but it does hit a smoother 120Hz refresh rate. You're definitely giving up some screen quality to land that extra storage.

While the keyboard is great, the touchpad leaves something to be desired. Your experience may vary.

Why is Microsoft concerned with reducing Windows 11 RAM usage?

Sure, Windows 11 could always be more streamlined, but this big push for more RAM efficiency is also a result of the ongoing memory and storage crisis.

See, AI data centers are eating up many of the foundational components of PCs, making the consumer side far more expensive.

RAM in particular has exploded in price; the same 32GB kit of DDR5 I bought for my gaming PC a few years ago, for example, is roughly 600% more expensive today. Storage isn't much better.

This is forcing PC makers to reevaluate their product lineups, as many consumers can no longer afford PCs with 16GB or more of RAM.

Cutting RAM in half is a huge cost saver and won't likely stop anytime soon (the RAM crisis could last for years to come), so it's great to see Microsoft taking user complaints about Windows 11's responsiveness (or lack thereof) seriously.

title: Microsoft details how it's made Windows 11 optimized for 8GB RAM PCs
author: Zac Bowden
summary: Windows 11 has gained a number of improvements and optimizations designed specifically for devices with 8GB RAM, and it's all already rolling out.
content:
Microsoft has detailed a number of changes and improvements that it has made to Windows 11 over the last handful of months that are designed to improve the OS for devices that have just 8GB of RAM. The company says that as of today, Windows 11 is more RAM-efficient and faster on PCs with limited memory compared to a year ago.

"On 8 GB PCs, Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test" Microsoft CVP Pavan Davaluri says. "We’re approaching this in three parts: making better use of the memory in every Windows 11 PC, protecting the interactions that need to feel instant even under load, and ensuring key apps and Windows require less memory."

Recent Windows 11 updates have changed how the OS preloads background services and apps on PCs with 8GB RAM. Now, the OS will no longer preload things like the Widgets Board on these devices with 8GB RAM or less, which frees up RAM for other tasks and activities.

Microsoft also says that it has worked with teams across Windows, Office, and Edge to reduce the amount of RAM these apps use, resulting in up to 900MB of RAM being given back to the system for other tasks. A large chunk of those savings came from Office apps, which add up to 350MB of RAM freed for the system.

There are also consolidation efforts around behind the scenes technology that should also free up system memory. A number of web-powered interfaces across the system are now powered by the same engine, rather than individual engines, and a number of web experiences are being rewritten as native WinUI experiences that use less RAM.

You may like
  • Microsoft made Windows 11 more responsive on these 8GB laptops
  • Does Windows 11 26H2 actually use less RAM? I tested to find out.
  • Windows 11 KB5101684 makes PCs with low RAM faster and more reliable

In fact, if you install Windows 11 version 25H2 from a year ago, and compared it to the latest version of Windows 11 with the latest OS updates installed, you'll find that even at idle, Windows is now using significantly less RAM compared to before. These improvements appear to be very real.

Additionally, the company is enforcing "memory budgets" on OEM hardware with limited RAM. This should stop hardware makers from preloading 8GB RAM devices with unnecessary bloatware, reserving preload for the most important services.

These improvements are all in the name of ensuring Windows 11 runs well on 8GB RAM. Windows 11's performance on limited RAM PCs was pulled into the spotlight earlier this year when MacBook Neo shipped, which revealed that macOS is well optimized for 8GB RAM.

Now, Microsoft is eager to let people know that it has made the necessary improvements to Windows 11 to ensure that it too is well optimized for 8GB RAM. Here's a rundown of some other improvements it has made to the OS over the last year:

  • Memory compression already helps Windows keep more of your work in faster memory. Next, we’re making it even smarter and more efficient to get the most out of your system performance.
  • Windows features and apps will share common parts instead of each carrying its own. Search and Widgets will share one web engine, and so will OneDrive and Photos for memory savings across all four apps.
  • Apps and experiences built on WinUI 3, including File Explorer, Notepad, Paint, and the new Windows search are being designed to open faster and use less memory.
  • Together with PC makers and silicon partners, we’re optimizing how much memory your PC needs to reserve for its hardware, leaving more available for Windows and the apps you use.
  • We’re also working with third-party app developers to help their apps use memory more efficiently.

Of course, Windows 11 technically officially supports 4GB RAM PCs, and I'm told these optimizations also apply to those devices too. If you're running Windows 11 on 4GB RAM, you should see notable improvements to performance and multitasking with the latest OS updates.

But are these improvements going to be enough for users? Let us know what you think in the comments below!

title: Does Windows 11 26H2 actually use less RAM? I tested to find out.
author: Cale Hunt
summary: Microsoft has been busy at work making Windows 11 more memory-efficient, and I decided to put the recent announcement to the test on an Acer Swift Air 14 with 8GB. The results are more impressive than...
content:
Microsoft has revealed the depths of its work to make Windows 11 feel less sluggish, with the company claiming, among other things, up to 20% better responsiveness on systems with 8GB of RAM.

Microsoft has claimed before that things "seem faster," but is there any juice behind this new claim? I decided to find out myself by running some tests on an 8GB laptop in my office.

The results will likely be surprising to some, especially once we get into the heavier workloads below.

How I tested Windows 11's responsiveness on an 8GB laptop

I installed a barebones version of Windows 11 25H2 (262000.7019) from about a year ago on an Acer Swift Air 14 with an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, and a 512GB M.2 PCIe 3.0 NVMe SSD.

I didn't touch the page file (4524MB), and I only installed the necessary drivers before beginning my tests. I used the Best Performance power profile for all tests.

Once I'd completed all tests on 25H2, I upgraded to Windows 11 26H2 (26300.9711), which was released in October. Same system, same drivers, same programs.

Microsoft used telemetry data from things like Search, Settings, File Explorer, and Snipping Tool to measure responsiveness. I took a look at RAM usage instead; lower usage generally means fewer hiccups and interruptions, leading to an overall better experience.

The older Windows 11 25H2 version was eating up 5.3GB of RAM in this scenario, leaving 2.3GB free. Windows 11 26H2 dropped RAM usage to 4.1GB, leaving 3.5GB free. That's a big drop.

Although both commits are the same at 9.5GB, Windows 11 26H2 uses slightly less at 4.4GB compared to 4.7GB.

TL;DR: Windows 11 26H2 is well ahead in the boot test where no additional apps are running, using significantly less RAM than 25H2.

Now that I've established a baseline, I put together a test to see how each PC handles an average user's daily workload.

I opened 10 tabs in Edge with a mix of Windows Central, Reddit, YouTube, Gmail, X, Amazon, etc. I also opened a Word document, Slack messenger, and the Spotify app.

Windows 11 25H2 climbed to 7.0GB RAM usage, while 26H2 hit just 6.6GB. That's about a 0.4GB improvement. Windows 11 26H2 was able to keep its cache larger while also committing less RAM at 10.4GB compared to 12.2GB.

For reference, committed memory indicates how much RAM the PC is setting aside for operations. In this case, 12.2GB of RAM committed includes physical system RAM and virtual memory (set by the page file). Committing less RAM keeps your system from clogging up, so this is good news.

TL;DR: Windows 11 26H2 keeps its lead under load, actively using less RAM and allocating less RAM overall.

Although the fresh crop of recommended Windows 11 laptops with 8GB of RAM aren't really meant to handle workloads this heavy, I knew it would be fun to really stress out the PC.

I opened Edge (with 20 tabs), a Word document, an Excel spreadsheet, Spotify, Slack, Microsoft Store, the Photos app, File Explorer, and GIMP simultaneously for this test.
