content:
Some attacks this week didn't need much of a trick. A fake support call, a trusted extension, a shared link, or a device with no password. Small things that people barely think about. Yet each was enough to cause serious trouble.

Then there were the bigger messes. Billions stolen, hidden networks of hacked devices, poisoned software, and attackers finding new ways to turn normal tools against their users. Even the places meant to keep money and systems safe ended up with problems of their own. The strange part is how often the damage started somewhere nobody was looking.

And that's before getting to the long list of fresh bugs, shady services, and scams making the rounds. Quite a bit to sort through. Here's what made the list.

⚡ Threat of the Week

N. Korea Sets New Record with Binance $6.43B Crypto Theft — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism.

Mythos: Map Attack Paths to Collapse Lateral Breach Routes

Access the Gartner® CTEM report to see how the Mythos platform continuously maps cross-domain attack paths and isolates key choke points to break active lateral movement to critical assets.

 Get the full report ➝

🔔 Top News

  • Volt Typhoon Uses Covert Silent Train Network in 0-Day Attacks — Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including to facilitate zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems. It's codenamed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation to minimize detection and attribution, and refreshes it continuously. Silent Train is a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices to hide the origin of its attacks. The findings highlight evidence of efforts to pre-position access within what it described as "strategic communications, critical infrastructure and other ecosystems that become essential during geopolitical tensions or crises." Silent Train is built around "rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices." The nature of these victims "indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region."
  • Polymarket Briefly Suspended Trading After Third-Party Hack — Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading after hackers compromised DebugBear, a third-party service, to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript that siphoned approximately $2.7 million in assets from 33 deposit wallets in under an hour. "Our DNS server records were compromised through our domain registrar. We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain," DebugBear said in an update shared on October 31, 2026. "Based on our initial investigation this attack targeted the website of a specific customer. We have not seen any indication of a compromise of our internal systems, though we will continue to investigate this." In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, leading to reported losses of around $3 million.
  • Shared ChatGPT Links Lead to Code Execution — Researchers from Parameter Labs disclosed a now-patched flaw in ChatGPT that turned an ordinary share link into an attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. "An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," Parameter Labs said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session." Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation, and send data from that conversation to an external server.
  • Official Claude Code Extension on Cursor Marketplace with SSH Backdoor — Two versions of the Claude Code extension distributed through Cursor Marketplace were tampered with to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems. Cursor said the incident impacted up to 5,000 users. In response to the incident, Cursor said it rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and worked with the cloud provider to take the server offline so that the reverse shell is no longer functional. It also stressed that no other extensions were maliciously modified as part of the attack. However, several questions surrounding the supply chain attack remain unanswered, including how the threat actor managed to publish a malicious extension under Anthropic's name on Cursor's marketplace and what level of access they were able to obtain.
  • FBI Seizes bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine — The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine. The DoJ said the service was being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct. However, the long-term impact of such crackdowns has been questioned. According to Intel 471, disruptions have driven customers to newer services operated by former resellers, fragmenting the market rather than eliminating demand. The disclosure comes as the Australian Signals Directorate said it gained backend access to Amadey's operations and severed its access to 180,000 computers across the globe.
  • Keystone to Destroy 18,835 Hardware Wallets — Keystone confirmed a security incident involving its official website where an attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool to escalate privileges and obtain some customer information and a key used to verify the authenticity of our devices. This included 25,964 records containing names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order information, along with 12,873 checkout records containing names, contact details, and shipping information submitted by users. Besides stopping the use of the old key, Keystone plans to destroy 18,835 devices in existing inventory that contain the old key. "Shipping of all unshipped orders from our official website has been suspended," it said. "Sales will switch to a preorder model until production of devices using the new key is complete, after which shipping will resume." In a related development, another hardware cryptocurrency wallet maker Trezor said it received credible reports about a suspected hardware crypto-theft implant in a Trezor Safe 5 sold by its reseller CryptoBilis in Southeast Asia. "If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards and are using it to store funds, please move your funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed as soon as possible," it said.
  • uCreator Android Spyware Can Clone WeChat Accounts — A commercial Android spyware offering called uCreator is designed to target ordinary users of mobile wallets and messaging applications across China and Southeast Asia, including GCash (Philippines), WeChat, WeCom, QQ, Telegram, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, and MoMo. It can also be used to clone WeChat accounts. Victims install repackaged copies of legitimate applications disturbed through sideloading or social engineering flows. The attack leverages a variation of on-device virtualization techniques observed in malware like GodFather to conduct fraud. "GodFather spins the banking app up inside a virtual container and drops a fake overlay on top to phish credentials: the victim is really typing into the attacker's screen," security researcher Ovi Liber said. "uCreator shares the substrate but it draws no overlay. This is a case really of overlay-the-app versus instrument-the-app, with the second being quieter and also not being confined to a login screen. As an operator, it scales to any app the vendor writes a module for."
  • Gheist Turns GitHub Actions into a Secret Extraction Service — An automated campaign dubbed Gheist has been observed planting a secret-dumping workflow named "sync-check" in every repository that stolen GitHub tokens can reach. "The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log," Wiz said. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later." The Google-owned cloud security company said it recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts. The campaign was first detected in mid-September 2026.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-115889, CVE-2026-115893 (Wasmtime), CVE-2026-90975 (Fireblocks mpc-lib), CVE-2026-91141 (COVESA vsomeip), CVE-2026-88781, CVE-2026-75775, CVE-2026-75779, CVE-2026-93489, CVE-2026-17518, CVE-2026-75753, CVE-2026-102438, CVE-2026-14911, CVE-2026-16528, CVE-2026-19386, CVE-2026-19396, CVE-2026-93495, CVE-2026-14157, CVE-2026-13313 (ASUS), CVE-2026-114573, CVE-2026-9082, CVE-2026-118539 (Drupal), CVE-2026-114595, CVE-2026-114596, CVE-2026-114597, CVE-2026-114598 (EPICS Base), CVE-2026-97631 (TianoCore EDK II), CVE-2026-115881, CVE-2026-115884 (GoAhead), CVE-2026-110720 (HashiCorp consul-k8s), CVE-2026-90885, CVE-2026-85250, CVE-2026-88901, CVE-2026-88900, CVE-2026-78165, CVE-2026-85251 (Apache Camel), CVE-2026-115547 (Okta), CVE-2026-114349, CVE-2026-111551 (Apache Kafka), CVE-2026-118306, CVE-2026-118331, CVE-2026-118348, CVE-2026-118344, CVE-2026-106378 (Google Chrome), from CVE-2026-117860 through CVE-2026-117954, from CVE-2026-118005 through CVE-2026-118017 (Mozilla Firefox), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-18672, CVE-2026-19219 (Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX), TRA-2020-14 (Kodi), CVE-2026-107239, CVE-2026-107238, CVE-2023-22793 (Veeam), CVE-2026-103401, CVE-2026-103402, CVE-2026-103403, CVE-2026-103404, CVE-2026-103405, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-103407, CVE-2026-103408, CVE-2026-103409 (Juniper Networks Session Smart Router), CVE-2026-111585 (TeamViewer), CAN-2026-2035970 (Intelbras IP cameras), CVE-2026-103594, CVE-2026-112709, CVE-2026-112710, CVE-2026-93857, CVE-2026-103593, CVE-2026-93865, CVE-2026-93866 (WatchGuard Fireware OS), CVE-2026-101296, CVE-2026-101356, CVE-2026-103119 (Apache Tomcat), CVE-2026-112816 (Canonical LXD), CVE-2026-93680, CVE-2026-110186 (Langflow OSS), and a preauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in TightVNC.

🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars

  • Learn How to Turn Identity Context Into Faster, Smarter SOC Response → Your security tools can detect suspicious activity, but without identity context, critical threats may go unnoticed. As machine identities and AI agents expand the attack surface, SOC teams need deeper visibility to respond effectively. Join this expert-led webinar to discover how connecting identity intelligence with security operations can help uncover hidden risks, accelerate investigations, and contain threats faster.
  • From Zero-Days to Exploits in Minutes: Are You Ready for AI Threats? → AI-powered cyberattacks are accelerating, shrinking the time security teams have to detect, investigate, and respond. Are your defenses ready to keep up? Join this expert-led webinar to discover how to strengthen AI threat readiness, improve attack-surface visibility, and build faster, more resilient security operations before attackers gain the upper hand.

📰 Around the Cyber World

  • A massive search-hijacking campaign called Searchjacked involving 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million reported installations hijacked users' searches through tracking servers, captured queries, and collected referral payments from Microsoft Bing and Yahoo. The findings from Socket expand on the April 2025 discovery of 57 Chrome extensions with six million users, adding 264 newly identified add-ons with another 8.7 million users. Although they are hosted on the Chrome Web Store, they are unlisted and don't appear in users' searches on the extension store. Instead, the extensions are promoted through sketchy advertisements shown as pop overs or pop unders on websites. Socket also discovered a cluster of malicious Firefox extensions that mimic Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys. A third campaign, documented by Am I Being Pwned?, involves 60 Chrome extensions with 2.3 million installs across 4 publisher accounts. Called OffiDocs, the extensions masquerade as document programs and exfiltrate all URLs visited by users to be shared with business partners, and other third-parties, or redirect users to one of their pages on redcoolmedia.net or runapps.org
  • Microsoft revealed details of two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. "Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths," Microsoft said. "This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure."
  • Threat actors are increasingly turning to vulnerabilities as a means for breaking into corporate systems, as exfiltration and extortion-only attacks emerged as the fastest-growing category in the third quarter of 2026.
  • Check Point detailed three anti-detect browsers, Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin, that could enable a single operator to silently manage thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms, and evade detection systems that look for scams and coordinated inauthentic behavior. "Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution," Check Point said. "These accounts can also be used to coordinate influence operations, which becomes an even greater concern ahead of elections. These tools already use AI integration, from built-in automation templates to offering a dedicated MCP server that pipes LLM-generated content directly into pre-warmed account profiles at machine speed. Running a large-scale social media operation now requires only a credit card instead of a technical team."
  • Russia and Ukraine both revealed their emergency alert systems were hit by cyber attacks. The attacks caused the two systems to send fake emergency alerts. Per BBC, Ukraine's air raid app sent false red-level air raid warnings nationwide. A few hours later, Russia said its alert app was also attacked, but said that it was only an "ancillary" service among sirens and other warnings. It’s not clear if the two incidents are connected.
  • A sophisticated Android malware campaign has been targeting the Indian banking sector since July 2025 using seven distinct trojan families that facilitate banking fraud through coordinated phishing, credential theft, and unauthorized cryptojacking. It is orchestrated by a financially motivated threat cluster codenamed CyberDakait that's operating in India since January 2025. The malware families are GhostBat, cyb3rx, godz, d-passive, d-shine, tenxen, and appkjl. Distributed via coordinated smishing and vishing campaigns, they are designed to harvest sensitive information, including bank mobile application credentials, credit card details, outstanding balances, through sophisticated overlay attacks. "The main goal of the campaign is the distribution of Android malware to conduct cryptojacking and elaborate banking fraud," Group-IB said. "The malicious applications are commonly hosted on GitHub repositories to maintain legitimacy and evade security controls, where the initial APK functions as a dropper that downloads and executes the main payload alongside a cryptocurrency mining module, enabling the threat actors to generate revenue through both direct financial theft and unauthorized cryptocurrency mining on infected devices." A total of at least 17,960 compromised devices have been identified, and about 7.6 million SMS messages were intercepted from victim devices.
  • A new phishing campaign has disguised credential theft as an invitation to a private AI event from Anthropic, and uses GoTo Webinar branding, a Zoom-style registration page, and convincing Google and Microsoft login pages to steal login credentials. "Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g., proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization," Cofense said.
  • A new campaign is using judicial-themed phishing emails targeting Colombian organizations to deliver XWorm via a multi-stage chain. The initial payloads resemble legitimate Colombian administrative or judicial correspondence, according to Arctic Wolf.
  • Multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. "The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance," Recorded Future said. "This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds." Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.
  • Nozomi Networks detailed a new Go-based malware for Linux called Kairos that turns a compromised machine into a node in the operator's DDoS botnet. "On command, the bot opens hundreds to thousands of TCP connections to a target chosen by the operator and keeps them open for the requested duration, sending a single near-empty keepalive byte every few seconds," Nozomi Networks said. "Initial access came through Telnet, using the default credentials (user root, empty password). The operator then staged the payload with a short shell sequence that downloaded it over HTTP from the same server the bot later calls home."
  • A previously undocumented Microsoft device code phishing kit codenamed MadApe is using business-themed PDF lures, configurable redirects, and fake document-sharing pages to trick victims into completing Microsoft device code authentication. It was first observed by Group-IB on January 7, 2026.
  • Threat actors behind Aur0ra ransomware, aka Gold Ogre, are extensively using AI to develop tools and to orchestrate and execute ransomware operations, Sophos said. The AI-assisted post-exploitation framework is developed with Cursor AI assistance. "The threat actors used Cursor to escalate from credential access to domain administrator in preparation for data collection and ransomware deployment," Sophos said. "AI guardrails were bypassed by framing the intrusions as authorized red team activity or 'diagnostics testing.' Intrusions were orchestrated by Cursor's Composer agentic coding model as well as AI models provided by Anthropic, xAI, and Moonshot." Although the threat actors initially used Anthropic almost exclusively, they have since introduced other models.
  • Malicious model repositories on Hugging Face are being used to fuel a cryptomining and backdoor campaign. "The payloads were written for GPU hosts running self-hosted inference, especially Xinference and GPUStack, along with rented GPU machines, shared research notebooks, and CI jobs that pull small test models without anyone reading the code," Pluto Security said. Instead of using poisoned weights or pickle exploits, the campaign abuses a Hugging Face option, trust_remote_code, that lets a model ship its own Python code. When this option is set to true, that code is automatically executed on a victim's machine as soon as the model loads.
  • Bitdefender and NETGEAR found that Smart TVs and connected plugs accounted for a large share of recorded security weaknesses. Televisions represented 22.7% of vulnerability observations, followed by smart plugs at 22.4%. "Before buying connected equipment, the support period deserves attention alongside the price and features," the 2026 IoT Security Landscape Report said. For equipment already in the home, knowing whether updates are still available is part of knowing whether it should stay connected.
  • A tech-support scam is directing victims to install the commercially available remote access application UltraViewer. Infoblox, which broke down details of the campaign, said it found links to a long-running QuickBooks phishing campaign. "That campaign uses over 350 QuickBooks-lookalike domains and directs victims to call scammers who attempt to steal QuickBooks credentials," Infoblox said. The scam has been found directing users to trojanized UltraViewer and UltraMailer, installers that lead to the deployment of DarkKometa and njRAT, respectively.
  • In an analysis of The Com ecosystem, Flare said the loose-knit collective comprises three distinct intrusion clusters, Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters, while SP1D3R HUNTERS (aka Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters) represents an amalgamation of all three. Security researcher Jon DiMaggio warned against attributing any activity post-2022 to LAPSUS, which ceased operating years ago. "LAPSUS$ operated at full capacity for roughly nine months, from its December 2021 attack against Brazil’s Ministry of Health through its concentrated campaign in early 2022, before a series of arrests in mid-to-late 2022 ended it as an organized entity," DiMaggio said. "Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$ overlapped by a few months at the start and by at least one individual across their lifespans, and they still ran different playbooks against different targets toward different ends." 

Conclusion

That's about it for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others worked because someone clicked the wrong thing, trusted the wrong tool, or left something exposed. Different methods, same result. And with so many systems connected to other systems, even a small mistake can travel further than expected.

The bigger concern is how normal some of these attacks have become. Nothing particularly clever is needed when the easy routes still work. Keep an eye on what has access, check what needs fixing, and don't assume familiar means safe. See you next week.

title: Google Disrupts 1.3 Million-Device Android Botnet, Says TV Box Maker Sold Criminal Access
author: The Hacker News
summary: A botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes, lost control of its servers in late October in a takedown led by Google.   Google says  it is highly confident that device maker Videostrong intentionally put a backdoor in the boxes and sold access to criminals.   They used the boxes for ad fraud and to pass other people's internet traffic through owners' home connections. The backdoor is still on the boxes, and owners cannot remove it themselves.   Videostrong, based in Shenzhen, China, makes Android TV boxes and other devices under its own name and for other brands. The backdoor, called x.cpe, was built into many device models and brands over several years. Google does not believe a rogue insider or a mistake was to blame.   Google used legal action to take down the domains and servers that controlled the botnet. It also took down the control domains of more than a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Japan's National Police Agenc...
content:
A botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes, lost control of its servers in late October in a takedown led by Google.

Google says it is highly confident that device maker Videostrong intentionally put a backdoor in the boxes and sold access to criminals.

They used the boxes for ad fraud and to pass other people's internet traffic through owners' home connections. The backdoor is still on the boxes, and owners cannot remove it themselves.

Videostrong, based in Shenzhen, China, makes Android TV boxes and other devices under its own name and for other brands. The backdoor, called x.cpe, was built into many device models and brands over several years. Google does not believe a rogue insider or a mistake was to blame.

Google used legal action to take down the domains and servers that controlled the botnet. It also took down the control domains of more than a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI worked with Google on the operation.

Because the criminals behind that malware also spread it in other ways, Google expects the action to cut off their access to at least 10 million more infected devices. It warns that backdoor operators and the criminals who buy from them quickly switch to new tools when one part of their setup is disrupted.

Google has cut ties with Videostrong. It banned the company, and any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices and from supplying software to other certified device makers.

What the Backdoor Did

The x.cpe backdoor runs as a system app inside the firmware, with system-level access, according to Google's analysis. It reports to the botnet's command-and-control (C2) servers and waits for orders. To install software silently, it first turns off the app checks in Google Play Protect, Android's built-in security feature.

Through the backdoor, the botnet's operators could install apps without the owner knowing, run commands, capture the screen and map the network the box sits on.

Google says it saw Videostrong's operators use some of these powers. They took live screenshots, sent keystrokes, copied out account details, device information, app lists and system logs, and opened reverse shells, which give a remote command line into the box.

Most of the criminals' modules, the add-on programs loaded through the backdoor, turned the boxes into residential proxies or sold their spare bandwidth. A residential proxy service sells access to a home internet connection, so a customer's traffic appears to come from an ordinary household. Other modules faked views of online ads.

Most infected devices are Android TV set-top boxes, but the backdoor also turned up on telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage.

TrendAI, Trend Micro's enterprise business unit, counted 1,472,554 infected devices across 206 models between June 3 and October 1, and says the real number is at least that high. Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan had the most. The U.S., Germany, the U.K., Australia and Canada each had about 26,000 to 42,000.

What Owners Can Do

Synthient, which tracks proxy networks and botnets, has published a list of 182 device model names seen in the campaign. The list warns that a model name alone does not confirm that a box is infected.

Synthient's report focuses on MECOOL-branded boxes, which it links to Videostrong. It bought a MECOOL KM9PRO Max and found the backdoor preinstalled. Plume, which makes Wi-Fi software for internet providers, found more than a dozen different devices using the botnet's control server, most of them from MECOOL.

Because x.cpe is part of the firmware, removing it does not stick. It reinstalls itself when the box restarts. TrendAI says the backdoor runs as a system app signed with the maker's key, so cleanup needs "vendor action, platform protection or replacement of the device."

Plume recommends a full factory reset, because the modules may have installed more backdoors, but it does not say whether a reset removes x.cpe itself. Synthient goes further, telling consumers to throw the boxes away for good because they pose a high risk of malware.

For organizations, Synthient recommends these steps:

  • Use its published indicators to find MECOOL or similar devices on the network.
  • Disconnect and throw away any that turn up.
  • Block the control domains and IP addresses its report lists.
  • Keep other smart devices on separate network segments, away from sensitive systems.

TrendAI advises companies with remote staff to treat unmanaged consumer devices on home networks as part of their attack surface, and to keep corporate access behind managed devices.

How Videostrong Was Identified

In Google's account, x.cpe passes settings from the C2 server to other Videostrong apps, including its YokaTV Player streaming app. One of the GitHub accounts that hosted the botnet's packages is named yf-videostrong.

Synthient, which worked with Google, also concluded with high confidence that Videostrong runs the operation. It points to a document signed by Videostrong's research and development director in an open folder on one of the botnet's servers, and to a Videostrong web domain that shares an IP address with the operators' control panel.

Plume found that Videostrong supplies both the firmware for these devices and tools to manage them remotely.

A Gap in Google's Device Tests

Google requires device makers to go through a set of compatibility and security tests. It says Videostrong hid its code to bypass a gap in those tests and loaded the malicious code after a device's first boot.

Google has changed its review process and is improving its checks of the firmware on certified Android TV devices.

As of November 2, Videostrong's own website listed products it calls "Google Certified Android TV Box" and "Google Certified Android TV Stick."

Plume says the botnet included both Google-certified devices and devices running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) version. Google's report does not say how many certified devices were affected.

When Google sued over the BadBox 2.0 botnet in July 2025, the more than 10 million devices involved were uncertified.

title: DarkBlinders Compromises Israeli Target and Iraqi Kurdish Government Cloud Environment
author: The Hacker News
summary: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026.   According to a report published  by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region.   The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders , an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups.   Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads.   Prev...
content:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026.

According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region.

The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups.

Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads.

Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685. 

Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets.

The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025.

The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire.

Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment.

The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood.

"The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said.

"The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]."

The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include -

  • gcc-sg[.]cloud/owa/auth/logon.aspx
  • mfakuwait[.]online/owa/auth/logon.aspx
  • moelcloud[.]online/drive/file/d/1JpH3ySmJpvX6TyGnF7C-S8qYiaoxyC5O

The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2.

The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software.

Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added.

"Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group."

Prince of Persia Hosts C2 in the U.S. for the First Time in a Decade

The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026.

The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor."

"We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims."

"The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."

title: Critical Langflow Flaws Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code on Servers
author: The Hacker News
summary: Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code,  IBM said last week . The four Langflow flaws in IBM's bulletin, first published on October 28 and updated the next day, are:
content:
Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week.

Langflow is an open-source tool for building AI agents and workflows, and its vulnerability reports go to IBM. Every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 has the flaws, and the only fix is version 1.13.0.

Neither flaw is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, as of the catalog's October 30 update. Six other Langflow flaws are listed there, most recently CVE-2026-9198, which was added in August.

The four Langflow flaws in IBM's bulletin, first published on October 28 and updated the next day, are:

CVE CVSS score (IBM) Account needed What IBM says it could allow
CVE-2026-93680 9.8 (Critical) No Bypassing security restrictions, because of improper authentication
CVE-2026-110186 9.8 (Critical) No Running arbitrary code, because of improper control of code generation
CVE-2026-110193 8.8 (High) Yes, a low-privileged account Making the Agentic Assistant generate or submit component code that runs operating system commands on the server
CVE-2026-110192 6.5 (Medium) Yes Getting sensitive information from insufficiently protected credentials

One of the flaws is "unauthenticated remote code execution exploitable through model context protocol tool enumeration," according to IBM. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Langflow can offer its flows as tools to AI apps that support MCP.

A module in the public Metasploit Framework already cites CVE-2026-93680, the authentication bypass. It connects to a Langflow server's MCP endpoint without credentials, starts a session, and lists the tools the server offers. It does not run code or commands on the server.

Its author lists Langflow 1.5.0 through 1.11.4 as affected, a narrower range than IBM's.

When automatic login is enabled, Langflow logs users in as superusers without prompting them to sign in. The setting LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN is enabled by default in Langflow 1.12.8. Its code description warns that it "bypasses authentication and should only be used in development environments."

The module was tested on Langflow 1.8.4 with automatic login turned on. Another of the four flaws is "an incomplete remediation of an auto-login security control," according to IBM. The bulletin does not say whether servers with automatic login turned off are vulnerable.

Upgrading to 1.13.0

Langflow 1.13.0 came out on October 22. Version 1.12.8, released the same day, still has the flaws, and PyPI lists no later 1.12 release as of November 2. IBM offers no workaround for servers that cannot upgrade yet.

Langflow 1.13 turns automatic login off by default. To upgrade:

  1. Back up the database, the secret key and uploaded files.
  2. If the server uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in, as Langflow's upgrade guidance describes.
  3. Upgrade the Python package with pip install --upgrade "langflow==1.13.0". For Docker, move to the langflowai/langflow:1.13.0 image and keep the deployment's persistent data.
  4. If you cannot sign in after upgrading, follow the recovery steps that the same guidance links to. Do not delete or reinstall Langflow to get access back, because Langflow's documentation warns this can permanently remove your flows.

On October 29, IBM also published CVE records for 29 other Langflow flaws and named versions 1.12.4 and 1.12.5 as their fixes. One of them, CVE-2026-104339, could also let an attacker with no account run arbitrary code, and IBM rates it 9.8. None of the 33 records, these four included, lists 1.13.0 as affected.

title: I uninstalled Windows 11’s worst app, the 2GB RAM-eating WhatsApp, and the website does...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: A year after Meta killed the native app, WhatsApp's WebView2 wrapper still lags. I tested WhatsApp Web, the Edge-installed web app (579.6MB hiding behind a 2.5MB entry), Smart Connect streaming at 83....
content:
WhatsApp for Windows 11 used 2,157.8MB of RAM on my PC while I was simply scrolling through chats, a year after Meta replaced its native app with a WebView2 wrapper. I’ve uninstalled it, and between WhatsApp Web, which now supports voice and video calls, and streaming WhatsApp from my phone, I’m not missing anything.

If WhatsApp were fast while eating all that memory, I could live with it. It isn’t, and the alternatives I tested use a fraction of the RAM. I honestly do not understand what Meta engineers are doing. Wasn’t AI supposed to give us better software?

WhatsApp for Windows 11 now crosses 2GB of RAM, and it’s still slow

In Task Manager, the WhatsApp process group shows 10 processes. The WhatsApp WebView2 tab takes 1,234.7MB, the WebView2 GPU process takes 521.3MB, WhatsApp.Root uses 245.1MB and the WebView2 Manager another 88.6MB, which was the amount of RAM used by the native version of WhatsApp from a year ago. This web slop (sorry, not sorry) also hit 28.6% CPU and 11.6MB/s of disk activity while I scrolled.

For context, Meta killed the native WhatsApp app in November 2025, and the new version simply loads web.whatsapp.com inside Microsoft Edge WebView2. When I first tested it, the old UWP app was under 100MB when idle and around 250MB while scrolling, while the WebView2 version used about 600MB idle and 1.2GB while scrolling. During video calls, it was roughly 900MB versus 316MB. This is enshittification at its best!

In June, WhatsApp was still eating 1.2GB of RAM on Windows 11. Now it’s crossing 2GB.

The RAM would be easier to forgive if the app was at least fast. Switching chats still takes about a second, scrolling is choppy, and the single tick on a sent message shows up late. Ironically, WhatsApp’s own help page once said its native Windows and Mac apps “provide increased performance and reliability”, and yet Meta logged users out to push them to the web wrapper.

WhatsApp Web uses less RAM, and it finally has calls too

Sadly, or rather, as expected, WhatsApp Web isn’t lightweight. In Edge’s Browser Task Manager, my WhatsApp tab used about 700MB.

The RAM usage continues to rise as we use WhatsApp Web, especially while scrolling through texts. But in my testing, it is smoother than WhatsApp Desktop. There’s an important thing to consider here. My default browser is Edge, and it is always open, so when I open WhatsApp Web in it, the reduction in performance is not as drastic as when I open WhatsApp Desktop, which is similar to how I opened an entire browser just to run WhatsApp.

When I opened my personal and WhatsApp Business accounts in two Edge tabs, they used 593.4MB and 562.8MB, or about 1.16GB for two accounts, still well under the 2GB that one account hit in the desktop app.

You can also install WhatsApp Web as an app, as Edge shows an “Install WhatsApp Web app” icon when you open the site.

I installed it and ran it next to the desktop app. At first glance, Task Manager shows “WhatsApp Web” using just 2.5MB, which is too good to be true.

The real work happens under Microsoft Edge, where “App: web.whatsapp.com” used 579.6MB. At that point, the WhatsApp desktop app was using about 720.9MB RAM.

Calling was the one reason to keep the desktop app around, and that’s gone now. In July, WhatsApp brought voice and video calls to WhatsApp Web, along with screen sharing, a Calls tab with history and favourites, call transfer between devices, waiting rooms for group calls, QuickHD video and noise suppression. The features are rolling out gradually, and my browser already shows the “Voice and video calling is now available” card.

WhatsApp Web also recently told me I can share message history with new group members, use chat themes and custom wallpapers, like a status with a heart, and export a chat as a file.

The only catch is Windows 11’s Resume feature for WhatsApp, which always opens the desktop app, so it won’t help if you use WhatsApp in the browser.

Streaming WhatsApp from my phone uses just 83.5MB on my PC

My other trick needs the right hardware. I use a Lenovo IdeaPad with a Motorola Edge 50 Neo, and since Lenovo owns Motorola, both come with Smart Connect, which is a match made in heaven. I just searched for WhatsApp in Smart Connect and opened the Android app in a window on my PC. As easy as that!

Since WhatsApp keeps running on the phone, Smart Connect used only 83.5MB on my PC, and that includes the Smart Connect app itself. I use it daily, and it’s been reliable. File transfers are also possible with the app, making it arguably better than anything we can do with what Meta has given to Windows users.

I understand that not everyone has a Lenovo PC and a Motorola phone. Fortunately, Microsoft’s Phone Link can stream apps from supported Samsung, HONOR, OPPO, ASUS, vivo, and Xiaomi phones, and we found that Windows 11’s new taskbar Search can now open apps from your Android phone in a Phone Link window.

It’s still in testing, but it could make streaming WhatsApp on your PC a lot more natural, like how it is in the iOS + macOS walled garden.

Telegram and a one-person project show what WhatsApp could be

I’m in Telegram groups that get thousands of messages a day, but Telegram Desktop uses only 340.1MB on my PC. In Task Manager, the only sub-process it lists is the active conversation, unlike the pile of WebView2 processes under WhatsApp. It’s not a fair benchmark, as the two apps don’t have the same people I talk with.

However, Telegram is better in features and usability when compared to WhatsApp. Its developers have also been very consistent with their Windows app, which I hugely appreciate. Remember, Telegram is tiny compared to Meta.

In other interesting news, Independent developer Carmine Paolino went ahead and built ZapFast, a native WhatsApp client written in Rust for Windows, macOS and Linux. It connects to WhatsApp as a companion device, without a browser engine. In his Linux test, Paolino says it used about 150MB of idle RAM versus 1.13GB for WhatsApp Web with Chromium, and the chat UI loaded in about just 0.7 seconds compared to 4.

Of course, I’m not recommending it. ZapFast doesn’t support calls, status, or communities yet, but that’s not the issue. Its web page warns that “Using an unofficial client may be against WhatsApp’s terms of service and could get an account suspended.” Anyway, the point is, if one developer can build a native WhatsApp client, what’s stopping Meta?

Meta has no excuse to keep WhatsApp a web wrapper on Windows

Windows has 1.6 billion monthly users, according to Satya Nadella, and WhatsApp is the most popular messaging app out there. On Steam’s September survey, Windows has a 95.03% share versus 1.92% for macOS. Sure, that’s a gaming crowd, but you get the idea. Yet Meta still ships a native WhatsApp app for Mac, while Windows users get web slop (I guess this is the right word).

I get why developers prioritise the Mac for paid apps, as the consensus is that Mac users are more willing to pay. But WhatsApp is free, so that argument doesn’t work here. Make it make sense, Meta.

Also, WinUI is in its best shape yet, with the framework finally getting basic controls it lacked for years. Microsoft’s design team even prototyped Windows 11’s new speed test in a day with an agentic AI workflow.

AI helped make this in a day, on one person’s spare time:

Meanwhile, Meta launched its Muse Spark AI model in April and expects to spend $135 billion to $145 billion on capital expenditure this year as it builds out AI infrastructure. Surely, a company with that kind of money can spare a few engineers, or a few AI agents, for a native Windows app?

Sadly, WhatsApp once loved Windows. I remember using the WhatsApp beta on Windows Phone, and later, the UWP app on Windows 11 was fast and smooth. Microsoft’s Teams is also a web app and eats a ton of RAM, but it isn’t nearly as laggy as WhatsApp. And no, I’m not giving Teams any credit here.

I know this is not how it works, but I wish Microsoft would talk to Meta, because an app as popular as WhatsApp shouldn’t be this slow on the Microsoft Store. Until Meta builds a native app again, WhatsApp isn’t coming back on my PC.

Are you still using WhatsApp for Windows, or have you moved to the web? Let us know in the comments.

title: Give Teams enough RAM or look worse in meetings, Microsoft warns, as it still...
author: Mayank Parmar
summary: Microsoft says it's fully committed to building native apps for Windows 11 and ditching WebView entirely, but Teams will remain a crap.
content:
Microsoft says it’s fully committed to building native apps and features for Windows 11 and ditching WebView entirely, but don’t expect Teams and Outlook to go native, probably, as it’s almost impossible at this point. Instead, Microsoft is rolling out a feature that could make you look worse in meetings if your PC has 8GB of RAM or less.

In June 2026, Microsoft said it made Teams launch faster on PCs and reduced the time it takes to load all your chats on mobile. I personally did not notice any visible differences, but Microsoft promised it was only the beginning, and that performance concerns remained its number one priority, without sharing a timeline for the next big update.

Now, Microsoft says it has begun shipping Efficiency mode, which I covered in June 2026 and found that it does help Teams run better on low-end PCs. In fact, it could also make a difference on a PC with 16GB of RAM because, at the end of the day, Teams itself is a resource hog, a bloated app, and it will not spare any hardware.

Microsoft says it has “continued to raise the bar,” but again, I have not seen anything change meaningfully outside Efficiency mode.

“From hardware-constrained devices to employees working on the go from mobile phones, delivering a consistent, high-quality experience across every platform remains a key focus for the Teams engineering team,” Microsoft noted in a support document seen by Windows Latest.

If your meetings suddenly look worse, it could be due to Teams Efficiency mode

Microsoft Teams usually adjusts the meeting resolution automatically, so you don’t have control over it. When Efficiency mode is turned on, you may notice that you look worse in meetings. This happens because Teams can reduce camera resolution to reduce resource consumption.

“This mode reduces processor, memory and network usage and is ideal for lower performance devices or those under heavy load. Turning this on may affect some functionality such as camera resolution,” Microsoft warns.

Microsoft calls it a “better experience,” but I don’t think that’s fair terminology because there’s a clear tradeoff here. And you shouldn’t have to make yourself look worse or make screen sharing terrible because your PC doesn’t have 32GB of RAM to satisfy Microsoft Teams’ RAM-hogging architecture.

According to Microsoft, Efficiency mode is meant for PCs with 8GB of RAM, and it argues that “Great collaboration experiences shouldn’t depend on having the latest hardware. Many of our customers rely on older devices, entry-level laptops…”

Fair enough, but when I opened Teams on my $2,500 HP Spectre with 32GB of RAM, I noticed that Efficiency mode was already turned on. It would, however, go into effect only when it detects that my PC is low on free resources.

There are three options under Efficiency mode:

  • Use only when resources are low (Default): Reduce processor and memory usage when reduced resources are detected.
  • Never use efficiency mode: Prioritise a richer experience, using more system resources.
  • Always use efficiency mode: Reduce processor and memory use at all times.

Although Efficiency mode can make you look worse in meetings and comes with other compromises, Microsoft believes the feature exists to ensure a “high-quality of experience across all configurations,” which is an “important priority” for the company.

Teams can launch faster on PCs with less RAM

Microsoft found that Teams can launch up to 20% faster on PCs with 8GB of RAM or less. Efficiency mode can also make compromises to camera, screen-sharing, or audio quality when resources are low.

However, as I showed above, it’s not strictly limited to PCs with 8GB of RAM. Even on a PC with 32GB of RAM, Teams can automatically enter Efficiency mode when the system is already using most of its resources.

Efficiency mode also keeps an eye on CPU usage, and your camera resolution can be reduced based on that. But if Teams has to choose between camera resolution and audio on a CPU-constrained PC, it will optimize for audio.

“As a result, users on hardware-constrained devices can maintain a high quality of their meeting experience despite the disproportionately higher thermal throttling rates,” the company explained.

Teams for Windows 11 and Windows 10 will eventually get another big upgrade, where you’ll see more optimizations applied when a PC doesn’t have enough RAM. For example, you can expect Teams to stop downloading images in the background or make similar changes to keep it efficient.

Efficiency mode is not a terrible idea, but I don’t think it was the right move to make it the de facto solution for faster performance on Windows. Instead, Teams should ditch WebView and consider moving to WinUI. Microsoft previously said it’s making WinUI faster and reducing overall RAM usage, which would benefit Teams.

Right now, Teams outside Efficiency mode is dependent on Chromium to reduce its memory footprint, which isn’t going to happen anytime soon.

With that said, Microsoft does understand that consumers “expect Teams to be fast, responsive, and ready when they need it,” but it still wouldn’t do anything about the underlying architecture.

title: Sanket lets you redesign GNOME’s date menu and Quick Settings
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Sanket is a GNOME Shell extension that lets you rejig how the desktop’s date menu, calendar, notifications and Quick Settings look and behave – and then some.

It can put notifications beneath the Quick Settings menu in a floating island, or embedded inside of it. Quick Settings toggles can shrink to dots when space is tight, and expand again as and when needed, Android-style.

As well as shrinking Quick Settings pills to dots, other menu tweaks let you show up two rows of controls and choose if volume and brightness sliders remain visible in compact mode. An ‘edit’ mode lets you drag and drop the order of controls too.

With notifications no longer having to sit inside the calendar popover, it becomes more of dashboard than a catch-all. Forecasts via GNOME Weather compact to a single animated icon, and timezones in GNOME Clocks can be shown with analog icons.

Sanket does change how notifications are managed, making only the most recent visible. A bit jarring to me since expanding the list (wherever it’s place) is more effort than simply seeing them. Notifications can be pinned, which is neat.

But what makes this more useful is that you don’t need to use everything it offers.

There is a lot that you can change using Sanket – or not. You can keep the stock layout and just use it for other things, like hiding the calendar header or ‘upcoming events’ lists.

I like that its settings includes visual previews of many layouts and options, so you know where elements shift without performing the ol’ ‘change something then work out what it did’ routine.

If you’ve never looked at GNOME Shell’s calendar or Quick Settings menus and thought ‘I wish I could change that bit’ then Sanket may not be that appealing.

But if you enjoy customising your desktop, or trying to make GNOME look more like other desktop environments or OSes – combined with Dash to Panel this can create a more ChromeOS-y inspired setup – then it’s well worth a look.

Sanket works on GNOME Shell 45 through 51. You can install it from the GNOME Extensions website (the desktop Extensions Manager app lets you browse and install extensions without needing a web browser).

Learn more about it on its GitHub page.

title: Stick with Outlook Classic for now, as Microsoft delays new Outlook’s unified inbox, a...
author: Mayank Parmar
summary: If you've been planning to finally ditch Outlook Classic for New Outlook's unified inbox, you might want to hold off.
content:
If you’ve been planning to finally ditch Outlook Classic for New Outlook’s unified inbox, you might want to hold off. While some Outlook Classic users will be automatically switched to New Outlook in 2027, with the option to switch back, you still have a choice between the two clients. And quite a lot of us have been waiting to see how the unified inbox works before making the switch.

Unified inbox, also known as All Accounts view, is not a new idea. It was part of Windows 10’s ad-free Mail and Calendar app before Microsoft killed it off, and you also have it in Gmail for Android and Outlook for Android.

For some reason, we don’t have a similar experience in Outlook Classic. You can use folders or groups as a workaround, but it’s not the same experience, and even New Outlook has been missing it.

But earlier this year, as I reported, Microsoft confirmed it was working on the All Accounts view for New Outlook. It did begin rolling out, and we were able to test it last week, but Microsoft now says it needs another month to complete the rollout.

Microsoft expects the unified inbox rollout to be completed by late November, and I wouldn’t be surprised if it gets delayed again or we have to wait until December or January to see it across all accounts.

However, you don’t need to pay for Microsoft 365 to use the unified inbox, as it seems to work with free accounts as well. Of course, with ads. Those are here to stay.

“We began rolling out in late September 2026 and expect to complete by late November 2026 (previously late October),” Microsoft noted in an admin portal update seen by Windows Latest.

Once it reaches your account, you may need to turn it on manually if it isn’t enabled automatically. For IT admins, Microsoft has new controls rolling out in the next few weeks, although they were originally planned for sometime in October 2026.

“Once available, admins will be able to manage whether Unified Inbox is enabled or disabled by default and whether users can change that setting,” the company explained.

For everyone else, you can toggle the feature on or off from Outlook Settings > Mail > Folder pane:

How does New Outlook’s unified inbox actually work?

If you’ve used Windows 10’s beautiful Mail & Calendar app that Microsoft killed in favor of New Outlook, you’ve probably already tried the All Accounts view. A similar experience is coming to New Outlook, but I think it’s better, and Microsoft also suggests the same because it’s powered by “AI.”

When you turn on the feature, you’ll see emails from multiple accounts in a single inbox, so you don’t have to merge mailboxes, go back and forth between folders, or navigate between mailboxes on the left sidebar of New Outlook. That can take a lot of scrolling when you have dozens of email accounts linked to the app.

Microsoft is not killing off separate inboxes, so you can still open each account’s regular inbox.

“Each account’s inbox stays separate, and All Accounts view brings messages together so users can triage mail from one place,” Microsoft explained.

You can also delete, move, archive, or mark messages from the unified inbox, and those actions will be reflected in the individual inboxes. For example, if you delete an email from account B in the unified inbox, you’ll also see it disappear from account B’s dedicated inbox.

“This feature provides a unified view across connected accounts in the new Outlook for Windows but does not merge mailboxes or move messages between accounts,” Microsoft explained in a document seen by Windows Latest.

My favourite part is the idea of searching all mailboxes without opening each one and repeating the same search until you find what you were looking for. However, when Windows Latest tested the feature, searching for older messages only searched one mailbox, so we’ll have to see how this works as the rollout expands.

Microsoft is also bringing Copilot into the unified inbox

Microsoft is planning to use the unified inbox as a new way to sell Copilot.

“The experience integrates with Copilot for AI-assisted email workflows and supports Search with Copilot for finding messages across the user’s primary account,” the company noted.

For now, the unified inbox is finally on its way, but you’ll have to wait a little longer if it hasn’t reached your account yet.

title: Windows 10 had it, but Microsoft says it’s never coming back to Windows 11...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Windows 11 lets you move the taskbar from Settings, and Microsoft says that's intentional. We revisit Tali Roth's reflow explanation, the hidden Left/Top/Right/Bottom menu in testing, and why power us...
content:
Windows 11’s taskbar can finally go to the top, left, or right of the screen, but only through Settings, as you still can’t drag it there like in Windows 10. Microsoft says that’s by design. Diego Baca, Microsoft’s Vice President of Design for Windows, says dragging the taskbar caused accidental movements, people rarely change its position anyway, and leaving drag-to-move out was a deliberate choice.

I understand the argument here, and the history of the Windows 11 taskbar is in his favour. But a lone developer has already added drag-to-move on top of Windows 11’s new taskbar positions, and Baca himself had a working prototype of a Windows 11 feature within a day with the help of AI.

So why not give the users what they want? Well, there are a lot of layers here.

Microsoft says dragging the Windows 11 taskbar leads to accidental movements

Baca was replying to a post on X saying you “still need” a third-party app to drag the taskbar. “I find headlines like these unnecessarily negative,” he wrote, suggesting “you can also use” one instead.

“From our research, dragging the taskbar to reposition it can lead to accidental movements, which is one of the reasons “Lock the taskbar” existed in previous versions of Windows,” says Baca, adding that changing the taskbar position “isn’t something people do frequently.”

As you’d know if you’ve used Windows 10, one careless drag could send the taskbar flying to the side. It happened to me when I first used the OS, but never later. Microsoft’s answer (for Windows 11) is a setting, which Baca calls “a more intentional and predictable experience,” available “just one right-click away.” He signed off with “It’s a deliberate design decision, not a missing capability.”

Microsoft’s Brandon LeBlanc replied, “Agreed,” which means this is the company’s present stance on this capability. Another user said he had accidentally moved the taskbar before.

Baca also wrote Microsoft’s May Windows Insider blog post, which called the movable taskbar “one of the most requested features,” and said the focus was to keep the experience “simple, predictable, and free from accidental taskbar movement.” Interestingly, that post also said Microsoft is “evaluating additional features like different taskbar positions per monitor and drag and drop.”

The Windows 11 taskbar was rebuilt from scratch, and dragging didn’t make the cut

Windows 11 shipped in 2021 with a brand-new taskbar that didn’t carry over the old code, and former product lead Tali Roth said the work needed to move it was “just huge,” because of “the reflow and the work that all of the apps have to do.” Microsoft’s data also said other taskbar features were in higher demand.

There was a design reason too. Former Windows and Bing boss Mikhail Parakhin said the vertical taskbar was killed for Windows 11’s “symmetric panes,” with notifications on the right, widgets on the left, and Start in the middle.

Five years later, Microsoft brought back taskbar positions with the August 27 optional update KB5120998, and the September Patch Tuesday restored the movable taskbar for everyone through a gradual rollout. You’ll find it under Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors. Funnily enough, Microsoft’s taskbar support page still says “there are no settings for moving a taskbar to the top or to the side of the screen.”

Strictly speaking, Windows 11’s taskbar didn’t have drag-to-move when it launched, so Microsoft didn’t take anything away. A small startup can ship whatever its users shout for, but a company handling a billion PCs goes by data, and refactoring a new component for a rarely used gesture has to pass through a ton of processes.

During the initial moving taskbar announcement, Microsoft tested buttons on the right-click menu on the taskbar to move it. We recently found that leftover code still exists in the right-click menu with Left, Top, Right, and Bottom buttons. I thought if such buttons existed, then it would be easier to map them to dragging motions, but apparently that’s not the case.

Also, interestingly, in the May 15 blog about Improving Windows Quality, Diego Baca said, “Touch gestures for alternate positions are still in progress.” Doesn’t a touch gesture equate to drag and drop?

Meanwhile, independent developer Michał Łeptuch has already built what Microsoft left out. His free app, Taskbar Location Options, adds Left, Top, Right, and Bottom to the taskbar’s right-click menu and lets you drag the taskbar to any edge of the screen. It needs Windows 11 26H2 (build 26300 or newer), and it works by writing the standard TaskbarLocation registry value.

Łeptuch was quick to clarify that his tool “doesn’t unlock any built-in Windows 11 features,” calling it “a small experiment” that “can stop working anytime.” He also added, “I don’t want to put bad light on the great engineers working on Windows 11.” Note that installing it means trusting a self-signed certificate, so it’s not for everyone.

Point taken, but if one developer can wire up drag-to-move for free, surely the 3.8 trillion-dollar company can too?

Windows 11’s taskbar still lacks a few Windows 10 conveniences

Microsoft has restored several missing taskbar features, but Windows 10 still offers a few conveniences that Windows 11 doesn’t fully match.

Feature Windows 10 Windows 11
Right-click customization More options Limited menu
Multiple app windows Visible stacked indicators Indicators appear on hover
Taskbar toolbars Supported Not supported
Calendar agenda Native agenda view No equivalent native experience

Microsoft’s data may be right, but Windows needs goodwill

I’m one of those very few people who change the taskbar position. Mine is on the right, which pairs well with Edge’s vertical tabs on the left and leaves more room to read. In Windows 10, I dragged it to the side while working in Word and Excel, and back to the bottom for movies or PowerPoint.

But that’s not the point. Decades ago, internal data decided what got built. Today, it’s what’s trending on X, Reddit and YouTube, where power users set the tone, and I see a ton of thumbnails of people excitedly switching to Linux or macOS, as if they’ve been liberated from Windows!

People who don’t even use a vertical taskbar (the huge majority of the 1 billion Windows 11 users) watch those videos, conclude that Windows doesn’t listen, and side with power users over the 3.8 trillion dollar company.

Microsoft’s Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22% last quarter, which the company puts down to last year’s Windows 10 end-of-support rush, excess inventory and a weaker PC market. Fair enough, but holdouts won’t switch if their feeds keep saying Windows 11 lacks simple features, even when it doesn’t.

AI was supposed to make small requests cheaper

On Friday, Windows CVP Marcus Ash explained that Windows 11’s new internet speed test in Quick Settings came from user feedback. When Windows president Pavan Davuluri asked Baca to take a look, “Within a day, Diego had a working prototype,” says Ash. The design and build work was driven by an agentic AI workflow guided by a person in their spare time!

Microsoft’s designers are also contributing code fixes to Windows with AI now. So, if AI can take a feature from idea to prototype in a day, shouldn’t Microsoft stop waiting for its data to justify small features? Just ship what people keep asking for, even if only a fraction of users end up using it.

As for accidental movements, Microsoft solved that problem decades ago. Baca himself mentioned that “Lock the taskbar” existed for this reason, and in Windows 10, the taskbar came locked by default. Bring back drag-to-move with that lock, and the people who don’t move their taskbar wouldn’t even notice it.

I want Windows 11 to get the love XP and 7 got, and Microsoft has done a commendable job this year. But it isn’t in a position to bargain with users, yet. For a while, it should stop defending and build what people ask for, so that Windows 12 can be everything users wanted Windows 11 to be.

Did you used to drag your taskbar around, or did you set it once and forget it? Let us know in the comments.

title: “Without AI slop”: Microsoft says AI built a Windows 11 feature, and it just...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Marcus Ash says Diego Baca had a working prototype of the Quick Settings speed test within a day. In our tests, it matched phone results in under 30 seconds. With WinUI finally gaining tables and char...
content:
Windows 11’s new internet speed test in Quick Settings went from an idea to a working prototype in a single day, according to Windows Design and Research lead Marcus Ash, and surprisingly, the design and build work was done by an agentic AI workflow that one person guided in their spare time. I tested it last week, and it’s one of the most polished little additions to Windows 11 in a while.

If one person can pull that off, that too during break hours, imagine what such an approach could do for the rest of Windows. Three things need to happen, and from the looks of it, all of them are already in motion.

Windows 11’s speed test went from idea to working prototype in a day

In his “Windows tip of the day” post on X, spotted by Windows Latest, Ash explained that the feature started with user feedback. “This came from feedback we heard about wanting a more integrated experience,” he wrote.

AI made this happen:

Windows president Pavan Davuluri then asked Diego Baca, Microsoft’s Vice President of Product Design, to take a look. “Within a day, Diego had a working prototype,” says Ash. After that, Microsoft’s connectivity team worked with partners to bring the experience into Windows.

As for how it was built, “The design and build work was driven by an agentic AI workflow, with a person guiding the process in their spare time,” Ash wrote, adding, “Getting from idea to customer value faster. Without AI slop.”

It’s not AI slop because a human steered the agents, and Microsoft engineers plus partners (the test is powered by Speedtest by Ookla) handled the integration. Ash didn’t reveal which AI models or tools were used, or how much of the code AI wrote.

Either way, AI or not, a prototype in a day, built in someone’s spare time, is a far cry from the usual pace of Windows development.

I tested Windows 11’s new speed test, and it works surprisingly well

Microsoft showed us the feature with the October 23 Experimental build, where Insiders can run a speed test and see the results in Quick Settings “without being redirected to a browser.” On my build 26340.9767, I had to turn on the “Quick Settings Speed Test” feature flag first.

You can start a test from the new Speed test tile, the Wi-Fi flyout, or by right-clicking the network icon on the taskbar and selecting “Test internet speed”.

On my virtual machine connected over Ethernet, the flyout showed 31.5 Mbps download, 34.4 Mbps upload, and 32 ms ping, all in under 30 seconds. The numbers are accurate, as I confirmed the speed on two Android devices, too.

I was half expecting it to break, as it was in an Experimental build, but surprisingly, it worked without hiccups even when I moved the taskbar to other edges of the screen, and it looks good in both light and dark themes.

If you’re on a Windows 11 PC, you’ll know that the Perform speed test shortcut just opens Bing in your browser, which saves no time over a regular search to find internet speed. Ironically, both use Speedtest by OOKLA, even when Bing had its own version in the past.

Three things need to happen for the rest of Windows 11, and they finally are…

First of all, WinUI has to be good. Microsoft’s native framework went years without basics like data tables, charts and pen inking, which is one reason Windows 11 has so many web apps. At Build 2026, Microsoft’s Chris Anderson admitted WinUI has “a ton of feature gaps in the platform.”

TableView and Chart finally arrived in the experimental Windows App SDK 2.5.4 on September 29, though Microsoft says they aren’t ready for production apps yet.

WinUI’s mainline development also moved to GitHub in August, but outside developers still can’t contribute code, as Microsoft is validating the process first.

Second, Windows has to be WinUI. After the Properties dialog was rebuilt in WinUI 3, March Rogers, Microsoft’s Partner Director of Design, said “our plan is to bring more of the Windows UI to WinUI3.” Since then, AutoPlay came next in line, and Print Management has become a standalone WinUI 3 app that even reached Release Preview quicker than I thought.

Microsoft’s telemetry also shows the new WinUI Run dialog opening in 94ms versus 103ms for the Windows 95-era version, which goes to show how fast WinUI is. Most of these are still limited to Insider builds, though.

My favourite so far is the new Windows Search, which Microsoft says is “built on WinUI 3” and is “faster and more efficient with resources.” Microsoft has rolled it out to Insiders, with a broader rollout planned later this year. To put it lightly, I love everything about the new Search.

Third, all of this has to happen fast, and AI is how it can. Diego Baca says, “AI has already helped our design team accelerate significantly,” with designers now contributing code fixes to Windows. Microsoft also published guides showing AI building a native WinUI app in about 30 minutes.

Microsoft’s own apps need the ‘speed test’ type of treatment next

The app I open almost every day is Clipchamp (don’t judge me). It’s surprisingly feature-rich for small edits, even on the free plan, but it’s a web app, and the UI lag doesn’t hide the fact. I would gladly pay for Premium if Clipchamp were native WinUI.

A fast, native editor could be the Windows Movie Maker of this generation, the app so many successful creators made their first YouTube videos with, including Marques Brownlee (MKBHD).

Then there’s the Weather app, a basic app every OS needs. In our testing, Windows 11’s Weather app used over 1.2GB of RAM while idle, with nine Chromium subprocesses, while Apple’s native Weather app on macOS used 246.7MB. A weather app eating over a gigabyte of memory is shameful, to say the least.

MSN News is another one. In the days of endless social media feeds, a fast, native MSN News app would be a nice antidote to brain rot.

And of course, Teams. A fresh install with no chats used 963MB of RAM doing nothing on our 32GB PC, and as of now, Microsoft has no plans to move it off WebView2. Everyone I know hates using it, and compared to MSN Messenger from decades ago, Teams has zero charm.

Still, after five years of slow progress, Windows is finally moving faster than ever, and I can’t believe I’m saying this: AI deserves the credit. If one person in their spare time could build the speed test, what’s stopping Microsoft from giving Clipchamp, Weather, and Teams some of that love?
