title: Ubuntu 27.04 ‘Tenacious T-Rex’ opens for development
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Development on Ubuntu 27.04, codenamed ‘Tenacious T-Rex’, has officially begun.

The tenacious archive is now open (30 October 2026), with auto-sync from Debian set to pull in a tranche of updated packages since the Ubuntu 26.10 release. Over the course of the next six months, those will be tested, set and form the basis of the final, stable release.

Ubuntu 27.04 is scheduled for release on 22 April 2027, with a beta preceding it on 1 April (not a joke). Ubuntu 26.10 saw its beta delayed by a week, but hopefully the new development cycle has fewer hiccups.

What to expect in the Tenacious T-Rex?

Ubuntu 27.04 is almost certain to ship with the GNOME 52 desktop and, depending on schedules, the Linux 7.6 kernel or later. There’ll be more Rust baked in, with Canonical signalling its plan to adopt ntpd-rs as the default sync tool in this release.

Its engineers will be ‘accelerating’ development of Ubuntu Core Desktop, an all-snap version of Ubuntu. That won’t be the default download, but a preview since it won’t be daily-driver ready for regular use-cases – work has to start somewhere.

Plus, expect the Ubuntu OS installer’s support for TPM-backed full-disk encryption to mature, more work around security-orientated system booting and packaging to prep the new HWE firmware initiative.

What about further AI integrations?

The Myna voice dictation tool is currently in tech preview on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and 26.10. The AI models to power it are too large to ship by default, but a user-facing opt-in on the desktop could be introduced.

And I recently covered a new AI-backed Ubuntu launcher concept built by a Canonical engineer after ‘design discussions’ at the company. It’s a simulated mockup, not a real tool, but it shows Canonical is exploring ways to infuse on-device AI within the desktop.

What are your hopes and would-like-to-sees for the next release? Let me know in the comments.

title: What really happens when you hold the power button to force shut down your...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Microsoft says crash dumps aren't collected unless you send Optional diagnostic data, but Required data still flags the long press itself. Here's what the Diagnostics & feedback page, Kernel-Power Eve...
content:
If your Windows 11 PC freezes and, instead of panicking, you hold the power button to kill it, the OS uses those last few seconds to save a snapshot of what went wrong. Eight seconds into the press, the kernel captures an emergency dump, which Windows can upload to Microsoft’s Windows Error Reporting service on the next boot, if your diagnostic data settings allow it.

Microsoft internally calls these “long power button hold” (LPBH) failures, and the ones caught on a completely black screen go to a dedicated team, which Microsoft veteran Raymond Chen is a part of, and as you might’ve guessed, he recently explained how this power button behaviour works.

Windows 11 starts capturing a kernel dump eight seconds into the press

When you press and hold the power button on your Windows 11 PC, and you continue holding for 12 seconds, the PC turns off at the hardware level without telling Windows, but four seconds earlier, “the Windows kernel realizes that the user is trying to do a force-power-off of the system,” says Chen, and it quickly takes a kernel dump. Sometimes four seconds isn’t enough, and the dump ends up incomplete.

Also, the 12-second figure isn’t universal. Microsoft’s debugger documentation mentions the firmware hard power-off at “usually about 10 seconds”, even shorter on some ARM64 laptops, and its Event ID 41 guide remarks forced shutdowns after holding the button for at least four seconds. However, if your laptop cuts power at five seconds, there’s no dump to speak of.

Windows also notes whether every pixel on screen is black. Those dumps are tagged “black screen LPBH” and analyzed by a virtual team that Chen is a part of. The culprit could be a broken video driver, the desktop compositor handing black pixels to a working driver, or nothing drawing to the screen, sometimes because the process responsible has hung.

Funnily enough, a black screen is when most of us reach for the power button anyway!

Does Windows 11 send the crash dump to Microsoft automatically?

It depends on your diagnostic data setting. According to Microsoft’s privacy documentation, Required diagnostic data tells the company when a crash dump file is created, but “crash dumps themselves are not collected without additional permissions, such as choosing to send Optional diagnostic data.”

The long press still gets reported, though. Microsoft’s list of required diagnostic events includes a LongPowerButtonPressDetected field that “identifies if the user was pressing and holding power button.”

The part about Optional data with Windows makes anyone anxious, as Microsoft says the memory state captured during a crash “may unintentionally include parts of a file you were using when a problem occurred.” Redmond hasn’t said what an LPBH dump contains.

To check, open Settings > Privacy & security > Diagnostics & feedback, and expand Diagnostic data. Turning off “Send optional diagnostic data” removes the main permission Microsoft names for collecting crash dumps. There’s no separate switch for power button dumps, but the toggle is also one of the settings that limit what Windows 11’s GDID tracker captures.

Note that the “Delete diagnostic data” button on that page doesn’t stop data from being sent, and it doesn’t clear data linked to your Microsoft account, which you’ll need to delete from the Microsoft privacy dashboard.

I, for one, would like a dedicated crash dump toggle, especially from a company that recently had to deny Windows 11 was spying on desktop PCs.

Microsoft already has a “release the power button” screen in Windows

Chen believes Windows Insider builds ask you to let go of the power button so the kernel can finish its dump. We couldn’t check, as we run Insider builds in a virtual machine.

Interestingly, Microsoft has documented a similar screen for years. With the PowerButtonBugcheck registry value set, holding the button for 7 seconds and releasing it before 10 seconds triggers Bug Check 0x1C8. Instead of the usual crash screen (which Windows 11 has already turned black), you see “Please release the power button. We just need a few more seconds to shut down.” with a percentage counter.

The option dates back to Windows 10 version 1809 and needs a GPIO-based power button. My guess is that the Insider prompt borrows from it, but Microsoft hasn’t confirmed anything.

To see if your PC logged a forced shutdown, check Kernel-Power Event ID 41 under Event Viewer > Windows Logs > System. Microsoft says holding the power button logs a nonzero PowerButtonTimestamp, and Windows 11 also lists LongPowerButtonPressDetected in the Details tab. However, Event ID 41 only confirms an unclean shutdown, and doesn’t prove Windows saved a dump.

With that said, a black screen isn’t always a Windows bug. Chen recalls a Windows 3.1 support call where a customer saw nothing after the logo, because they had set every color in the Colors control panel to black, window text included. Hardly a job for the black screen LPBH team.

title: Microsoft killed Android apps on Windows 11, but they’re back in taskbar Search, streamed...
author: Gareth Smith
summary: Windows Latest found that Windows 11's new taskbar Search lists Android apps from your linked phone as Mobile App results. Selecting Bluesky opened it on my Samsung A26 and mirrored it to my PC via Ph...
content:
Windows Latest has found that Windows 11’s new taskbar Search can open apps from your Android phone. When I typed Bluesky into Search on my Surface Laptop, it showed the app installed on my Samsung phone as a “Mobile App” result, and clicking Open launched Bluesky on the phone and mirrored it to my PC through Phone Link!

Microsoft has since confirmed that Search can call, text, and toggle Do Not Disturb on a connected phone, but its release notes don’t mention opening phone apps. I found it while testing the new Search, and truth be told, it’s one of the neatest Windows and Android tricks I’ve seen.

Windows 11 Search now shows Android apps from your phone

For this test, I used my Surface Laptop 7th Edition on Windows 11 26H2, build 26340.9767, in the Experimental channel, paired with a Samsung Galaxy A26 running Android 16.

I searched for Bluesky and saw a result named Bluesky with “Mobile App” underneath, right at the top. Below it were the usual Bing suggestions and a couple of PNG files from my PC, so Search treats the phone app like any other app result.

Search gives linked Android apps the same entry point as Windows software. To me, it looks like another attempt to reduce instances of us having to open the Phone Link app first and then mirror an app from our Android phone. You just type the app’s name and press Open. That’s convenience for the win!

Selecting the result mirrors the Android app through Phone Link

Clicking Open launched Bluesky on my phone, and a “Phone screen” window from Phone Link appeared on my PC a moment later, showing the app with my phone’s status bar on top.

Just to be clear, Bluesky isn’t installed on Windows. The app keeps running on the phone, and the PC gives it a bigger screen, a keyboard and a mouse. Microsoft killed the Windows Subsystem for Android in March 2025, so streaming from the phone is now the only official way to use Android apps on Windows 11.

Yes, you could already open supported Android apps in Phone Link, add favorites, pin them to Start or the taskbar, and even run them almost full-screen. Search adds another way in, without creating a shortcut first, and if you usually open apps by typing their name, this feels a lot more natural.

My test only covered opening the app. I haven’t used it long enough to judge how reliable it is day to day, or if it works with multiple apps.

Microsoft confirms phone actions in Windows 11 Search

On October 30, Microsoft released build 26340.9843 with more features for the new Windows Search. “With a supported phone connected through Phone Link, you can now call or text a friend and access phone actions such as Do Not Disturb,” Microsoft says, adding that “Android support is available now with iPhone support coming early next year.”

In Microsoft’s screenshots, typing “dnd phone,” “text Melissa” or “call Melissa” shows an Action result for the phone with an Apply, Send or Call button. Opening phone apps isn’t shown yet, but it fits right in with these actions and with the phone controls Microsoft is testing in Quick Settings.

Which Android phones work with apps in Windows Search

Only some phones that pair with Phone Link can stream apps. According to Microsoft’s Phone Link Apps requirements, you need select Samsung, HONOR, OPPO, ASUS, vivo or Xiaomi phones with Link to Windows preinstalled, running Android 10 or newer, connected to the Wi-Fi network your PC uses. Pairing for calls and messages doesn’t mean app streaming will work.

The new Search is also rolling out gradually to Insiders, and Microsoft hasn’t said when Phone Actions will reach everyone, let alone my discovery of phone apps shown in Windows Search. Either way, results may differ between setups, so take my test as a first look.

Credit where it’s due, typing an app’s name on my PC and having it open from my phone feels like the kind of Windows and Android integration that Apple fans brag about with iPhone Mirroring. I just hope Microsoft keeps it reliable when it reaches everyone.

title: Windows 11 is full of web apps eating 1GB+ RAM because Microsoft neglected WinUI,...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Microsoft promised a DataGrid and charts for WinUI at Build 2026. TableView, Chart and InkCanvas are now in an experimental Windows App SDK release, almost five years after third-party vendors started...
content:
Microsoft is finally giving WinUI, Windows 11’s native framework for modern apps, a data table, charts, and pen inking, which are three basics needed by finance tools, admin panels, and note-taking apps. Without them, building on the web might’ve been the easier route. TableView and Chart came to Windows App SDK 2.5.4 Experimental on September 29 along with reworked inking controls, and WinUI Gallery 3.0 lets developers try them, but Microsoft says these are not yet ready for production apps.

At Build 2026, Chris Anderson from Microsoft’s Windows UI team admitted WinUI has “a ton of feature gaps in the platform,” and said DataGrid and Charting were “up and coming.” It was also the conference where Microsoft pushed developers toward WinUI over web frameworks and dropped the “3” from the name to convince them that the company isn’t planning yet another framework.

For context, WinUI is the UI framework, and the Windows App SDK is the package of Windows APIs and tools that ships it.

WinUI 3 is finally getting the basic controls developers have been asking for

The experimental release brings three first-party building blocks to WinUI 3 apps.

  • TableView, a native table for displaying, sorting, filtering, grouping, and editing large sets of records
  • Chart, a native control for line, area, and bar charts
  • InkCanvas and InkToolbar, which let users write and draw with a pen, finger, or mouse

Until now, developers had to buy these from third-party vendors or borrow them from community projects, maybe even build them by hand. TableView’s code showed up in WinUI’s GitHub repository in September.

TableView brings a native data grid to WinUI 3 apps

When Windows App SDK 1.0 came in November 2021, Syncfusion, DevExpress and Telerik were already advertising their WinUI DataGrid and Chart controls. Microsoft’s version took almost five years!

“For a long time, the community has asked for data table support in WinUI 3,” Pranav Gupta from the WinUI team wrote in the TableView announcement.

Users can click a header to sort, resize and freeze columns, and switch between Compact, Standard and Comfortable row density. Developers get template columns for richer cells like status pills or progress bars, filtering and grouping through a shared TableViewSource, editing with validation, and virtualized rows, which is how Microsoft’s Contoso Sales Ledger demo handles 5,000 deals across eleven columns.

An inventory app, for example, could let users sort products by stock, filter by supplier, group by category, and fix a wrong price in place, without the developer stitching a grid together from basic controls.

Ironically, Microsoft promised a DataGrid at Build, but its TableView documentation says the control “isn’t a DataGrid replacement and doesn’t provide spreadsheet-style interaction.” Users can select only one row, sort by one column at a time, and group by only one level, and columns can’t be reordered. Microsoft says hierarchical views and app context menus are already in the works.

WinUI 3 finally gets its own native Chart control

A finance dashboard needs revenue against expenses, a cash balance trend and maybe a portfolio curve, and considering how common such apps are, WinUI developers had to do the hard work of pulling in a third-party charting library to make such apps.

Microsoft’s Chart control comes with line, area, and bar series, category and date-time axes, numeric value axes, legends, data labels, and markers. Multiple series can share axes, and the WinUI Gallery sample shows a series updating live from an ObservableCollection.

In Gupta’s Contoso Finance demo, columns compare monthly revenue and expenses, a line tracks cash on hand, and horizontal bars break down spending. The chart only draws prepared data, though. “Calculations such as savings rate, cash runway and category totals belong to the app, not the chart control,” Gupta wrote.

Developer feedback has been mixed, to say the least. One simply asked, “there is no pie chart, why?” while others want zoom and pan, and an issue already complains that the control doesn’t follow Fluent design.

Microsoft is bringing InkCanvas and InkToolbar to WinUI 3

UWP apps have had InkCanvas for years, but when developers moved those apps to WinUI 3, the control “simply was not there,” as Gupta put it in the inking announcement.

Inking first came with Windows App SDK 2.4.1 Experimental in August with InkCanvas, InkToolbar and InkPresenter, plus clipboard and high-contrast support. The 2.5.4 release lets InkToolbar drive an InkPresenter without an InkCanvas and adds InkSynchronizer, so apps can themselves render committed ink.

The toolbar has pen, pencil, highlighter, eraser, and ruler buttons, and strokes can be saved as a regular GIF that still reloads as editable ink. Gupta says the controls mean “a note app stops being a drawing engine you have to write yourself,” which helps anyone signing a PDF or scribbling meeting notes on a Surface.

I’ve always felt Windows hardware, with its pens and convertibles, is miles ahead of Apple’s, so it was odd that Microsoft’s modern framework couldn’t handle a pen!

WinUI Gallery 3.0 lets developers test experimental controls sooner

“Until now, new controls usually showed up in the Gallery after they reached a stable Windows App SDK release,” Senior Product Manager Niels Laute wrote on October 13 while announcing WinUI Gallery 3.0, the reference app where developers try WinUI controls and copy sample code.

Version 3.0 runs on the experimental Windows App SDK and ships it self-contained, so developers don’t have to install anything extra. Laute says the idea is to get sample code out sooner and collect feedback while the APIs can still change. Experimental pages will have a badge, and the Gallery also has samples for WrapPanel, LayoutPanel, PagerControl, and new Window width and height properties.

Unsurprisingly, one developer under the post asked, “So it now has ‘experimental’ capabilities that existed in WPF for decades?”

WinUI’s development has taken years, and Microsoft is still opening it up

I was surprised to know that WinUI 3 has been around for seven years, and the push to fully open up its development only started last year. Well, better late than never…

Date Milestone
November 2019 Microsoft introduces the WinUI 3 direction.
February 2020 WinUI 3 Alpha arrives.
May 2020 WinUI 3 Preview 1 adds Win32 support.
March 2021 Project Reunion 0.5 ships with WinUI 3.
June 2021 Project Reunion 0.8 arrives.
November 2021 Windows App SDK 1.0 ships.
May 2022 Windows App SDK 1.1 adds features and improvements.
November 2022 Windows App SDK 1.2
April 2023 Windows App SDK 1.3
August 2023 Windows App SDK 1.4
February 2024 Windows App SDK 1.5
September 2024 Windows App SDK 1.6 adds Native AOT support.
March 2025 Windows App SDK 1.7
July 2025 Microsoft announces its phased WinUI open-source plan.
September 2025 Windows App SDK 1.8
April 2026 Windows App SDK 2.0 ships.
May 2026 Microsoft completes Phase 3 of its WinUI open-source plan.
August 2026 Mainline WinUI development moves to GitHub; Phase 4 completes.
August 2026 Experimental WinUI 3 inking support arrives.
September 2026 Experimental TableView and Chart controls arrive.
October 2026 WinUI Gallery 3.0 showcases new experimental controls.

 

“This isn’t a flip-the-switch moment, it’s a deliberate process,” Microsoft’s Beth Pan wrote when she announced the open-source plan in July 2025. Microsoft has since completed Phase 4, moving mainline WinUI development to GitHub in August 2026. Microsoft engineers now create branches, open pull requests, review and merge code in public. But that doesn’t mean outside developers can contribute yet. Microsoft says it is still validating the contribution process, while the XAML compiler remains partly closed and cannot yet be built entirely from source.

Ironically, a developer under the Chart announcement pointed out that the new controls ship in a closed source package!

Better native controls could give Windows apps a reason to ditch Electron

Developers pick Electron because one HTML, CSS, and JavaScript codebase runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Chances are that you’ve already used multiple Electron or WebView2 apps and saw the RAM usage climb like it’s rendering a game!

Electron uses Chromium and Node.js to run web-based desktop apps, while WebView2 embeds Microsoft’s Edge-based web rendering engine. Both let developers reuse web technologies, but they also come with extra browser-related processes and memory usage.

When I tested the new WhatsApp for Windows, the WebView2 version used about 600MB of RAM while idle, and the old native app was under 100MB. Personally, I’m still holding on to Outlook Classic, and I’d switch to the New Outlook (WebView2 app) the day it becomes a native app.

That said, WinUI isn’t automatically efficient. Microsoft admitted WinUI apps can hog RAM, and fortunately, Anderson’s priority list at Build included this. “The first and foremost is performance, fundamentals, quality, fixing a lot of bugs,” he said.

The 2.5.4 release takes care of some of that memory growth by fixing a resource-tracking bug that grew memory when apps repeatedly created visual-state storyboards or resolved static or theme resources, and by improving cleanup of unreachable native WinUI objects in .NET apps after a tab or page closes. Smaller stuff is still missing too, like the Shift+click scroll bar shortcut that even Electron apps support.

For now, a developer prototyping an accounting app in WinUI can build the ledger, the dashboard and the signature box with Microsoft’s native controls. Of course, this doesn’t mean fewer web apps on your PC all of a sudden, as it depends on how quickly these leave the experimental channel, and whether Microsoft finally gives developers the Visual Studio visual designer they keep asking for.

title: This app lets you manage Nothing & CMF earbuds on Linux
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Adjusting active noise cancellation (ANC) on Nothing or CMF earbuds means taking out your phone, opening the official mobile app and twiddling a setting there.

EarA, a new open-source tool, aims to nix that palaver. It’s a GTK4 app (with a CLI for those who prefer the terminal), and lets you change settings on earbuds like the Nothing Ear (a) and CMF Buds 2, from your Linux desktop.

Noise control/ANC levels can be switched with a click. There are toggles to disable personalised ANC and in-ear detection and use low latency. Gesture behaviours (on supported devices) can be set as well.

The app, available as a Flatpak, AppImage and DEB, also shows battery levels for each bud and the charging case, works with Find My Earbuds and offers an 8-band equaliser, EQ presets and bass enhancement for fine-tuning the sound.

Despite being made with GTK4, EarA’s user-interface doesn’t look especially native, not based on the screenshots and the “live demo” webpage. Does it matter? Maybe not; it’s a utility you open as needed, then close again.

Budslink may be a better fit

EarA is not the only option available for Nothing/CMF devices.

I wrote about Budslink earlier this year. That’s available on Flathub, studiously update and supports Nothing and CMF earbuds, alongside audio devices from Apple, Samsung, Google, Redmi, OnePlus and others.

An app isn’t needed to pair earbuds with a Linux desktop and play audio through them. That all works over Bluetooth as standard.

But for advanced features, things like ANC controls, a low-latency mode, codec options and reliable battery readings for each bud, you will find that a companion app like EarA or Budslink is worthwhile.

Where to get EarA

You can see a full list of supported/tested devices on the project’s GitHub page. This should work with hardware in the ‘same protocol family’. Some settings do rely on hardware, so if in doubt, look up what your model is supposed to support.

That’s where you can download the latest release to try. There’s a DEB installer for Ubuntu as well as a standalone AppImage runtime, though the latter is only available for x86-64 devices.

title: Tested: Windows 11’s 2026 feature update is just 174KB, but your PC still needs...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Windows 11 24H2, 25H2 and 26H2 share one servicing branch, so 26H2 is a tiny master switch for up-to-date PCs. Windows 11 23H2 is on the older 22H2/23H2 branch, so it needs a full OS swap built on a 5...
content:
Windows 11 26H2 is a tiny enablement package if your PC is already on Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2, but if you’re still on 23H2, you need a full feature update of around 6.5GB. I downloaded the official Windows 11 26H2 enablement package, KB5121794, and the whole file is just 173KB, or 177,535 bytes.

I know it sounds crazy that the 2026 annual Windows feature update is just 174KB, and it’s not a compressed installer that later downloads gigabytes of files. The shortest explanation is that 26H2 features are already on up-to-date 24H2 and 25H2 PCs, and the package’s duty is just to turn them on.

I downloaded the Windows 11 26H2 enablement package, and it’s 173KB

I grabbed the x64 package for 26H2 using direct Microsoft links. My File Explorer showed it as a Microsoft Update Standalone Package (.msu) with a size of 173KB, and it takes up just 176KB on disk.

Use the following links to download the Windows 11 26H2 enablement package for your PC, directly from Microsoft servers:

  • AMD64 PCs (Intel/AMD): Direct download link (.msu)
  • Arm64 PCs (Qualcomm): Direct download link (.msu)

When we first explained the 174KB size in June, we used Microsoft’s white paper as a reference; now we have the proof. According to Microsoft’s KB5121794 support document, “Windows 11, versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 share a common core operating system with an identical set of system files.” The new features already come to PCs through monthly updates in a partially disabled state, and the package works as “a small, quick-to-install ‘master switch'” that turns them on.

Note that this doesn’t mean that all features will be disabled. Microsoft gives new features to Windows PCs every month, but due to controlled feature rollout, some of them might not reach all PCs immediately.

Anyway, Microsoft describes four steps in its white paper. Code flags change from disabled to enabled, the PC restarts, the new features are enabled, and the build number changes from 26200 or 26100 to 26300. It’s also why 26H2 installs in under five minutes.

Why Windows 11 23H2 needs a 6.5GB upgrade

Windows 11 23H2 is on a different source code branch. Microsoft’s June 2026 white paper, Windows and the Shared Servicing Model, says there are two shared branches for Windows 11: “the 22H2/23H2 branch and the branch for 24H2/25H2/26H2.”

The newer branch also includes the Long Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) editions of Windows 11, which Microsoft says is why “it is a separate branch from Windows 11, version 23H2.” Since 23H2 PCs don’t receive the disabled 26H2 code in their monthly updates, there’s nothing for a master switch to turn on. Windows has to do what Microsoft calls an “OS swap,” which replaces the whole operating system.

Microsoft’s example in the white paper is a 23H2 PC moving to 25H2, using x64, US English, Business editions. The upgrade includes the 5.3GB base image of 24H2 and an 887MB final cumulative update that “contains the complete payload for additions for 25H2.” Microsoft says the complete feature update is “close to 6.5GB,” which is why the enablement package is “about three-thousandths of one percent” of its size.

To be clear, Microsoft measured this for 25H2, not 26H2, and the two listed components add up to about 6.2GB. A 23H2 PC moving to 26H2 goes through a similar full upgrade, but the final download size depends on your edition and the latest cumulative update.

Which Windows versions get the 174KB update

  • Windows 11 24H2: Enablement package, if you have the September 22, 2026 update (KB5124010) or later.
  • Windows 11 25H2: Enablement package, with the KB5124010 or later prerequisite.
  • Windows 11 23H2: Full feature update, around 6.5GB.
  • Windows 10: Full Windows 11 upgrade, only if your PC meets the hardware requirements.

Interestingly, 22H2 and 23H2 share a branch too, which is why 23H2 was actually an enablement package for 22H2 PCs in 2023. It just doesn’t help with 26H2, though.

More importantly, if you’re on 23H2, you can’t stay put for long. Windows 11 23H2 Home and Pro already stopped getting updates in November 2025, and Enterprise and Education editions stop getting updates on November 10, 2026.

How to get Windows 11 26H2 the easy way

If you’re on 24H2 or 25H2, open Settings > Windows Update and click Check for updates. If you see “Windows 11, version 26H2 is available,” click Download & install. Microsoft’s John Cable, VP of Windows Servicing and Delivery, says this gives you “minimal download size, quick installation, and a single restart.”

Our 26H2 installation guide has every method, and if you’re on 23H2 or doing a clean install, note that the 26H2 ISO is around 8GB.

There are good reasons to move. Once you’re on 26H2, your PC gets noticeable performance improvements and lower RAM usage. On my dad’s 8GB laptop, memory use after a restart dropped from 5GB to 3.3GB. You can check what’s new and whether you’re on 26H2 by running winver.

title: Gelly is a GTK desktop music player for Jellyfin and Navidrome
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
If you run your own music streaming server using Jellyfin or Navidrome/Subsonic, and you want a solid desktop player to browse and stream your library in, Gelly is worth a look.

It bills itself as a “native, lightweight music player” for the aforementioned streaming servers (along with compatible ones). It’s written in Rust and GTK4/libadwaita and, as any good player should, it lets you browse, play and control music playback.

And it does all of that with a modern design and layout.

Having recently set up Jellyfin on my Raspberry Pi 4 (to replace its ageing installation of dust and lint), seeing Gelly on Flathub’s front page this week felt like awfully good timing.

Having recent set up Jellyfin1 on my Raspberry Pi 4 (to replace its ageing installation of dust and lint), seeing Gelly surface on Flathub’s front page felt like awfully good timing.

A modern Jellyfin desktop player

Gelly is not a standalone desktop music player, so it won’t do anything until you point it at your Jellyfin or Navidrome server. Thankfully, the app has a straightforward setup wizard that takes care of that.

You enter http://your-server-ip:8096 and your server credentials and, after a short loading screen, your music filters in. Options let you trigger a rescan on the server (for new files, updated metadata, etc) and refresh the data in Gelly itself.

The default view is albums, with large art displays in a grid (I enabled compact mode in the player’s Preferences, which is what you see in my screenshots). There are also artist, playlist and track views. Sorting options are available in most views.

One feature I liked is the “play similar” action, which you can apply to a selected song, album or artist. If you’re migrating back from streaming music services like Spotify, these may be a nice creature comfort.

As this is a frontend, you won’t find many advanced settings (no metadata editing, Jellyfin dashboard, plugins etc). All of that is done via your Jellyfin or Navidrome setup.

Gelly supports MPRIS, so any media controllers you use (including extensions like Dynamic Music Pill) can relay and report playback info from it. Gelly can also display lyrics (with line sync, if available2) if you fancy a sing-along.

Other features include ReplayGain, gapless playback and track favouriting.

Options let you disable the ‘extra eye candy’, nixing fancier flourishes like blurred background effects, and enable a compact mode. You can also prevent the system from suspending during active playback and set specific transcoding settings (if needed).

I’ve only started using Jellyfin recently, so my needs are simple. I had been using MPD locally, and while I could run and access my music remotely through that, a dedicated setup seemed more sensible.

I rather gelled (don’t groan) with Gelly. If you want to see if you do too, it’s available to install on Ubuntu from Flathub (Arch users will find it in the AUR).

Get Gelly on Flathub

  1. Installing Navidrome on Ubuntu is moderately easy too, just a few commands and careful reading. I didn’t pick Jellyfin for any specific reason compared to other clients; it was the first one I remembered. ↩︎
  2. The lyrics plugin for Jellyfin supports downloading timed lyrics. ↩︎

title: We added a manual dark mode toggle to the site (cos you asked)
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
You may have noticed OMG! Ubuntu looking a little cleaner lately. Earlier this month, Sam and I finally rolled out a refreshed site backend, along with some changes to the bits you look at when you come here.

Boring stuff to read about, I know. But a few of the changes were done because readers asked for them, so I wanted to quickly mention them.

Firstly, the mobile homepage is now more info-dense.

Recent posts appear in a compact list, so you can see more of the latest articles at a glance rather than needing to scroll (and scroll, and scroll, etc) large thumbnails.

Secondly, there’s a manual dark mode toggle in the masthead. The site still follows your OS dark mode preference automatically, but you can override with this simple two-state switch: light or dark mode.

Thirdly, we updated the code blocks with a simple “copy” button to help newbies screw up their system faster make copying terminal commands easier than selecting text manually:

This has a copy button -->

The rest of the changes? Minor fluff.

A mix of things that are a bit different (new meta bar treatment, new ‘accent’ font, reworked mobile breakpoints) or just better (faster homepage cache loading, page transitions, AVIF for images1 and no more satsuma header background).

While I’m in salesman mode: I also added dark mode styling to the OMG! Ubuntu Chrome extension. The article list pop-over now uses dark mode when your system is in dark mode. That update rolled out on the Chrome Web Store this week.

Work isn’t done. If you’re especially keen-eyed you’ll see further refinements in the coming weeks. There are still a few rough edges to iron out and plan to revisit components, like the sidebar widgets, that haven’t changed in years.

I’m not generally one for talking about the site on the site. But I don’t use it in quite the same way you use do, so your feedback helps me know what’s working, what’s not and, if we’re honest, where I’ve made a typo.

  1. I don’t plan to go back and convert old images in old posts, or images in the archive. Newer posts may continue to have WebP images if I’m using something from the archive. If you have a website, AVIF is worth considering. The quality:size savings are impressive. Most of my WebP files go from ~400kb to <100kb, with no noticeable drop in quality (screenshots often have a lot of text, which can suffer most from compression). ↩︎

title: You won’t need Adobe or random sites to merge PDFs on Windows 11 soon,...
author: Mayank Parmar
summary: You don't have to pay Adobe if you just want to edit, extract, merge, or organize PDFs on Windows 11, thanks to Microsoft Edge.
content:
You don’t have to pay Adobe if you just want to edit, extract, merge, or organize PDFs on Windows 11, as Microsoft Edge is about to get one of its biggest updates.

Microsoft Edge is getting a built-in PDF merger alongside other new capabilities in January 2027, so you may no longer need to browse random websites to merge PDFs or buy Adobe Acrobat. Windows Latest understands it’s one of the biggest updates to Edge’s built-in PDF reader since Microsoft replaced its own solution with Adobe’s.

For those unaware, Microsoft maintained its own PDF engine for Edge, but in early 2023, it decided to ditch it in favour of the Adobe Acrobat PDF engine. It’s been more than three years since Edge started using Adobe’s engine, and Microsoft has mostly focused on migrating all of its legacy features to Adobe’s solution.

In fact, it still offered an “opt out” that allowed you to ditch Adobe and go back to Microsoft’s original PDF engine, but that toggle has now been removed with Edge 156.

That frees up Microsoft’s resources and will allow the company to once again focus on making Edge the preferred PDF reader on Windows 11, even if most people prefer Google Chrome for browsing the web. And if you’ve used Edge as a PDF reader, you’re not going to deny that it’s indeed far better than everything else available on Windows.

Right now, Edge’s PDF reader is mostly read-only, so you cannot reorganize pages or edit text, but you can highlight text, embed your own text, rotate the document, and do a few other things, like zoom in or out. I wouldn’t call it “editing,” but Edge still does a great job as a “viewer.” That could change soon.

Microsoft Edge will let you merge and organize PDFs

Microsoft quietly confirmed that it’ll let you organize and merge PDF files in Edge. You’ll be able to open a PDF in Edge, then open another PDF and merge both or select pages. You can also extract content from documents, even if they are scanned documents, and reorder pages as well.

“You can also merge the open PDF file with other PDF files that are open in Microsoft Edge tabs or stored on their device, to create a single PDF file,” Microsoft noted in a roadmap update spotted by Windows Latest.

The feature rolls out in January 2027, and Microsoft has told me that it’s not going to send your files or documents to Adobe’s cloud or any cloud for that matter.

“Files are processed on the device, and the original files aren’t modified,” the company noted, which means a fresh file would be created when you edit a PDF.

There’s also a new “notes” pane coming that will have all your ink notes, comments, highlights, and more in a single place. You can open a PDF, go to the pane, and revisit anything you’d like.

“Users can search and filter their annotations, jump to each one in the document, and edit, delete or add comments from the pane,” Microsoft noted in another roadmap update spotted by Windows Latest.

Edge for Windows and macOS will be getting all these new features.

Edge will also let you translate PDFs

Last but not least, you’ll also be able to translate all pages of PDF files in Microsoft Edge. Since it’s powered by Adobe’s solutions, I am expecting the browser to translate documents in up to 62 languages.

You might argue that Microsoft could have used Bing Translate, but I don’t think it would have been ideal for PDFs, particularly scanned PDFs, which is something Adobe can take better care of.

In any case, I am pumped that Edge’s built-in PDF reader, and soon editor, remains its best feature. But if you’re looking for something more powerful and free, I’d recommend using PDF Arranger, which is fully open source.

What do you use to open PDFs on Windows 11? Let me know in the comments below.

title: GitHub Universe 2026 Trip Report
author: Jorge O. Castro
summary: Bluefin was fortunate to get nominated for a "Ship and Tell" session at GitHub Universe.
content:
Bluefin was fortunate to get nominated for a "Ship and Tell" session at GitHub Universe.

A little while ago we had a thread in our discussions about the nightmare that is printing on Linux. What started as a joke turned into an actual thing that we built. It was such a cool story that Martin Woodward mentioned us in his closing keynote at Universe!

I've gotten feedback in the Discord from multiple people who have these working. We could really use more data/feedback/reports from those of you who have printers that need these drivers.

It was also a great event to spend time with Kyle Gospodnetich (co-creator of Bazzite). This gave us an opportunity to catch up on a bunch of things. Bazzite's build system just got reworked into a Python for a super clean design. It was exciting to hear Kyle talk about the new people that are coming on board. Just a week prior I had spent time with Cameron Knauff, the maintainer of StillOS. Same enery, the cloud native experts are starting to show up in larger numbers and everyone is accelerating.

We had a great 30+ minute discussion with Godot developers. Kyle spent a good deal of time explaining the Flatpak process to them, you love to see it.

We had some great sushi too:

Overall we had a great show, and it was awesome. I was inspired by the Home Assistant and AutoGPT developers as well, we have lots of experts to learn from! This was a bucket list event for me, we had to get nominated before even being submitted, it's very hard to get a talk here so it was great to be able to present your work in front of these developers!

A huge shoutout to GitHub for their direct support to Bluefin, it's not the first time!

title: Microsoft explains why Task Manager freezes right when you need it most on Windows...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Microsoft's own docs say Task Manager's ancestor ran at high priority to respond under any load, but Raymond Chen says priority can't help a thread stuck waiting on a lock, a slow network file or Wind...
content:
Windows 11’s Task Manager and taskbar can stop responding right when you need them to kill a runaway app. Microsoft engineer Raymond Chen says running them at high priority wouldn’t fix it, because a high-priority thread can still get stuck as it waits for a resource that another, slower thread is holding.

I have certainly experienced this when a game, or Chrome with too many tabs, or some heavy app maxes out my PC, and I desperately press Ctrl+Shift+Esc, hoping Task Manager could save the day to help me end the task, but instead, it takes forever to open or looks like it’s stuck.

Why Task Manager can freeze when your PC runs out of CPU time

Your CPU can only run so many threads at once, and Windows picks who goes next using priorities from 0 to 31. When a heavy app hogs the CPU, everything else waits, including Task Manager, which needs CPU time to draw its window, refresh the process list, and react to clicks.

“If a system becomes CPU-starved, all processes begin to suffer,” Chen wrote on October 27, 2026. “This includes the taskbar and Task Manager, even though they are often the tools you want to use to stop whatever it is that’s making your system suffer.”

Ironically, Microsoft’s documentation names the Task List, Task Manager’s ancestor, as an example of the high priority class, because it “must respond quickly when called by the user, regardless of the load on the operating system.” So why isn’t that enough?

Giving Task Manager higher priority wouldn’t fix the real problem

Priority only decides who gets the CPU first. It doesn’t let a thread skip a lock, file or other shared resource that another thread is already using. A thread waiting on a lock isn’t even in the queue for the CPU, so raising its priority does nothing until the lock is free.

Chen compares it to a supermarket. “Your priority checkout pass gets you to the front of the line, but if the person at the register has a large shopping cart full of groceries, you just have to wait until they are done before you get your chance.”

Windows does have a fix for one version of this, called priority inversion, where a high-priority thread waits on a low-priority one that can’t finish because other work keeps taking the CPU. According to Microsoft, a feature called AutoBoost raises the priority of the thread holding the resource “to the maximum priority of the waiter until it releases the resource.”

But a faster cashier doesn’t help if the cart is full. Chen says you are “still stuck waiting” if the owning thread is busy with slow work, “like, say, accessing a file over the network.” No amount of CPU priority makes a slow network respond faster.

Windows already prioritizes the app you’re using, but that has limits

Windows already favors the app in front of you. Microsoft’s Priority Boosts documentation says the foreground app’s priority class is raised to at least the level of any background process, and when a window gets keyboard or mouse input, “the scheduler boosts the priority of the thread that owns the window.” In-focus apps also get High Quality of Service, while apps that aren’t visible drop to Low and, on battery, can be moved to power-efficient cores.

“So if you can get focus onto the taskbar or Task Manager, you are doing about as well as you can,” Chen says.

The caveat is UI code. “For UI code, this problem is particularly acute because you will eventually have to call into the UI system, and now you’re duking it out with all the other UI threads in the system,” he explains. Task Manager can get its turn on the CPU and still have to wait for parts of Windows that every other app is hammering.

One reader under Chen’s post said big builds make the taskbar nearly unusable, and raising Task Manager’s priority helped only slightly.

Why Microsoft can’t make Task Manager unbeatable

“The problem is that it’s hard to fix a runaway system from within that same system,” Chen wrote. Task Manager runs on the Windows it’s trying to rescue, and the tools you’d use “may already have been compromised.”

He made a similar point back in 2010, when someone suggested running Task Manager at real-time priority. Running it at real-time “won’t help, and it would be wrong,” Chen said, because “nothing in the user interface runs with real-time priority,” including the thread that processes your keyboard and mouse input.

Just to clarify, Chen isn’t describing a new Windows 11 bug. Taskbar freezes can also come from explorer.exe reliability issues, and Task Manager had an insane bug last year that left multiple copies running in the background.

What you can do when Task Manager or the taskbar stops responding

If Task Manager won’t open, press Ctrl+Alt+Delete. The security screen runs on its own secure desktop and lets you open Task Manager, sign out, or restart, though it can lag too when Windows is badly stuck.

Remember to turn on End task in the taskbar from Settings > System > Advanced. For a single frozen app, just right-click the app’s icon and press End task to kill it without opening Task Manager.

In my opinion, instead of finding a way to make Task Manager responsive in situations where the CPU gets maxed out, I would be more impressed to see Windows not freezing an app just because it’s too much for the PC to handle. A warning sign about the load, which prevents the app from freezing by pausing it, would be a better way to handle such situations.

title: Microsoft killed Windows 10 to push Windows 11, but Windows sales crashed 27% as holdouts still refuse to switch
author: Windows Latest
content:
Microsoft’s Windows OEM revenue fell 27% in the July to September 2026 quarter, and Microsoft says it was “driven by the Windows 10 end of support demand in the prior year, inventory drawdowns by OEM and channel partners, and weaker PC market demand.” As it turns out, the people who rushed to buy PCs before Windows 10 support ended last year don’t have a reason anymore to upgrade…

Meanwhile, a big chunk of PC users still hasn’t moved on. In September 2026, nearly a year after Windows 10 support ended, Steam’s hardware survey shows Windows 11 at 71.34% with 0.37% growth, while Windows 10 had 0.71% growth and 23.61% market share.

Windows OEM revenue fell 27% as Windows 10’s upgrade boom faded

During the FY27 Q1 earnings call on October 28, CFO Amy Hood said Windows OEM revenue “was below expectations” and fell 27%, or 28% in constant currency. “Inventory levels remain elevated,” she added.

Windows OEM revenue is what Microsoft earns from PC makers like HP, Dell and Lenovo for preinstalling Windows. It’s part of a larger category, Windows OEM and Devices, which also includes Surface. Revenue in that category fell 22% from $4.55 billion to $3.55 billion, according to Microsoft’s earnings release. Microsoft doesn’t share revenue from only Windows 11, which I feel is odd.

Anyway, what I find interesting is how the inventory story flipped so quickly. Back in July, Hood said Windows results were “ahead of expectations as OEM and channel partners continue to build inventory.” Three months later, these partners are selling through that stock and buying fewer Windows licenses.

Ironically, Bing and Edge did just fine. Search advertising revenue grew 12%, helped by “higher volume and rate across LinkedIn, Edge, and Bing.” This comes as Microsoft is reducing Bing’s presence in Windows!

Windows 10’s end of support sold a lot of Windows 11 PCs in 2025

If you look at it from another angle, the 27% drop looks so bad because the comparison is with a quarter when businesses and consumers were rushing to replace Windows 10 PCs.

In the third quarter of 2025, global PC shipments grew 8.2% to nearly 70 million units. “Worldwide PC shipments were driven by the Windows 10 end-of-support (EOS) refresh cycle in most regions,” Gartner’s Rishi Padhi said at the time. By the end of 2025, shipments grew 9.1% for the year, with fourth-quarter demand “fueled by the Windows 11 upgrade cycle,” according to Gartner.

PC makers weren’t hiding the facts. In August 2025, Dell COO Jeff Clarke said he expected growth “driven by an aging installed base and the Windows 10 end of life.” Microsoft admitted in July that it was up against “a high prior-year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support,” which is why we said Windows 10’s end of support was the real Windows 11 sales driver.

Unfortunately for Microsoft and its partners, a deadline only works once. Many people who needed a new PC bought one before October 2025, and they’re not buying another one a year later.

Windows 10 holdouts still aren’t switching

The rest are holding on (I personally know a few). Lansweeper found that Windows 10 still ran on 16.9% of Windows PCs it tracked in July 2026, and 21.4% in small and mid-sized businesses. I understand the conflicting numbers can be confusing, but tracking OS market share can only go so far. However, the interesting bit is that, from the numbers Lansweeper found, only about 2.8% of those PCs can’t run Windows 11, so most of them could upgrade if their owners wanted to.

HP’s CFO Karen Parkhill said in May that “roughly 30% of the installed base” is still on Windows 10. Microsoft didn’t help its case either, when the company extended free consumer security updates for Windows 10 to October 12, 2027. “We understand that moving to a new PC can take time,” Microsoft said.

Then there’s the giant elephant in the room: buying a new PC is now insanely expensive thanks to the memory shortage. Counterpoint says global PC shipments fell 21% in Q3 2026, blaming higher prices for RAM, SSDs and processors, along with a Q3 2025 that was boosted by Windows 10’s deadline. It’s not a secret anymore now that all major industry analysts confirmed the effect of Windows 10’s end of service on Windows 11 PC sales.

To be clear, Microsoft didn’t say that Windows 10 holdouts caused the 27% drop. But as long as they stay put, the software giant can’t count on another wave of Windows 11 upgrades, especially as Copilot+ PC branding didn’t do much to drive sales.

Microsoft expects Windows revenue to fall even further

For the October to December quarter, Microsoft expects Windows OEM and Devices revenue to “decline in the mid-thirties.” Hood said, “Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand, and a prior-year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support,” adding, “We expect these trends to continue through the rest of this fiscal year.”

Three months ago, Microsoft expected a decline “in the high teens” for the full fiscal year. Now, it’s guiding for a drop roughly twice as steep in a single quarter.

The seemingly stoic Satya Nadella talked about “making every PC a secure agent box” that runs AI models locally on new chips from AMD, Intel, Qualcomm and NVIDIA. On the call, he also said, “We think of Copilot as the new OS for work.” I’m not sure Windows fans will love hearing that from the company that makes Windows.

Meanwhile, IDC believes Apple’s $599 MacBook Neo is “putting real pressure on the entire PC ecosystem,” and is continuing to do so. Apple also launched the new Touch enabled MacBook Pro, giving another reason for Windows 10 holdouts to switch to the other side. Not a good sign for the Windows PC ecosystem!

Windows 11 needs a reason to upgrade that isn’t a deadline

Windows 11 has to sell itself on being fast and reliable, which is why fixes like the faster right-click menu in KB5127936 do more for Windows than any AI or agentic capabilities in the OS.

If Microsoft wants the remaining Windows 10 users to upgrade, it has to give them a reason to want Windows 11, and my top picks would be better privacy, no ads and recommendations, faster and cleaner.

title: Ghostty 1.4 brings big Linux improvements
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
A major new release of Ghostty, the open-source terminal emulator, is out.

Ghostty 1.4.0 brings a varied set of changes after seven months of development. There are welcome performance optimisations on Linux and macOS, a more capable SSH implementation and an easier way to rearrange tab splits – dragging them!

This update to the Zig-based app offers complete Kitty graphics protocol support (including animation and relative placements) – the first terminal besides Kitty to do so. If you use TUI tools or script to render images in the terminal, this is a major feat.

Devs say performance is improved hugely with this update. Notably, Ghostty 1.4.0 now compresses off-screen scrollback when the terminal is idle. This lowers the amount of physical RAM used by text-heavy histories by up to 90%.

Content is decompressed if you scroll back or you make use of the text search feature that was added in the Ghostty 1.3.0 update earlier this year.

On Linux, Ghostty’s GTK app renders text sharply at fractional display scales such as 125% and 150%, which should resolve oft-mentioned issues with blurry text.

The update also replaces GtkGLArea with an EGL rendering pipeline that runs on a separate thread and passes frames to GTK using DMA-BUFs. This requires a system EGL library; if a GPU can’t export DMA-BUFs, slower CPU-based copying is used.

And terminal splits in the GTK build can be rearranged using drag. When a tab has two or more splits, each split has a drag handle that can be grabbed and the split dragged and dropped onto another split.

Other changes include:

  • Standalone SSH wrapper
  • Better terminal emulation accuracy
  • Kitty clipboard protocol implemented
  • Misc performance improvements across platforms

Linux changes of note:

  • Desktop notifications dismiss if the terminal is focused or closed
  • Noto emoji font update so newer ZWJ sequences render as one glyph
  • Dolphin’s ‘Open Ghostty Here’ opens new window in running instance
  • Split resizing no longer flickers and can no longer be made too small
  • Mouse cursor keeps its text shape while selecting text
  • Command palette uses terminal colours if window-theme = ghostty
  • URLs now open through the XDG desktop portal

And configuration options on GTK builds include gtk-horizontal-tab-scroll, which can be set to false to disable two-finger scrolling from changing tabs, and gtk-tabs-inverted, to move the close button to the start of each tab.

Install Ghostty 1.4.0

Ubuntu 26.10 includes Ghostty in the repos, putting it an apt install ghostty away. But, that won’t get you the newest version. For the changes mentioned above, you’ll need to use an alternative method.

Plenty are available.

You can install Ghostty on Ubuntu using an unofficial community-maintained Ghostty DEB (and that has its own Ghostty PPA for easy updates). There’s also a Ghostty AppImage, and an unofficial Snap.

On macOS, Ghostty provides official binaries (recommended; supports in-app updating), and it’s also available via Homebrew and other CLI package managers.

Ghostty drops support for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS

As Ghostty 1.4.0 requires GTK 4.18 and libadwaita 1.7, per the terminal’s GTK/Adwaita version policy, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS no longer meets the requirements. This means a DEB version of Ghostty (e.g. from the PPA above) can no longer be installed.

As an aside, the underlying libghostty terminal emulation library will be powering terminals in future versions of JetBrains’ IDEs. Linux Mint’s new terminal app, Velocitty, doesn’t use that, but its design is said to have been inspired by Ghostty.

title: Ubuntu Core Desktop ‘accelerating’ development ahead of 27.04
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Canonical has announced it’s ‘accelerating’ development of Ubuntu Core Desktop, its immutable, snap-based version of its desktop OS.

Ubuntu Core Desktop was announced in 2023 and made available in preview for enthusiasts to try. But a lack of of obvious progress and direction (not to mention up-to-date builds) had left many wondering if Canonical was running cool on the idea.

Now, things are finally kicking up a gear, says Jon Seager, VP of Engineering at Canonical.

A newly-formed Ubuntu Core Desktop team within the company will work on bringing Ubuntu Core Desktop into shape, with builds available ahead of the 27.04 release next year. Seager says the classic, Deb-based Ubuntu desktop is not going away.

Ahead of Ubuntu 27.04, which will begin offering daily builds of Ubuntu Core Desktop, three use-cases will be worked towards:

  • Browser-based workflows
  • Developer workstations
  • Gaming systems

Don’t expect miracles too soon.

Creating all-Snap Ubuntu experience is on-par with a classic Deb-based desktop will not be trivial. For one, the entire desktop stack needs to be made into a snap that’s modular so that parts can be replaced (the KDE Plasma desktop will be available too).

There’s also an “app gap” problem. A swathe of popular Linux software folks rely on for their day-to-day computing isn’t available on the Snap Store – officially, or is, but not all features work, and so on.

It’s not as simple as “make snap versions” other, as developer in particular will want access to alternative packaging systems, even Flatpak, that virtualisation and containerisation will need to account for – in a way users aren’t bewildered by.

Plus, the rest of the things that a standard desktop build offers that a sandboxed, immutable desktop shouldn’t.

Simply, a lot of technical challenges are in the way – but some call that the fun part!

Ubuntu Core Desktop default?

Seager says the long-term ambition is to make Ubuntu Core (and snaps, to an extent) the “de facto target for Linux applications and workflows, and the default Ubuntu experience on the desktop, in the data centre and at the edge”.

Ubuntu Core Desktop will offer a “safer, more resilient, more trustworthy and future-proof Ubuntu”, Seager says, that users will “have a blast using”.

Me? I’m glad there’ll be another Ubuntu development cycle with plenty of hashtagcontent to cover.

To keep tabs on all that in the coming months, why not bookmark this site, stick it in your RSS feed reader or follow us over on social media – let’s have a blast together.

title: Windows 11’s faster, customizable right-click menu released, enable it right now using these steps
author: Abhijith M B
summary: I tested the new File Explorer context menu on my daily PC, and it opens instantly with just eight items by default. Settings now let you add Print, Send to and Copy as path, move Ask Copilot or Clipc...
content:
Windows 11’s redesigned right-click menu is now rolling out to everyone with the October 2026 optional update, KB5127936. I installed it on my daily-driver PC, and as expected, the new context menu opens instantly. For all the unwelcome app extensions, you can also pick which among them show up when you right-click a file. Options like Send to, Print, and the legacy menu can all be customized from a new Context menu Settings page.

However, Microsoft is rolling it out gradually, so installing the update doesn’t mean you’ll see the new menu right away. Fortunately, ViVeTool can turn it on in a couple of minutes, and we’ll tell you how to enable the new right-click menu.

How to enable the new Windows 11 right-click menu

Step 1 – Install KB5127936

Open Settings > Windows Update and click Check for updates. If KB5127936 doesn’t show up, turn on “Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available” and check again. Install the 2026-10 Preview Update (KB5127936) and restart your PC. Run winver to make sure you’re on Build 26200.9818 or 26300.9818.

Step 2 – Check if you already have it

Right-click any file in File Explorer. If you see “Customize menu” at the bottom, consider yourself lucky, and you don’t need ViVeTool. If you didn’t get it, like the rest of us, follow the steps below:

Step 3 – Download ViVeTool

If you still see the old menu, download ViVeTool from its official GitHub page. Pick ViVeTool-v0.3.4-IntelAmd.zip for Intel and AMD PCs, or ViVeTool-v0.3.4-SnapdragonArm64.zip for Snapdragon PCs. Extract the zip to a folder named ViVeTool in your C drive, so that ViVeTool.exe is in C:\ViVeTool.

Step 4 – Run the command

Right-click the Start button, open Terminal (Admin), and run these two commands one after the other.

cd C:\ViVeTool

vivetool /enable /id:60813048

You should see “Successfully set feature configuration(s).” Restart your PC and right-click a file again.

Step 5 – Try the other IDs if it doesn’t show up

Some PCs need a second ID. Run this command and restart.

vivetool /enable /id:49453572,60813048

If that still doesn’t work, there’s a third ID for some builds.

vivetool /enable /id:49453572,60813048,61934903

On my PC, 60813048 was enough. Before that, I tried 61456288, which is intended for the redesigned Temporary files page in Settings.

If you want to undo the change, run the command again with /disable in place of /enable. Do keep in mind that ViVeTool turns on features Microsoft hasn’t rolled out to your PC yet, so use it at your own discretion.

Windows 11’s new context menu is rolling out with KB5127936

KB5127936 was released on October 28 for Windows 11 25H2 (Build 26200.9818) and 26H2 (Build 26300.9818). In the release notes, Microsoft says the new menu “opens more quickly, reduces clutter, and gives you more control over the commands and app extensions that appear when you right-click.”

Back in August, Microsoft admitted that the Windows 11 menu “became cluttered and sluggish,” after years of extensions like Ask Copilot and Edit with Clipchamp loading late and making you click the wrong item. Its first attempt at a fix, a Manage file submenu for less-used actions, only made the menu a few lines shorter.

The new menu has a “Customize menu” button at the bottom, which opens Settings > Personalization > Context menu. According to Microsoft, “No action is required to use the default configuration,” and if you still wish to see the old Windows 10-style menu, just hold down Shift and right-click on your desktop or the file.

I tested Windows 11’s new right-click menu, and it’s finally fast

When I first tested the new menu in August, it was on an Insider build which I ran on an underpowered VM with 4GB RAM. For this test, I’m using my daily PC, where even apps like Google’s Quick Share add their own right-click options.

Before the update, right-clicking an image gave me 20 items below the Cut, Copy, Rename, Share, and Delete icons. Among them were AI actions, Send to My Phone, Share with, Rotate right, Rotate left, and Copy as path, plus seven app extensions (Send with Quick Share, Ask Copilot, Edit with Clipchamp, Edit in Notepad, Edit with Paint, Edit with Photos, and Add to Share hub) and Show more options. This was insanity, and I don’t even use most of these.

The old menu took a good one to two seconds to settle. In my screen recording, it first shows up with AI actions greyed out and the icons missing, and the app extensions are clearly what made it jittery.

The new default menu for that image has just eight items, which are Open, Open with, Compress to, Set as desktop background, Add to Favorites, Properties, App extensions, and Customize menu. All seven app extensions moved to the App extensions submenu, with a new Manage extensions option. AI actions, Send to My Phone, and Share with are gone from the default menu.

And it’s instant. In my recording, the menu shows up fully loaded in the first frame. Since the app extensions only load when I open the submenu, they can’t slow down the main menu anymore.

Every setting you can customize in the new context menu

Settings > Personalization > Context menu has three sections, and Microsoft notes that “Only relevant items will be displayed,” based on the file you right-click.

File actions

  • Send to adds the Send to submenu. I don’t use this and kept it disabled.
  • Print adds Print (of course), which is handy for documents and images, but most of us may not need this anyway.
  • Create shortcut adds an option to create a shortcut to the file, which I kept disabled.
  • Copy as path copies the file’s full path, and I know power users who use it often, but I later disabled it.
  • Rotate image adds Rotate left and Rotate right, but this option shows up in the ribbon when we select an image, so I kept this too disabled.

App extensions

Microsoft describes this as “Choose which app extensions appear in the main context menu instead of in a submenu.” On my PC, there are toggles for Send with Quick Share (shown as “Context menu” in the screenshot below, which is a bug), Copilot, Microsoft Clipchamp, Notepad, OneDrive, Paint, Photos, Smart Connect (courtesy of Motorola), and Terminal. Your list will change based on the apps you’ve installed.

Turning on an extension moves it to the main menu. Ask Copilot showed up above App extensions by default, while the rest were in the submenu. It’s fine, though, as I can turn it off easily, and I did. Kudos for not having Copilot in the Context menu!

The “Show app extensions submenu” toggle is interesting, and shows just how customizable Windows can be. When it’s on, extensions that aren’t in the main menu appear in the submenu. When it’s off, they don’t appear in the context menu. So, if you don’t want Ask Copilot, Clipchamp, or any other extension when you right-click, keep their toggles off and turn off the submenu.

Additional options

  • Arrange primary actions inline replaces the row of icons with Cut, Copy, Paste, Rename, Share, and Delete as regular menu items, in a vertical way, which was how Windows 10 did it.
  • Keep cloud storage actions in their own section shows OneDrive and other cloud storage actions in a separate section, but only in folders managed by that provider. When it’s off, they show up with other app extensions.
  • Show more options brings back the legacy Windows 10-era menu entry. Microsoft’s Marcus Ash said it’s “off by default” and “can be turned on in settings if a user has legacy extensions.” If you use old apps like 7-Zip that only show up in the legacy menu, turn it on. Otherwise, there’s no reason to.
  • Move Properties to the bottom of the context menu puts Properties last, like in Windows 10. If you combine it with inline actions, the menu feels a lot like Windows 10, with a modern look.

Windows 11’s right-click menu is finally something you can make your own

Along with the faster File Explorer launch from June, Microsoft has now fixed the two things that made right-clicking in Windows 11 annoying: the frustrating delay and the annoying clutter. The fact that you don’t need registry hacks or third-party apps to clean things like Copilot and Clipchamp is definitely a win in my books.

There’s nothing to complain about here. If the new menu isn’t on your PC yet, ViVeTool is there for you. Note that if you skip the Optional update, your PC will still get this new context menu in the mandatory November 2026 update.

title: Tim Cook compared touchscreen Windows laptops to a toaster-fridge, now Apple is selling one...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Five years ago, John Ternus said the Mac was built for indirect input and Apple had no reason to change. Now, as Apple's CEO, he is selling a touchscreen MacBook Pro using a classic pre-emptive claim,...
content:
Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is the first Mac with a touchscreen, and Apple is pitching tapping, scrolling, and pinching to zoom as “a whole new way to interact with your work.” Windows laptops have supported these gestures since Windows 7 in 2009, while Apple executives spent the next decade and a half explaining why touch didn’t belong on a Mac, including John Ternus, who now runs the company.

Ternus defended the Mac’s touch-free design five years ago to the day. Now, he says, “You’ve gotta touch it to believe it.”

Really? I mean, I’ve been believing since 2012…

Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro ad explains touch like it’s 2007

Apple’s announcement on October 28, 2026 calls it “Touch for the first time on Mac,” and the launch video’s description tells you the display is so good that “you’ll want to reach out and touch it. And now, you can. Tap, swipe, scroll, and pinch to zoom directly on your screen.”

The product page is hilariously explaining each gesture as if we haven’t seen touchscreen laptops before. Scroll is “Move through content by sliding your finger across it.” Zoom is “Pinch to zoom in on photos, documents, web pages, and more.” The section is titled “Magic on tap.” There’s nothing magical here, Apple!

Apple also says the touch sensor is “built directly into the display panel” and “not layered on top of it,” which reduces latency. Samsung Display announced OLED laptop panels with touch sensors built into the panel in January 2023, and offered them to other laptop brands. Again, not a new technology.

That said, the display is excellent. The tandem OLED panel hits 2,000 nits peak brightness with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and the MacBook Pro got lighter and thinner while adding touch. It’s great, but what’s not is the way Apple tries to sell them.

Apple is using a marketing trick from decades ago

SPOILER ALERT: In the very first episode of Mad Men, Lucky Strike’s owners explain how their tobacco is grown, cured, and toasted. Don Draper stops them at “toasted,” because that’s the ad. Everyone else’s tobacco is poisonous, but Lucky Strike’s is toasted (as if that makes it less poisonous!)

The funny thing is that heating tobacco was common practice across cigarette makers. Advertisers call this a preemptive claim, where a brand talks about a common feature first, so it starts to look like its own. Claude Hopkins did it over a century ago, selling Schlitz beer in sterilized bottles that other breweries also used, and “It’s toasted” was a real Lucky Strike slogan from 1917.

Apologies for the mention of old Cigarette and Alcohol ads, but there’s a reason why those sold in millions, and Cupertino is planning the same.

Apple is doing this with touch. For a Mac user who hasn’t used a touchscreen laptop, it’s toasted.

Apple executives said touchscreen Macs were a bad idea for 16 years

Steve Jobs said in 2010 that “touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” and that “your arm wants to fall off.” Of course, Jobs couldn’t have been more wrong here.

Last week, as Apple prepared to launch the touchscreen MacBook Pro, ex-Windows boss Steven Sinofsky didn’t let the double standards slide, as he mocked the naysayers who suddenly changed stands.

When an analyst asked whether Apple would merge tablets and laptops like Microsoft was doing with Windows 8, Tim Cook said in April 2012, “You can converge a toaster and a refrigerator, but those aren’t going to be pleasing to the user.”

Apple’s software chief Craig Federighi told CNET in 2014 that the “Mac is sort of a sit-down experience,” and that Apple “experimented with all the technology, but we found it just wasn’t good.” In 2016, he said, “Grafting touch onto something that was fundamentally designed around a precise pointer really compromises the experience,” while Phil Schiller said about touch and pointer input, “You can’t optimize for both.”

By 2018, Federighi was calling touchscreen laptops “experiments,” and said “lifting your arm up to poke a screen is a pretty fatiguing thing to do.”

Then, in October 2021, Ternus, who was Apple’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal, “We make the world’s best touch computer on an iPad. It’s totally optimized for that. And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.”

John Ternus now says touch on a Mac is “comfortable and handy”

When WIRED’s Steven Levy asked Ternus whether Apple was breaking its touchscreen taboo, his answer was, “Who knew?”

“The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch,” Ternus said. He added that Apple “needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way.”

While on the new CEO, let’s not forget the old one’s new vision. Tim Cook tweeted: “We brought Touch to the Mac!” Sure, you have. It’s been here all along.

Marketing chief Greg Joswiak said, “There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.” Of course they do. They grew up on iPhones and iPads, and many of them on Windows laptops with touchscreens!

So, what changed, the technology or Apple’s priorities? According to Bloomberg, Apple hopes premium features will help it charge more, and the touch MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. Well, the technology matured in the past decade…

Microsoft sold this idea with Windows 8 and Surface years ago

Windows 8 built its whole interface around touch in 2012, and Microsoft followed it with the Surface Pro. At the Surface Pro 4 launch in October 2015, a CAD model of a toaster-fridge showed up in Panos Panay‘s demo, a dig at Cook’s comment.

Today, touch is so ordinary on Windows that Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra announcement mentions its “PixelSense Ultra touchscreen” once, in passing. Add the flips, 2-in-1s and detachables from every major OEM, and Windows hardware is miles ahead in form factors.

As someone who once promised himself he’d buy a Surface Studio after watching its launch video, I’m sad Microsoft didn’t double down on hardware. And Apple is still ahead where Windows OEMs keep cutting corners, with six speakers with force-cancelling woofers and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR.

Windows laptops had touch first, but that won’t stop Apple from making it look new. What Windows OEMs can do is fix their speakers and webcams (and build quality in general), because touch no longer sets them apart from a MacBook.
