title: Windows 11 KB5127936 out with big changes, direct download links for offline installer (.msu)
author: Mayank Parmar
summary: Windows 11 KB5127936 lets you customize the context menu, which means you can now choose what appears when you right-click anywhere.
content:
Windows 11 KB5127936 is rolling out, and it FINALLY lets you customize the context menu, which means you can now choose what appears when you right-click anywhere. Microsoft has published direct download links for the KB5127936 offline installer (.msu), but in most cases, you should use Windows Update.

KB5127936 is an optional update, and it won’t download or install automatically on PCs where the toggle “Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available” is turned off. This update is listed as “2026-10 Preview Update (KB5127936) (26300.9818)” on PCs with Windows 11 26H2.

In case you’re on version 25H2, you’ll see Build 26200.9818, but the KB ID won’t change. Also, if you’re still on Windows 11 24H2, you won’t be getting today’s optional update or any updates going forward, as the OS version reached end of support on October 13. You should verify your Windows version under Settings > System > About.

Note: If you do not install an optional update like the one rolling out today, you do not miss out on anything.

Optional updates are considered “production quality” despite the “preview” label (not to be confused with the Windows Insider Program), but you don’t have to rush installation, as everything included in Windows 11 Build 26300.9818 will roll out to everyone on November 10, as part of Patch Tuesday.

Download links for Windows 11 KB5127936

Windows 11 KB5127936 direct download links: 64-bit and ARM64 | As with all updates, you again have the opportunity to use the Microsoft Update Catalog to download offline installers for today’s update and update multiple PCs with or without an internet connection.

I personally recommend Update Catalog only when Windows Update is not working.

The size of the update is usually under 2GB if you use Windows Update, but if you use Update Catalog and manually download offline installers, you’ll be downloading a whopping 5GB .msu installer. Windows 10 updates used to be less than 700MB via Update Catalog, but as Microsoft bundles AI models, even for unsupported PCs, the download size is higher.

Build number Size OS version Architecture
26300.9818 5180.8 MB Windows 11 26H2 x64-based
26300.9818 4973.5 MB Windows 11 26H2 arm64-based
26200.9818 5180.8 MB Windows 11 25H2 x64-based
26200.9818 4973.5 MB Windows 11 25H2 arm64-based

Today’s update is a cumulative release, so it comes bundled with all previous changes, including those that rolled out in August 2026. That means if you skipped or paused updates, you can unpause them and get all the changes in a single update.

What’s new in Windows 11 Build 26300.9818 (26H2) / Build 26200.9818 (25H2)?

Windows 11 Build 26300.9818’s changelog is not huge, but I think there are quite a few notable changes, and my personal favourite is the ability to customize the right-click menu. However, like every monthly update, you’re not getting everything out of the box, as changes roll out gradually.

Microsoft confirmed that the new context menu is also rolling out gradually and won’t show up on all PCs. You can consider turning on the “Get the latest updates…” toggle on the Windows Update page to increase your chances. But don’t expect most of these improvements to show up after applying today’s update.

1. The context menu can now be customized in Windows 11

Microsoft previously confirmed that it sees the Windows context menu, commonly known as the right-click menu, as “cluttered and sluggish,” and it also admitted that Windows 11 failed to address Windows 10’s context menu problems. In fact, Windows 11 made it worse, but it’s finally getting a big update.

With Windows 11 KB5127936, you can now choose what appears when you right-click a file. I installed today’s update and right-clicked on an image in the Downloads folder, and the context menu looks decluttered straight out of the box:

There’s a new “Customize menu” option in the right-click menu. If you click Customize menu, you will be taken to a new page in Windows Settings > Personalization.

From here, you can choose to turn on or off options like Send to, Print, Create shortcut, Copy as path, and Rotate image. For example, if you don’t want Print, Send to, Create shortcut, or Rotate options to show, you can toggle them off as I did:

You also have other customization controls, such as the ability to show “cut, copy, paste, rename, share, and delete” inline in the menu, which could make the context menu a bit wider, but shorter at the same time. Finally, you can even enable the “legacy context menu,” so it appears right away without you having to hold Shift and right-click.

Now, if you look closely, there’s another feature called “App extensions,” which lets you manage extensions like “Open in Paint” or “Edit in Notepad.” You can choose what appears from third-party apps or first-party apps when you right-click. You can hide anything, including the Notepad option for .txt files:

Finally, if you turn on the “Show app extensions submenu” toggle, all extensions like “Notepad,” “Paint,” “Photos,” and any third-party app will appear inside a new menu called “App extensions.” Here’s what it looks like after I turned on the feature, with all the options now clubbed in a new submenu:

And this change won’t break legacy apps, so if you right-click and go to the legacy menu, you can still access apps like 7-Zip:

Last but not least, after installing Windows 11 KB5127936, you will also notice that the right-click menu now opens much faster:

Microsoft told Windows Latest that making Windows 11 more customizable is one of its top priorities, and a customizable context menu is a step in the right direction. But it’s not the only customization improvement that landed this year.

Microsoft now also lets you customize the Start menu and choose what appears, so you can have just the “Pinned” section if you prefer, or only “All apps,” letting go of the “Recommended/Recent” section entirely.

2. File Explorer is getting better

Microsoft says it’s making the search results page more “consistent,” whether you launch a search from a specific volume, This PC, or Home. Regardless of where you begin searching in File Explorer, information like the date, location, or name will appear in a better layout. It looks less of a mess compared to what we have now.

There’s another notable improvement, and it’s to the squiggly keyboard key, ~, which didn’t have much of a use on Windows. Now, after you install Windows 11 KB5127936, you can open File Explorer, click on the address bar, and use ~ to go to your profile folder or its subfolders, including the famous AppData.

That means you can now use ~\AppData in File Explorer or Windows Run to quickly open this particular location. Last but not least, today’s update begins rolling out dark mode support for the Folder Options dialog in File Explorer!

However, we’re not seeing signs of the modern Properties sheet with WinUI and dark mode yet, as the feature still appears to be under development.

title: Windows 11’s “Restart now” button is a trap if updates are still installing, and...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Microsoft's Jen Gentleman and Aria Hanson say the Restart now button that appears mid-install is meant for people who want a ready update applied right away. But users have complained about it on Micr...
content:
Windows 11’s Windows Update page can show a “Restart now” button while the monthly security update is still installing. Microsoft says the button is there on purpose, for people who want to restart as soon as a specific update is ready, but they’re now looking at changing the experience after a Microsoft MVP said he keeps falling for it, and it keeps happening to others too.

If you click Restart now too early, your PC still has to finish the remaining installation, and depending on what’s pending, you may need another restart later, which takes even more time!

Windows 11 asks you to restart even with the security update at 2%

Nathan McNulty, a security solutions architect and Microsoft MVP, posted on X: “The number of times I’ve clicked Restart Now thinking updates were finished while updates were still installing… I don’t understand why we can’t grey that option out while updates are in progress.”

In the screenshot he shared, the October 2026 Security Update (KB5127648) shows “Installing – 2%,” while a .NET Framework update and an audio driver update are at “Pending restart.” Above them, Windows Update says “Restart required (estimate: 6 min),” with a big blue Restart now button, tantalizing enough to make users want to click it.

That said, the problem isn’t new. In December 2020, a Windows 10 user on Microsoft’s forum asked why “Restart now” appeared while cumulative updates were still installing, and later noticed it happened after the .NET update finished first. “Apparently no one from Microsoft wants to respond to this,” he wrote. More than 30 people upvoted they had that question too.

Almost six years later, Microsoft has finally explained why.

Microsoft says some people want to restart before everything installs

Microsoft’s Jen Gentleman explained under McNulty’s post, “Some of the updates are ready, if you wanted to restart immediately to install them.”

Aria Hanson, a Principal Group Product Manager working on Windows management, including Windows Autopatch and Intune, added that some people, and certain test cases, do want that. According to Hanson, most people who open the Windows Update settings page are advanced users, or open it from a notification, which only shows up after everything installs. Microsoft MVP James Robinson made a similar point in the thread.

But AskWoody publisher Susan Bradley pointed out that .NET updates “sometimes indicate that it’s ready to reboot and the main Windows patch is still coming,” and McNulty’s screenshot shows the .NET update doing that.

Since July 28, 2026, Microsoft has been holding .NET, driver and firmware updates on personal PCs so they install with the monthly security update and share one restart. So, it’s no surprise to see them waiting at “Pending restart” next to a cumulative update that’s still installing.

Microsoft is looking at changing the Restart now experience

In a reply to McNulty, which we spotted on X, Hanson said Microsoft is already looking at it.

“Appreciate the feedback, we’re looking at changing this to better enable the users on both sides (restart ASAP since the thing I care about is ready / don’t restart till everything is installed). In either case, we will not notify you about restarting till everything installs. :)”

To be clear, Microsoft hasn’t shared how the new experience will look or when it will roll out, only that it wants to keep the early restart for people who need it.

“Love to hear it,” McNulty replied. “Promise I’m not complaining, just flustered every time I restart before it was ready.” And it’s not just McNulty. The replies that came under his post is proof. Of course, for someone like me, who waits for Windows updates and watches the percentage rising, this is a non-issue.

One early click can mean a long wait or a second restart

In a follow-up to his original post, McNulty asked, “why would I want to reboot after checking for updates and in the middle of the big update still applying?” He said it’s easy to do “when you bounce between lots of windows,” which, as someone who checks for updates and goes right back to writing, I can relate to.

Joel Coehoorn (also a Microsoft MVP) noted that the big monthly cumulative update is usually the one still in progress, and when you restart, it has to finish before the PC is ready again, leaving you with an unusable machine “for sometimes > 1/2 hour.” Adam Juelich, who is an IT Professional with experience in Microsoft Intune, added that “Now you may end up with two reboots,” and Stephen Morning (also an IT Professional) said the restart icon in the system tray also shows up early.

Windows Update needs to show what’s still installing

I replied to McNulty’s original post suggesting a different color, like orange, while updates are still installing, and blue only when everything is at “Pending restart.”

McNulty’s idea is even simpler. Windows could show “Installing updates” and move “Restart anyway” to the dropdown, which, by the way, is already right next to the Restart now button.

Ironically, Microsoft has spent 2026 giving us more control over Windows Update. You can now pause updates for as long as you want, shut down or restart without installing pending updates, and Microsoft has explained why some updates take longer to install even after a quick download.

But control only helps if Windows tells you what’s happening. Until Microsoft brings the change, expand the list of updates before you click Restart now, and make sure nothing says “Installing.”

title: Ubuntu plans firmware HWE to prevent issues on older kernels
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Ubuntu is planning a new linux-firmware-hwe package, in an effort to reduce the risk of firmware updates for newer kernels causing problems for users running older ones.

On Ubuntu long-term support (LTS) releases, you can stick with the standard (GA) kernel it was released with for the duration of its support period, or you can install the HWE update, which brings newer Linux kernel versions to existing Ubuntu LTS releases. 

Right now, both kernels share the same firmware package, which means firmware updates designed to work with HWE kernels can cause problems for users who stick with the GA kernel.

Ubuntu developer Juerg Haefliger noted that a firmware backport for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, intended for its Linux 7.0 HWE kernel, introduced two AMD regressions for users running the Linux 6.9 GA kernel.

Thus, a new approach is needed.

The plan, laid out by Haefliger, is for HWE kernels to use a linux-firmware-hwe package, which pulls in HWE versions of existing firmware subpackages. Ubuntu’s firmware packages were split into subpackages for 24.04 too, in case you missed that news.

The change would let users who stick with the GA kernel continue using the standard firmware set, without receiving updates intended for HWE kernels.

But both firmware sets would continue to receive targeted fixes for reported issues from Canonical for the duration of their respective support periods.

Well, albeit with a rub.

Most of us running LTS releases will, at some point, have a GA and HWE kernel installed on the same device. As only one firmware package can be installed, systems with both kernels will need a workaround of some sort.

But this change, it seems, is now coming.

Firmware packages in Ubuntu 26.10 are in the process of being packaged as ‘hwe’ versions, ahead of their upcoming backport to Ubuntu 26.04 in early 2027.

title: Windows XP had built-in video calls 25 years ago, and Microsoft has been killing...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: Long before Zoom, Windows Messenger let Windows XP users video chat, share apps and call landlines through paid providers. MSN Messenger was a different app altogether, and after Windows Live Messenge...
content:
Windows XP shipped on October 25, 2001, with Windows Messenger, a built-in app for text chat, voice and video calls, and application sharing, almost two years before Skype even existed. Microsoft also said it would work with the nearly 32 million people already using MSN Messenger.

Twenty-five years later, Microsoft has retired every consumer messenger it built from that original idea, from MSN Messenger to Skype, and only Teams is left standing, which everyone loathes.

Windows XP is now 25 years old; when we installed it in a virtual machine, Solitaire still worked fine, but Messenger was offline.

Windows Messenger could do video calls, app sharing and remote help in 2001

Microsoft showed Windows Messenger to beta testers on June 4, 2001. “Windows XP delivers the next level of communications through real-time audio- and video-conferencing, application sharing and online collaboration,” Microsoft said in its announcement.

Bill Gates, then chairman and chief software architect, said Windows Messenger would “help make the world a more connected place.” But what surprised me the most were Microsoft’s examples. The company said students “will be able to collaborate on homework assignments,” and families “will have the chance to hold impromptu online reunions no matter where they are in the world.” Replace Windows Messenger with Zoom, and you have a 2020 lockdown ad.

It also worked with XP’s Remote Assistance, so users could “easily obtain online help if they have a problem or question.”

On October 11, 2001, Microsoft announced a Windows Messenger update for XP’s launch day that let people use their PCs “to make voice calls to telephones virtually anywhere in the world.”

These calls weren’t free, though. Depending on their location, users could pick IP telephony providers like Net2Phone, Dialpad or TELUS, keep an account with them, and “track their current call account balances all from within Messenger.” Basically, Skype Credit, before Skype was a thing.

Windows Messenger and MSN Messenger were two different apps

MSN Messenger, which turned 27 this July, came first. Microsoft launched the MSN Messenger Service on July 21, 1999, as a free download that “tells consumers when their friends, family and colleagues are online,” and it could even exchange messages with AOL Instant Messenger users (imagine WhatsApp and Telegram exchanging messages). Windows Messenger came bundled with XP two years later, and people on both apps could chat with each other.

The naming confusion got so bad that Microsoft published a 2005 document titled “Windows Messenger vs. MSN Messenger: What is the difference?”

According to Microsoft, Windows Messenger “is designed for use in a business environment,” while MSN Messenger was for friends and family, and its “Communications are not encrypted, as they are with Windows Messenger.” Windows Messenger 5.1 could also search your company’s address book and show a coworker’s presence inside Office and SharePoint.

Both had a whiteboard, file transfer, voice and video, and Microsoft said they could run side by side on one PC. If a company writing a whole document to explain its own app names sounds familiar, you’ve probably tried to figure out Copilot vs Microsoft 365 Copilot.

Microsoft kept replacing its messengers, and that we don’t have one (not counting Teams!)

MSN Messenger became Windows Live Messenger in 2006, and it only got bigger. In November 2008, Microsoft called it “the No. 1 instant messaging service worldwide with more than 330 million active customers.”

Then was the grant entry of Skype. On May 10, 2011, Microsoft agreed to buy Skype for $8.5 billion, which sounds normal by 2026 standards, but was huge back then. This was when it had 170 million connected users and over 207 billion minutes of calls in 2010.

In November 2012, Tony Bates, president of Microsoft’s Skype division, wrote, “We will retire Messenger in all countries worldwide in the first quarter of 2013,” with mainland China as the only exception. In his farewell post, Windows Live general manager Brian Hall wrote that “Messenger enabled each of us to communicate and share with the people we care about.”

Ironically, Microsoft’s post announcing the switch was titled “Transition From Windows Messenger to Skype Begins April 8,” even though the service being retired was Windows Live Messenger. China kept it until October 31, 2014.

Sadly, Skype didn’t survive. Microsoft retired it on May 5, 2025, to “streamline our free consumer communications offerings,” as Jeff Teper wrote in the announcement. Contacts and chats moved to Teams Free, and even leftover Skype Credit got pushed to a dial pad on the web.

Expectedly, the business side of Windows Messenger ended up in Teams. Windows Messenger 5.1 was a client for Live Communications Server 2005, the platform that later became Lync and then Skype for Business, and Microsoft retired Skype for Business Online on July 31, 2021, asking customers to upgrade to Teams.

Yes, these were different products, and the Windows Messenger in XP didn’t simply get renamed to Skype. But every path Microsoft took from that idea in 2001, personal or professional, now ends at Teams.

Teams has 320 million users, and Microsoft built it for work

In October 2023, Satya Nadella said Teams had “more than 320 million monthly active users making Teams the place to work.” Back in 2001, John Frederiksen, then general manager of Windows, called Windows Messenger “an easy way for people to communicate with friends, family and co-workers anywhere.” Co-workers came last. (To be fair, Teams is a workplace platform, so its numbers aren’t directly comparable to Messenger’s.)

Messenger was where you set a status message, showed off the song you were listening to, and nudged friends until their window shook (remember that?). Teams is where your manager reminds you of the impending deadline. Hardly anyone opens Teams to talk about their day!

Apple figured this out with iMessage, which works properly only on Apple devices, and yet people associate Apple with their daily lives. Microsoft had a cross-platform answer in Skype and stupidly let that go.

On the technical side, Windows Messenger was a native Windows app, while the new Teams uses WebView2 “as the host” and React for its interface, according to Microsoft. In our testing, a fresh Teams install used about 963MB of RAM while idle with zero conversations, and Microsoft had to add an Efficiency mode for PCs with less RAM.

As someone who despises web apps on Windows, I find it funny that Microsoft is now promising developers that WinUI isn’t being killed, while its biggest communication app is a web app in a desktop shell.

Should Microsoft bring back MSN Messenger?

Yes, but not now.

A free MSN Messenger that’s end-to-end encrypted like Signal, and works on Windows, Android, iPhone, and the web, would give people another reason to use Windows.

But right now, whatever Microsoft does is met with skepticism, even the good stuff, such as the new, good features in Windows 11, including the ability to check internet speed right on the taskbar.

It’s not just Windows things. On Monday, Microsoft offered voluntary exit packages to about 60,000 employees, and the headlines immediately asked if layoffs were around the corner, with social media already deeming it a mass layoff. It’s like everyone forgot what the word voluntary means.

If, and that’s a big if, Microsoft makes Windows lovable again, with transparent privacy and fewer bugs, a Messenger revival makes sense. I’ve said this before; Windows 11 is not a free OS, and OneDrive and Microsoft 365 subscriptions could easily grow when and if people trust Redmond.

Microsoft should remember that the XP nostalgia won’t last forever. A generation that grew up on WhatsApp and iMessage has no memory of a nudge, and the company needs to become more people-focused before deciding to only make software for work.

title: Windows 11’s Bing-free Search is showing up on more PCs, and it shows Bing...
author: Mayank Parmar
summary: I'm sure most of you have run into this at some point: you quickly press the Start button, start typing to find your app, and hit Enter, only to realize that you're opening a...
content:
I’m sure most of you have run into this at some point: you quickly press the Start button, start typing to find your app, and hit Enter, only to realize that you’re opening a Microsoft Edge tab with a Bing search. But you can now turn off these web results, as Bing-free Windows Search has begun rolling out to more users this week.

Microsoft began rolling out the Bing-free Windows Search experience in August 2026, but the gradual rollout meant most of us were hanging around without the actual feature, and we never knew when it would “fully” become available. In fact, it’s still not available to everyone, but turning on the “Get the latest updates…” toggle on the Windows Update page should bring it up for even more PCs.

How to turn off Bing and Microsoft Store results in Windows Search

Now, you’re not going to wake up and find Bing turned off by default in your search experience. Microsoft has no plans to kill off Bing by default, and this toggle is only for those who actually understand why Search is trash in the first place.

If the server-side change has reached your PC, you should be able to turn off Bing as well as Microsoft Store results by following these steps:

  1. Open Settings > Privacy & security.
  2. Open Search.
  3. Right below the indexing status, you’ll see the “Show suggested search results” section, with two toggles for web and Microsoft Store suggestions.
  4. Turn off web searches and, for the best results, Microsoft Store suggestions. Then reopen Windows Search.

Microsoft doesn’t call it Bing in Windows Search, but “web searches,” because in regions like Europe, you can set a search engine other than Bing as your preferred source.

Funnily enough, you can’t find this toggle by searching for it in Settings. I typed “web search” and “turn off bing” in the Settings search box, and both returned “No results.”

The only way to get there from Settings search is to type “search” and pick “Suggested search results.” That list also still includes “Change the search provider in Internet Explorer,” which is a nice reminder that some parts of Windows haven’t moved on since 2022.

Also, turning off web searches doesn’t make Windows Search completely offline. Right below it, there’s a “Search my accounts” section with “Microsoft account” and “Work or School account” toggles, and both are turned on by default. When these are turned on, Windows Search can still pull results from services like OneDrive and Outlook. If you want Search to stick to your PC only, you should turn these off as well.

Windows Search feels much better without Bing. Seriously.

Now, if you open Windows Search, you’ll notice that the homepage no longer has Bing-related widgets, such as trending keywords, quizzes, and the so-called lesser-known facts of the day. All the Bing- and MSN-related adware instantly disappears from the Search homepage.

You’ll now be staring at a clean homepage with a few of your recent searches, and of course, even those will only include local searches. You can also hover over the items and remove whatever you want. I cleaned it up, and here’s what it looks like on my PC:

It’s a breath of fresh air, but if you’ve ever used the Windows Registry or third-party tools to force-disable Bing in Windows Search, this experience will feel familiar.

Then, I pressed the letter S on my keyboard, and it instantly brought up apps starting with S, including Spotify. I also noticed Windows settings, files, and folders that start with the letter or include it somewhere in the name.

Now, try doing it on your PC with Bing search turned on, which is the default behavior. I bet you’re going to find a few Microsoft Store listings and queries from Bing alongside Spotify. And it wouldn’t be nearly as fast as Windows Search without Bing.

And I’m not even using the “Enhanced” mode, which indexes your entire PC. My laptop is on the default “Classic” mode, which only covers Documents, Pictures, Music, and the desktop, and Windows Search has still indexed 218,100 items with zero pending.

You usually won’t run into a blank result if you’ve got everything indexed. But if nothing on your PC matches your query, you’re more likely to see “No results found” than you would with Bing enabled.

Moreover, Windows Search is now much better at understanding typos, so if you type “Otl” when looking for Outlook, you’ll still get the email client in the search results. The same goes for “Putlook.”

That said, it’s not magic, and there are rough edges that Microsoft still needs to address. For example, when I typed “ntpd” for Notepad, Windows Search came back with “No results found.” It is entirely possible Microsoft is still trying to get it right, but based on my understanding, Search handles misspellings well. However, it won’t guess an app from an abbreviation with the vowels removed.

Settings, apps, and app shortcuts show up instantly

Windows Search is also pretty good at plain-English questions about settings. I typed “make text size bigger,” and the best match was the exact system setting, with an Open button in the preview pane. And this is not powered by any large or small language model, so it’s entirely a simple query-matching algorithm.

But there are two problems with the above test. As you can see, the preview pane still shows a “Get quick help from web” section with a “Making text larger on screen” link, even though I have web searches turned off. So Bing hasn’t fully left the building, and that explains why Edge-based WebView2 process is still running in the background.

Second, look at the Documents section. Windows Search is showing “SettingsCache.txt” and two “settingssynonyms.txt” files, which appear to be internal files Windows uses to match Settings queries. I wasn’t expecting these files to show up as I’ve only enabled classic indexing.

Next, I searched “chrome”; Windows Search showed Google Chrome as the best match, along with jump list actions like “New window” and “New Incognito window,” and my most-visited sites. Without Bing, there’s no “chrome download” web suggestion pushing me towards Edge.

It also picks up Chrome’s web apps, such as WhatsApp Web, Cloudflare, and Google Meet, which are listed as regular apps.

What you lose without Bing in Windows Search

Of course, turning off Bing isn’t free. The first thing I noticed is that Windows Search no longer does math for you. I typed a simple multiplication, and it returned “No results found.” With Bing enabled, you’d get the answer inline, so you’ll now have to open Calculator.

When I searched “weather,” I didn’t get a forecast card like the one Bing used to show. Instead, Windows Search listed the Weather app as the best match, followed by Lively Weather, Weather for Command Palette, and a bunch of old screenshots on my PC that have “weather” in their names.

Honestly, I don’t mind. I’d rather open the Weather app than wait for Bing to load a card I didn’t ask for.

I’ve never been so impressed with Windows Search, and it’s quite interesting how turning off Bing just made everything better. Microsoft could have done it years ago, and that would have saved the company from all the embarrassment.

While this new Windows Search is available for more people, it’s still being “rolled out.” That means there’s a high chance some of you may not get it this week as well.

title: Windows 11 still needs TPM 2.0, but Microsoft quietly changed who provides it on...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: On 2026 AMD and Qualcomm silicon, Windows 11 gets TPM 2.0 from the chipmaker’s firmware TPM or a discrete chip, while Pluton stays for other security work. Existing Pluton PCs keep their TPM, but firm...
content:
Starting with chips released in 2026, Microsoft’s Pluton security processor won’t act as the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) on AMD and Qualcomm PCs. Windows 11 will instead use the chipmaker’s firmware TPM or a separate TPM chip, and Microsoft also lists Intel PCs under that arrangement. Pluton will be inside these processors for other security work, and PCs already using Pluton as the TPM will keep getting updates.

BitLocker and Windows Hello will work as usual. However, the change is in who fixes your TPM if (or when) an unthinkable security flaw shows up.

Microsoft confirms Pluton won’t be the TPM on 2026 AMD and Qualcomm chips

Microsoft added the change as a note to its Pluton as TPM documentation, which was last updated on September 16.

“Beginning with 2026 silicon, Microsoft Pluton no longer serves as the TPM on AMD and Qualcomm platforms. On these platforms, as well as on Intel, TPM 2.0 functionality is instead delivered through the vendor’s firmware TPM (fTPM) or a discrete TPM.”

Some reports mentioned it as Pluton losing its TPM role on Intel too, but Microsoft names only AMD and Qualcomm for the change. Intel’s Core Ultra 200V and Core Ultra Series 3 chips have Pluton, while Intel PCs typically get TPM 2.0 from Intel’s own firmware TPM, called Platform Trust Technology (PTT), or a discrete chip.

The company hasn’t explained the decision, and it hasn’t listed which chips count as “2026 silicon.” For example, Snapdragon X2 laptops were unveiled at CES 2026, but Qualcomm announced the chips in September 2025.

Ironically, Microsoft’s main Pluton page, updated in May, still says “Microsoft Pluton is designed to provide the functionality of the Trusted Platform Module (TPM).”

Windows 11 still requires TPM 2.0, and a firmware TPM can meet it

A TPM is a tamper-resistant security module that stores the keys protecting your PC. When BitLocker encrypts your drive or Windows Hello signs you in with a PIN or your face, the keys are kept in the TPM, so, theoretically, malware can’t easily copy them. The TPM also helps confirm that nobody tampered with the boot process before Windows unlocks your drive.

Windows 11’s minimum requirements still list “Trusted Platform Module (TPM) version 2.0,” and Microsoft called it a non-negotiable standard in late 2024.

According to Microsoft’s TPM recommendations, TPM 2.0 comes in three forms. A discrete TPM is a separate chip on the motherboard, an integrated TPM is built into a chip package but kept logically separate, and a firmware TPM runs in a trusted execution environment on the processor.

Windows doesn’t pick favorites. “Windows uses any compatible TPM in the same way. Microsoft doesn’t take a position on which way a TPM should be implemented,” the company says, while also admitting that “There are variations in the security properties of different TPM implementations.”

To see which TPM your PC uses, press Win + R, type tpm.msc, and look under TPM Manufacturer Information. Microsoft says the Specification Version should show 2.0, and the Manufacturer Name field shows the vendor.

Pluton isn’t going away, and current Pluton PCs keep their TPM

Microsoft’s note confirms that existing laptops aren’t affected:“Devices built on 2025 or earlier AMD and Qualcomm silicon that ship with Pluton configured as the TPM remain fully serviced and supported.”

“The Pluton security processor will continue to be present and supported on existing and future Windows devices to provide a hardware isolated security environment for Windows,” Microsoft added.

Microsoft announced Pluton with AMD, Intel and Qualcomm in November 2020. Microsoft’s David Weston, now Corporate Vice President of AI Security, explained that attackers with physical access can “target the communication channel between the CPU and TPM,” and Pluton’s design “removes the potential for that communication channel to be attacked.” Pluton PCs “will first emulate a TPM,” Weston wrote at the time, and the design borrowed from Microsoft’s work on the Xbox One and Azure Sphere.

By May 2024, Microsoft said Pluton “will be enabled by default on all Copilot+ PCs.”

Losing Pluton as the TPM changes how your PC gets security fixes

Pluton’s big selling point was updates. Microsoft says it “allows for other Pluton firmware and OS features to be delivered over time via Windows Update,” and at startup, Windows loads newer Pluton firmware if it has one.

A firmware TPM is part of the chipmaker’s firmware, so usually, fixes come as a BIOS update from your PC maker. In August, AMD disclosed two high-severity flaws in the TPM 2.0 reference code that affect its firmware TPMs, and told users to “contact your OEM for the BIOS update specific to your product(s).” If your laptop maker is slow with BIOS updates, your TPM could be unpatched for longer.

AMD’s fTPM has a bad reputation, too. In 2022, it caused random stutters on some Ryzen PCs, and the fix came through BIOS updates with AGESA 1207 or later. A year later, TU Berlin researchers broke AMD’s fTPM on Zen 2 and Zen 3 processors with about $200 of hardware and several hours of physical access.

If you install a BIOS update, keep your BitLocker recovery key handy, as firmware changes can trigger the BitLocker recovery screen.

Then again, Pluton came with compatibility baggage. Lenovo shipped its 2022 Ryzen 6000 ThinkPads with Pluton disabled by default, and Linux needed kernel 6.3 to support Pluton’s TPM, after developer Matthew Garrett added support without any documentation.

A firmware TPM also runs inside the processor, so it isn’t exposed to the CPU-to-TPM bus attacks Weston described. However, a discrete TPM chip is vulnerable.

In my opinion, Microsoft gave up a core part of the Pluton pitch in a documentation note, with further explanation. If you’re buying a 2026 AMD or Snapdragon laptop, check how often its maker gives BIOS updates. Who would you trust to patch your TPM: Microsoft or your laptop maker?

title: iOS 26 can run on an Android phone, and a developer proved it on...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: SmuOS shared exclusive photos of iOS 26.5.2 running natively on Microsoft's abandoned Surface Duo 2, with Settings and the Phone app spanning both screens. He explains how Apple's open-source XNU kern...
content:
Developer SmuOS, also known as None24, has booted Apple’s iOS 26 natively on Microsoft’s discontinued Surface Duo 2, a dual-screen Android phone powered by a Snapdragon 888. Both screens and touch now work, the Phone and Settings apps stretch across the two displays, and iOS calls the device an “iPhone 17 Pro Max.” It isn’t emulation. The port boots Apple’s open-source XNU kernel with a custom UEFI loader, and the developer shared exclusive photos and details with Windows Latest.

Microsoft stopped supporting the Surface Duo 2 in October 2024, and Apple’s two-screen iPhone Duo went on sale last week. Until now, Apple using the Duo name was the joke for me, but now, the joke is on multiple levels. So, while Apple sells its own take on Microsoft’s idea for $1,999, a talented hobbyist turned Microsoft’s abandoned phone into an iPhone Duo of sorts.

iOS 26 on the Surface Duo 2, in exclusive photos

SmuOS sent Windows Latest photos of his test device running iOS 26, and the Settings app’s About page leaves nothing to doubt. It shows iOS 26.5.2, the model name “iPhone 17 Pro Max,” 5GB of capacity, and N/A for the serial number, Wi-Fi address, and Bluetooth.

iOS thinks of both screens as one large canvas. Settings shows its sidebar on the left screen and the selected page on the right, Liquid Glass and all, which is how it would look on an iPad.

The Phone app is where the dual-screen layout gets awkward, in a funny way. The keypad is centered on the full canvas, so the 1, 4, 7, and * keys found their place on the left screen; 3, 6, 9, and # are on the right, and the middle column disappears into the hinge, along with half the green call button. That said, getting the iOS Phone app to open on an Android-powered Surface Duo, of all phones, is impressive, to say the least.

Don’t mind the glitchy color bands and a badly cracked right display. “The device im using is my test device which is why its cracked. I wonder how much i could aution it off for on my non broken device (mostly joking),” SmuOS wrote on X.

The progress over the past few days has been wild to watch. On October 24, he posted that iOS 26 had booted natively, though “nothing but 1 display works at the moment.” Hours later, he reached the iOS setup screen, and that post crossed 54,000 views. Photos from that stage show the language picker on both displays, with a boot log overlaid on top.

It’s hard to expect more, but surprisingly, by October 25, the developer wrote that “Both displays run at 37fps– it used to be 3-10 fps,” followed by “TOUCH IS WORKINGGG,” which is nothing short of spectacular.

How iOS 26 boots on an Android phone

Apple publishes the source code of XNU, the kernel in iOS and macOS, on GitHub. Since iPhones and most Android phones use ARM chips, a developer can build that kernel for a Qualcomm processor. Yes, I made it sound simple, but of course, it’s not, and it takes an incredible amount of work.

“A person would essentially build the XNU kernel from source to run on ARM for whichever SOC they have. The iPhones still use ARM based chips which makes this possible. So its all about how much you can make compatible with iOS,” SmuOS told Windows Latest.

The second piece is UniXNU, an open-source project that describes itself as a way “to run iOS and macOS on non-Apple ARM64 hardware through UEFI,” similar to OpenCore for Hackintoshes. “You boot a custom loader like open core, and you can port either ios or macos to your device with enough technical know-how,” he explained. UniXNU already includes the Surface Duo 2, codenamed zeta, among its community ports, with SmuOS as the maintainer.

According to his GitHub repository, the port uses the official iPhone 17 Pro Max restore image for iOS 26.5.2 (build 23F84), with a kernel built from Apple’s XNU source for iOS 26.5. The firmware and Apple’s files aren’t redistributed, so you can’t simply download it and flash it, in case you were wondering.

Getting Apple’s kernel to boot is only the start, though. “You either port or build drivers from scratch. And the Surface Duo 2 ships with the Snapdragon 888 SoC. So i both had to build drivers from scratch and a metal translation layer but also find a way to make the displays compatible with ios26 as there hasnt been an Apple device with 2 screens until the iPhone Duo,” he said.

The “metal translation layer” is needed because iOS draws everything with Apple’s Metal graphics API, while the Surface Duo 2’s Adreno 660 GPU doesn’t speak Metal. UniXNU’s documentation describes its approach as translating Metal to Vulkan and running it on Turnip, which is the open-source Vulkan driver for Adreno GPUs.

Apple’s chips also use a security feature called pointer authentication, and iOS code is compiled for it, under a format called arm64e. The Snapdragon 888 doesn’t support it, and his repository notes that 29.6 million of these pointer signatures were stripped from iOS’s shared cache. “Some parts of the build by default use ARM64e, i rewrote them to arm64 for better performance,” SmuOS said.

Interestingly, he says the kernel wasn’t the hardest part. “The more difficult parts of the build you might think is the kernel but its actually the graphics stack. There are so many small things that can break spingboard, backboardd etc. Having a decompiled ipsw (that i did myself) helps to understand ios under the hood much better.”

It took two months, and SmuOS had iOS running before the iOS-on-Android wave

In case you missed it, iOS on Android became a trend this month. HackiOS runs iOS 16.5 on a Poco X5 Pro, ios-sweet runs iOS 16.7.16 on a Redmi Note 10 Pro, and UniXNU’s lead device, the Xiaomi Pad 6S Pro, runs iPadOS 17. Of course, I find SmuOS’s port the most impressive of the lot, simply because it runs iOS 26, with Liquid Glass, across two screens, on a Surface Duo. I doubt if the irony can get any deeper.

He says he got there first, too. “Prior to any news about iOS ports being done on android I had iOS 26 running on the Surface Duo 2 and the Pixel 10 Pro Fold headless (without graphics). I initially wanted to keep it to myself because I wanted to show it off when graphics were fully working and I would’ve been the first to do it with a foldable. Lol.”

“It took 2 months of investigating, headaches and trial/error to do it,” he said, while also working on an Android 16 port for the Duo. He’s upfront about using AI, too. “Some is my effort some was Chatgpt helping me to understand bits about the XNU kernel that I never knew about.”

The project started as a way to keep the Surface Duo alive. SmuOS initially set out to port Linux Mobile and Android 16 and 17 to the Surface Duo and Surface Duo 2, as he felt the phone “didn’t get much love over the years.” Along the way, a few people who worked on Microsoft’s Duo development team helped him understand “the inner workings of the duo framework.”

If it wasn’t clear from the images already, iOS on Surface Duo 2 is still a research build. The wallpaper renders black, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth show N/A in Settings, and the developer’s repository documents ongoing graphics fixes.

Like one of the replies SmuOS got on X, it is indeed funny to see “getting custom OS’s to run on hardware they were never designed to run on.”

SmuOS isn’t done working on iOS on Surface…

Surface Pen as Apple Pencil and an iOS 27 “iPhone Duo” build are next

SmuOS told Windows Latest that two things are coming: “Surface Pen to Apple Pencil spoofing and the iPhone Duo’s iOS 27 build.”

The iOS 27 build is a tougher ladder. “I am working through moving the project up to iOS 27 which is more difficult of a task since no kernel tags exist yet for it publicly,” he explained. He also has an idea for bringing the iPhone’s Action Button to a phone that doesn’t have one.

The Surface Duo isn’t his only Microsoft experiment either. He’s porting Windows Andromeda, the dual-screen version of Windows that Microsoft cancelled in 2018 and that the Surface Duo’s firmware hinted it was first designed for, to Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold. He’s also rewriting the Nintendo GameCube’s boot menu in ARM64 to build an OS for the Ayn Odin 2.

“I do these for fun,” he said, and that’s the best part of this story. SmuOS went from 50 followers to over 300 in a weekend, and we wish he’d get more support. He also tells other porters not to give up. “If you port something that someone else already did, just make sure it’s the best or collaborate with that person.”

“Modding communities are wonderful places because they inspire the mind. And I think the world should encourage that more.”

Microsoft gave up on the Surface Duo, but the community clearly hasn’t. Would you be interested in a Surface Duo with iOS, as the original Duo didn’t have to deal with ‘crackgate’?

title: Firefox 159 released with Wayland Linux fixes
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Firefox 159 is out, with a fresh set of improvements and some Linux-specific fixes.

Now that Mozilla’s browser hews to a faster release cadence, with two releases a month rather than one, some changelogs may look minor on their own, as they’re smaller, if more frequent slices.

So what’s changed?

The Passwords tool in the browser sidebar (added as an option in Firefox 145) is now shown by default. This lets you find credentials in the same window as a web page, no mousing through menus or juggling with floating dialogs.

It’s also a smidgen easier to search your open tabs. A new keyboard shortcut has been added to activate the tab search filter. The feature isn’t new (it could be triggered using the ‘List all tabs’ button), but a memorable shortcut aids discoverability.

On Windows or Linux, press ctrl + shift + a1 to trigger the tab search. It focuses the address bar and you type some words to return any matches from open tabs on your device or open on your synced devices (if signed in to your Mozilla account).

Wayland Linux tab terrors

On Linux, Firefox 159 resolves a couple of Wayland issues that were affecting tab behaviour.

In some situations, click on a tab could make it detach into a standalone window (which isn’t super helpful if you were just trying to select or move it). Conversely, dragging a tab upward on Linux desktops using Wayland wouldn’t detach the tab.

And Linux system with AMD GPUs who noticed Firefox consuming excessive memory on sites like ChatGPT when Mapbox GL JS maps were displayed, will be pleased to hear that issue is now resolved.

AI & Smart Window tweaks

Smart Window testers can use a new /watch command to get their AI backend of choice to monitor a web page for any changes, like a price drop or new post. Check interval and notification method are configurable.

Safari in macOS and iOS 27 debuted a similar feature backed by Siri AI. Like Apple’s offering, Mozilla’s version lets you easily manage, edit, pause, force check and, of course, delete watches.

When using an AI chatbot in the sidebar, the “summarise” page now shares the website address with the AI provider, rather than the page’s text. Firefox 160, out 10 November, will include a new AI chatbot provider: Yahoo! Scout.

Other changes

On the web compatibility side, Firefox 159 adds support for scroll-driven animations, a CSS feature that lets web developers tie an animation’s progress to, well, scrolling or a specific on-page element being moved through the viewport.

Bug fixes include:

  • Bookmarks not being imported from signed-in Google Chrome profiles
  • File upload dialog opening in the last folder a file was saved to
  • Cherry picked patches for better Vulkan ffvpx handling on Linux
  • Browser UI animations are turned off if OS Reduce Motion setting is on
  • Sites (including Slack) often failed to load instead of using HTTP/2

Plus, security patches and plenty of other, smaller fixes. Firefox 160 is due for release in 2 weeks time, on 10 November 2026.

Auto-PiP when switching window

If you use picture-in-picture mode often, you may be interested in testing a new behaviour that’s coming. It triggers picture-in-picture mode when a page playing video is obscured by another window or the browser is minimised.

To try it out, go to about:config and find the enable-when-occluded setting. Double-click to set the value to true. If the ‘keep playing in picture-in-picture mode’ setting is enabled, videos will pop-out when switching window too.

Get Firefox 159

Firefox 159 is free, open-source software. You can download the new release from the Mozilla FTP server or wait for the links to the same builds to appear on the Firefox website from 27 October.

Existing users get updated to the new version in-app on Windows, macOS and Linux (binary builds), or through the app store or package repository it was installed from.

On Ubuntu? This update arrives like the rest, i.e., an automatic, background update from the Snap Store.

  1. This shortcut previously opened the Add-ons and Themes page. To get to that in v159, press Ctrl + Shift + F. ↩︎

title: Trash talking Ubuntu’s confusing British bin labels
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Every operating systems needs somewhere to put the files you delete (and give you chance to rummage through to find the ones you want to keep).

But, if you’re a Brit using Ubuntu, the name of that place varies based on where you look.

It seems Ubuntu’s UK English translation team don’t agree on what to call a bin. The dock hover label says Trash. That opens a Rubbish Bin in the file manager, and that show an action bar button to Empty Wastebasket…

Right-click on a file in the tr… Er, file holding area, and you have the choice to Delete From Wastebasket… or Restore From Rubbish Bin – both in the same menu.

If you delete to clear out the cruft, the confirmation dialog is headed ‘Empty Wastebasket?’ with the affirmative action being ‘Empty Rubbish Bin’.

At least no-ones calling it a Recycle Bin, I guess!

It seems the identity crisis is solely in the British English terminology, as Ubuntu’s US translations are consistent in calling trash Trash (pronounced Traaash, in your best American drawl accent).

GNOME’s own British English translation guidance says “Trash should be translated to Wastebasket”, so that’s where that term comes from (though ‘wastebasket’ still reads as American to me1).

Lost in translation

Consistency in interface language matters (the same way it does in icons and controls). While the various UK labels are obvious as to what they are, the changing terminology adds a bit of unnecessary friction since your eyes will scan for the shape of the word you expect.

Not a major papercut, and with Ubuntu’s translations split across GNOME, third-party extensions and its own integrations, each maintained by different teams, it’s not surprising there are some locale quirks.

But if the US locale can use one term, can’t the UK bin the ones it doesn’t need?

  1. We call that a waste-paper basket, darling. ↩︎

title: Microsoft confirms Windows 11 26H2 is now available for everyone, and it installs in...
author: Mayank Parmar
summary: Microsoft has confirmed version 26H2 is now available for everyone running versions 25H2 and 24H2, and next milestone is forced installation.
content:
Windows 11 26H2, aka Windows 11 2026 Update, began rolling out on September 29, but until now, not everybody has been offered the annual update. Today, Windows Latest noticed that Microsoft has confirmed version 26H2 is now available for everyone running versions 25H2 and 24H2, and it could now be only a matter of weeks before Microsoft begins force-updating PCs.

In a support document updated quietly on October 21 and first spotted by Windows Latest, Microsoft noted:

“The Windows 11, version 26H2 phased rollout has reached full availability for devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2. You can check for the update by going to Settings > Windows Update and selecting Check for Windows updates.”

If Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available is toggled on, Windows 11 26H2 can automatically download and install on your PC.

Here’s what Windows Update looks like on a PC still on Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2, and note that I did not click on “Check for updates”:

If you don’t see Windows 11 26H2, it’s entirely possible you already have the feature update installed. I recommend going to Settings > System > About and checking the OS version and build number under Windows specifications. If it says version 26H2 and Build 26300, you’ve already installed the annual update.

In other cases, it could be due to an upgrade safeguard if Microsoft has detected a compatibility issue on your PC.

“During rollout, we might place safeguard holds on devices where we detect a known compatibility issue that could impact the update experience,” Microsoft explained in a blog post last month.

However, this can only happen on PCs running Windows 11 23H2 or older, since Windows 11 26H2, 25H2, and 24H2 are the same release in a nullshell, so you won’t run into compatibility issues when you jump between these updates.

The next major milestone is a forced rollout

Windows 11 26H2 has reached full availability in less than a month of its release. That shows Microsoft’s confidence in the annual update, and it shouldn’t surprise anybody, as it’s a small upgrade if you’re already on 24H2 or 25H2.

I’m told that Microsoft is also preparing to begin force-installing Windows 11 26H2 on PCs soon.

Microsoft has been force-installing Windows 11 25H2 on PCs still running Windows 11 24H2 or 23H2. But over the next few weeks, I believe it could open the floodgates and let Windows 11 26H2 automatically install on PCs nearing the end of support or those that have already reached it.

What about a PC running Windows 11 25H2? Will you be upgraded to Windows 11 26H2 without your permission? I believe that would happen in the middle of 2027, well ahead of Windows 11 27H2, which is expected to be a big release.

Windows 11 26H2 is still a nothingburger update

I call Windows 11 26H2 a nothingburger update because it doesn’t come with new consumer features, but it still ships with the improvements from recent monthly updates toggled on by default.

In our tests, Windows Latest has observed that Windows 11 26H2 actually makes 8GB RAM PCs use less memory. Microsoft has also confirmed memory improvements and says Windows 11 is now up to 20% more responsive.

However, these improvements are also rolling out to Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2, so nothing here makes Windows 11 26H2 a special update.

Windows 11 26H2 is based on the same underlying platform as Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2, and it uses a small enablement package to flip the OS version and build number.

If you choose to install Windows 11 26H2, it’s highly likely that you will not see any visible changes, and my tests show that the update finishes installing in less than five minutes because the enablement package is just 174KB in size. It’s also smaller compared to monthly cumulative updates, which can go well above 2GB via Windows Update and over 5GB on the Update Catalog.

Windows 11 26H2 resets the support lifecycle

Regardless, it’s an important release because Windows 11 24H2’s Home and Pro support has already ended, and the same editions of Windows 11 25H2 have less than 365 days of runway left.

If anything, Windows 11 26H2 is the kind of release that resets the Windows lifecycle and gives you peace of mind without a major platform upgrade.

Windows 11 26H2 is supported for two years for consumer editions, including Home and Pro. If you use Windows 11 Enterprise or Education, you get an additional year of support on top of those two years. And that’s the standard for annual Windows 11 feature updates.

Here’s the Windows product lifecycle:

Windows 11 version Servicing branch Home and Pro support ends Enterprise and Education support ends
Windows 11 24H2 24H2 / Germanium October 13, 2026 October 12, 2027
Windows 11 25H2 24H2 / Germanium October 12, 2027 October 10, 2028
Windows 11 26H2 24H2 / Germanium October 9, 2028 October 8, 2029

You might argue that Microsoft could have skipped Windows 11 26H2 if it’s the same update all over again. But that’s not how Windows could actually work when you look at the broader picture.

As I’ve reported previously, Windows 11 27H2 is planned as a new platform release, expected in October 2027. Since Windows 11 25H2 support wraps up at the same time, you’d be staring at a forced update to that big release if Windows 11 26H2 didn’t exist.

At that point, Windows 11 26H2, a nothingburger release, would look like a golden release, as it gives you the opportunity to stay on the same branch through October 2028.

By the time that support wraps up, Windows 11 27H2 should be more stable, and Microsoft could already be preparing Windows 11 28H2.

title: Tested: Windows 11’s new Outlook now beats Outlook Classic at one thing (unified inbox),...
author: Gareth Smith
summary: Microsoft is rolling out All Accounts to the new Outlook for Windows, a unified inbox that combines Inbox, Drafts, Sent, Archive and Junk from every account while keeping mailboxes separate. I tried i...
content:
The new Outlook for Windows now has an All Accounts view, Microsoft’s take on a unified inbox, which shows email from every connected account in one list while each mailbox is kept separate. It’s rolling out to everyone now, and I’ve been using it on my Windows 365 Cloud PC to go through mail from my work and personal accounts in one pass.

Of course, unified inboxes aren’t a new idea. The old Windows Mail app could link inboxes, and Outlook for Mac, iOS and Android have had one for years. But when Microsoft shut down Mail and Calendar and impelled people to the new Outlook, the feature didn’t come along.

New Outlook’s All Accounts view puts every inbox in one place

Before this update, I had to check each inbox one by one. Pinning inboxes to Favorites saved a little clicking, but it still didn’t give me one combined message list.

Microsoft confirmed the All Accounts view in June, and according to Message Center post MC1519843, the rollout started in late September and should finish by late October. “Users can read, delete, search, move, archive, and mark messages across accounts without switching between mailboxes,” Microsoft says, adding that it “does not merge mailboxes or move messages between accounts.”

Once it’s on, a new All Accounts section appears in the folder pane above your individual mailboxes. It’s not the typical Inbox, as it also includes combined Drafts, Outbox, Archive, Sent Items, Scheduled, Deleted Items, and Junk Email folders. A combined Inbox with 70,495 unread emails could make some feel overwhelmed, though!

How to turn on All Accounts in the new Outlook for Windows

My Cloud PC got the feature through Targeted Release on new Outlook version 1.2026.922.300, while my laptop still hasn’t. To turn it on, open Settings > Mail > Folder pane and check “See emails from all your accounts in one place” under Show all accounts.

Some users may find it already enabled. Microsoft says admin controls are coming later this month, which will let IT teams decide if Unified Inbox is on by default and if users can change it.

Using one inbox for multiple Outlook accounts

My usual first pass is to handle urgent mail, archive reference messages and leave the rest for later. All Accounts let me do that once instead of repeating the process in every inbox, and I could archive or mark messages as read without leaving the combined list.

It also helped with quieter accounts. New mail from my secondary account showed up in the combined list, so I no longer had to open its folders or keep an eye on unread counts.

I still open individual mailboxes for focused work, and the combined view is right above them, so switching is just a click away.

Cross-account search and shared mailboxes are still missing

Microsoft mentions search among the actions you can do across accounts, but in the version I tested, searching for older messages only initiated a search in one mailbox, and I had to open the right account to find them. Microsoft also says Search with Copilot only finds messages in your primary account.

Shared mailboxes aren’t part of the view either, and Microsoft says support will come later. If you manage a team inbox, you’ll still be opening it separately, even though the new Outlook’s shared mailbox handling has improved this year.

All Accounts should have been in the new Outlook from the get-go

If you only have one email account, this doesn’t matter to you in the slightest. But if you move between work, personal, and other accounts every day, All Accounts removes a frustratingly tedious account-by-account routine, and I’m glad it’s finally here.

Still, the new Outlook launched as the replacement for both Mail and Outlook Classic without a feature that the free Mail app had. It’s a web app that can be painfully slow next to Outlook Classic, and with Microsoft set to make it the default for businesses in 2027, it still has plenty of catching up to do, as was evident from our 3-day testing.

title: Everyone says disabling SysMain speeds up Windows 11, so I benchmarked it on two...
author: Abhijith M B
summary: SysMain, formerly Superfetch, preloads your frequently used apps into spare RAM and prepares startup data for Fast Startup. I timed restarts, Word and Photoshop launches and RAM use on a 32GB PC and a...
content:
Disabling SysMain, the Windows service formerly called Superfetch, won’t make most Windows 11 PCs faster. SysMain uses spare RAM to preload apps you open often, and Microsoft says it also preps startup data for Fast Startup. In my tests on two PCs, turning it off barely changed boot time, and even made cold app launches slightly slower. The case for disabling it is limited to specific problems, like a PC with 4GB of RAM and a slow hard drive.

Search “speed up Windows 11” on YouTube, and SysMain is almost always on the list of services to kill, right next to deleting Prefetch, which we found doesn’t help either.

Windows 11’s SysMain service is supposed to make apps open faster

Open Services, and Windows describes SysMain as, “Maintains and improves system performance over time.” In Task Manager, it shows up as “Service Host: SysMain,” which is usually how people find it, usually while it’s using CPU or disk after boot.

SysMain learns which apps you use, then loads parts of them into RAM before you open them. Mark Russinovich, now Microsoft Azure’s CTO, explained in 2008 that whenever memory frees up, SuperFetch asks Windows to reload recently evicted data “at a rate of a few pages per second with Very Low priority I/Os so that the preloading does not impact the user or other active applications.”

The preloaded data goes into the Standby list, which Task Manager calls “Cached.” Russinovich wrote that Windows gives every page in that cache a priority from 0 to 7, and “takes pages from low-priority lists first” when an app needs memory. Basically, cached RAM is borrowed, and Windows does take it back if an app asks.

SysMain also helps boot. Microsoft’s hardware assessment documentation says Superfetch “pre-fetches data that is frequently accessed on startup” and stores it in the hiberfile for Fast Startup, “to avoid excessive disk accesses on resume.”

Do not confuse SysMain with Prefetch. Prefetch writes small .pf files that tell Windows what an app reads when it starts, while SysMain decides what to keep in RAM. SysMain’s database files are also stored in C:\Windows\Prefetch, a folder that keeps a record of the apps you run, as we found earlier.

On Microsoft’s Q&A forum, a thread from June 2023 asked what SysMain is and what happens if you disable it. An answer from Independent Advisor John Jefferson Doyon, marked helpful by over 40 people, says “it’s important to note that disabling it may negatively impact system performance,” and recommends keeping the defaults.

Does disabling SysMain make Windows 11 faster?

I tested disabling SysMain on my 16GB PC and a 4GB test PC, both on Windows 11. The 16GB one is my daily driver, and the other is an underpowered VM that I use just to test features.

Unsurprisingly, I saw little to no change in the boot time and app launch time on my regular PC before and after disabling SysMain. However, on the VM, there were some changes:

Before disabling SysMain:

Restarting the PC took 42.83 seconds (yes, the VM is pretty slow)

Opening ClipChamp took 3.14 seconds

Here is the RAM usage before disabling SysMain:

After disabling SysMain:

Restarting PC took 35.18 seconds, which is a respectable improvement.

But opening ClipChamp took 8.48 seconds

Here is the RAM usage before disabling SysMain:

The truth is, you don’t have to take the effort to disable SysMain for your daily driver PC, unless it’s too old.

The RAM numbers are where most “SysMain eats my memory” claims fall apart. Apart from some minor changes, there isn’t anything to write home about. After several tries, I did see a lowered Cached memory, but only by 100MB, and that doesn’t change system performance in any way. A lower Cached number doesn’t mean apps get more memory, as Windows would’ve handed that cache over anyway.

Microsoft’s caching argument is far from new. Back in 2007, Tom’s Hardware found that on a Windows Vista PC with 512MB of RAM, SuperFetch and ReadyBoost cut OpenOffice Writer’s launch time from 9 seconds to 2-4 seconds, and Outlook 2007’s from 10 seconds to 2-4 seconds. Tom’s Hardware tested it on a hard drive, though, and Microsoft said in 2009 that Windows 7 turns Superfetch off on SSDs with good random read performance, as these features were “designed to improve performance on traditional HDDs.”

It’s not just me, though. Others who recommend disabling SysMain mostly agree that you won’t feel it on a modern PC. XDA’s Ty Sherback noticed little difference on his Ryzen 7 7800X3D workstation with 64GB of RAM and NVMe storage, though older, low-RAM systems felt better shortly after boot. Even he says PCs with 8GB of RAM or less should probably leave SysMain on. Another XDA writer admitted you “probably won’t notice an immediate performance uplift.”

Forum threads on NVMe systems mostly end with people saying they saw no difference either way: “I have seen absolutely no difference in performance whether it is enabled or disabled, except for one less background service.”

When should you disable SysMain, and when should you keep it on?

SysMain using CPU or disk for a few minutes after boot is normal, as it’s reloading what it thinks you’ll need. But it’s a problem if it keeps doing that for hours.

One user on that Microsoft Q&A thread said SysMain was using 96% of the CPU on a small HP all-in-one, which they thought had 4GB of RAM, right after a Windows update. On a PC like that, with little RAM to cache into and an old drive, stopping SysMain makes sense, at least until you can upgrade the RAM.

Microsoft has also documented a specific Windows 7 bug, KB2723033, where SysMain spiked the CPU for 1-2 minutes, over and over, when a 64-bit app was compiled with a particular flag. It’s an old, niche issue, but it shows that a misbehaving SysMain is usually a bug and doesn’t mean that the service is useless.

If you suspect SysMain, check Task Manager first and confirm that “Service Host: SysMain” is the process using resources, and that it continues after the first 10 minutes. Then, stop it from Services without changing its Startup type, and use your PC for a day. If nothing improves, start it again. Only set it to Disabled if the problem goes away and comes back when you turn it on.

How to disable SysMain in Windows 11 PC

  • Press Win+R to open Run, and type services.msc. Press Enter.
  • From the Services menu, scroll till you see SysMain.
  • Right-click SysMain and select Properties.
  • From there, look for the dropdown menu in Startup type, and select Disabled.
  • Click Apply, then OK, and restart your PC.

Having an SSD isn’t a reason to disable SysMain, and neither is a high RAM number in Task Manager. Microsoft is already working on faster app launches in Windows 11 from other angles, like skipping an extra process for apps that are already running, and SysMain was built for that goal long before.

Like the page file, SysMain is a Windows memory feature that looks like waste in Task Manager but exists to help. If your Windows 11 PC isn’t struggling, don’t mind that it’s on. Have you disabled SysMain on your PC?

title: Ubuntu users can now file bugs against specific Launchpad PPAs
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Launchpad now offers bug tracking for personal package archives (PPAs), making it easier for users to report issues specific to software within a PPA.

Why does that matter? Well, not all PPAs are maintained by their upstream counterparts – folks who, frankly, aren’t always minded to care about quirks in their software that might be down to someone else’s packaging methods.

Plus, PPAs are often used to provide newer or experimental versions of software that the version in the standard Ubuntu repositories, and different PPAs can distribute different versions of the same software.

With the new tracking support, users can finally problems against the packages they’ve installed from that PPA. Bugs can be about the PPA a whole, an individual source package within it or a build for a specific Ubuntu version.

Canonical’s İlker Emre Koç illustrated the benefit in an announcement.

A user installs a newer version of Example Editor from a testing PPA, then encounters a crash. Rather than report an issue against the package, which would imply the version in the Ubuntu repos is affected, it can now be filed against the version in the testing PPA.

For software developers who use PPAs to distribute their own software and for maintainers packaging other people’s software, this long-awaited ability should reduce the burden of triaging and fixing bugs.

PPA bug tracking is live on Launchpad. Developers can head to their PPA and select View bugs to explore the features available – as can users who want report something’s askew.

In other Launchpad news, the code-hosting site is retiring its blueprints feature at the end of the 27.10 cycle (so not for another year) due to low usage. It’s also mulling the creation of a ‘modern, purpose-built translation platform’ on top of Launchpad.

title: Windows 11’s new “better performance” toggle shows up, but your current PC will never...
author: Mayank Parmar
summary: Windows 11's recent preview builds include a new toggle called "Advanced Performance Extensions," aka "APX," and on supported hardware.
content:
Windows 11’s recent preview builds include a new toggle called “Advanced Performance Extensions,” aka “APX,” and on supported hardware, it could actually make your PC run faster. According to Microsoft, letting Windows use APX allows your PC to have “better performance.”

This new hardware requirement could finally give Microsoft another opportunity to push you into buying a new PC, especially as Windows 10 is now less than a year away from the end of extended support in 2027. So far, Windows 11’s Copilot+ PCs with NPU support have done little to nothing to convince Windows 10 holdouts, and it makes you wonder if APX, or the idea of “better performance,” could change that.

Existing Windows 11 PCs can still benefit from Low Latency Profile, though, and it doesn’t need APX support.

If you haven’t seen the toggle yet, it’s because it popped up in Build 29695, released to Windows Insiders on October 23, so at this point, we are not sure when the feature will roll out in production. For consumer PCs, Intel’s upcoming Nova Lake is the family to watch.

What is Intel APX, and what are CPU registers?

Now, time for some backstory to better understand why APX even exists as a toggle on Windows 11 in the first place.

Intel has been around for several decades now, and it has continuously changed its architecture for “emerging workloads” and other requirements, such as better battery life, where Qualcomm has raised expectations. While Intel hasn’t had much luck with efficiency or even AMD-like performance, APX is another attempt to improve performance without significantly increasing power consumption.

Originally, Intel’s x86 architecture defined eight 16-bit general-purpose registers. Over time, that increased to 16 registers, each 64 bits wide. This happened long before Windows 11, which requires a 64-bit processor.

But what are these “registers”? According to Intel, registers are small but very fast storage locations inside processors, and they hold the values required for running processes. As you can imagine, if you have more values stored there, the processor needs to move fewer of them to and from memory.

APX builds on that idea. Intel introduced it in 2023, and it expands the x86 instruction set with access to more registers and other performance improvements.

“The extensions provide efficient performance gains across a variety of workloads without significantly increasing the silicon area or power consumption of the core,” Intel explained in a technical document updated in October 2024.

“Intel APX doubles the number of general-purpose registers (GPRs) from 16 to 32. This allows the compiler to keep more values in registers,” the company noted.

How APX could make Windows 11 apps faster

Microsoft and Intel are working closely to make the most of APX, and the performance improvements in Windows 11 will go beyond just OS-related areas.

Intel confirmed that APX has an interesting approach to helping apps run faster, and I am not talking about Windows 11’s recent Low Latency Profile. With APX, software can reduce some of the work the processor needs to do.

“As a result, code compiled with Intel APX contains 10% fewer loads and more than 20% fewer stores than the same code compiled for an Intel® 64 baseline,” Intel explained.

Intel also confirmed that it found 10% fewer instructions in code compiled with APX, so it could even help developers compile their apps faster. It’s one of the areas where Intel has been lagging behind. However, these figures come from a prototype, so the numbers are not final and could go either way.

This also doesn’t mean Windows 11 will run 10% or 20% faster when this change becomes available, and Microsoft hasn’t yet provided benchmark results for this toggle.

Right now, if the CPU makes the wrong guess about which path a program will take, it has to spend more time recovering and sideline other tasks it could have undertaken.

Intel says the new instructions let Windows apps avoid more of these hard-to-predict branches, and that should technically reduce the time wasted on recovery. This could improve performance in apps where these mistakes happen frequently.

However, flipping the APX switch in Windows 11’s settings won’t make every existing app faster. Intel says developers may need to update their apps to use APX. They can take advantage of it through “simple recompilation,” and “source code changes are not expected to be needed.”

Which CPUs will support APX, and will it come to existing PCs?

Windows Latest understands that Nova Lake will support APX, and Intel’s own compiler documentation confirms APX for Diamond Rapids.

Processor family APX support Are you getting it?
Intel Nova Lake APX is listed in GCC’s processor documentation. An upcoming consumer CPU family expected to benefit once Windows and software support are ready.
Intel Diamond Rapids Intel has documented APX support. A Xeon server family, rather than a processor upgrade for your existing Windows laptop.
Intel Alder Lake, Raptor Lake, Meteor Lake, Lunar Lake, Arrow Lake, and Panther Lake These families do not support APX. A Windows update cannot add the missing CPU capability.

And yes, APX could eventually reach AMD processors too. AMD’s Robert Hormuth has discussed APX as part of its collaboration with Intel, but that doesn’t confirm a particular Ryzen model or make an existing Ryzen PC APX-compatible, so I have not included it in the above table.

Existing PCs can already benefit from the Low Latency Profile, and it could cover more of Windows

You can’t simply force-enable APX on existing PCs because it requires CPU-level changes, but Microsoft is testing other performance improvements for all existing PCs.

As you may be aware, Windows 11 now supports Low Latency Profile, which originally covered the Start menu, Search, Notification Center, and Quick Settings, before Microsoft expanded it to app launches with the August 2026 update. In Windows Latest’s tests on an existing Raptor Lake PC, apps such as Chrome, Calculator, and even the WebView2-based Weather app opened faster after the update.

Low Latency Profile is enabled by default and simply uses a brief CPU boost when you launch apps or OS-related features. You don’t need a new instruction set for that, and in our earlier tests, the difference was easier to notice on older or lower-end PCs.

Windows Latest understands that Microsoft eventually plans to expand Low Latency Profile to cover more of Windows, including file launches and OS settings.

If anything, Windows is clearly getting faster for all PC owners, and we’ll learn more about Microsoft’s plans early next year.
