title: Canonical dev mocks up an Ubuntu launcher that uses AI
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
What would deeper AI integration on the Ubuntu desktop look like? Well, you don’t need to think too hard to find out.

A Canonical engineer has published a prototype launcher that simulates how on-device AI could be used to enhance and aid users of the Ubuntu desktop.

But the warty-prototype1 snap by Didier Roche-Tolomelli (aka didrocks) is not a real launcher. It’s a semi-interactive, automated mockup. It simulates things a user could do, and that includes interacting with a (theoretical) on-device AI model to complete tasks.

The Snap Store listing refers to it as a ‘design-discussion prototype of the next Ubuntu launcher’.

An intriguing choice of words – that’s as far as I’d read into it for now, though. A hint of a possible future feature perhaps, but not quite a commitment to shipping or actually building this as a real thing.

A launcher and a prompt box

I installed the prototype and ran through the simulated tasks to get an idea of what (there’s a menu full of them). The launcher itself is triggered by a small Ubuntu logo in the top panel and is only ostensibly interactive.

One simulated task saw the launcher used to find a local image file (using the file filter). The launcher’s AI box is used, and the model is asked to set the image as the desktop wallpaper and adjust the system accent colour to match.

In another, the “Followup with AI…” is used to find a suitable app the user can install to open an ePub. Matches from the Snap Store filter back inside of the launcher, complete with install buttons, which then trigger an installation. Nice.

And another, and to my mind more impressive use-case demo tasks AI with creating an add-able calendar itinerary from a handful of items selected from the clipboard history. Press play on the video embed below to watch that:

It’s intended to function as a regular launcher too, e.g., opening apps, findings files, picking emoji, clipboard history, finding open browser tabs and reviewing recent ‘tasks’.

Throughout the simulation results appear with all kinds of icons and actions to manipulate or manage them inside of the launcher, making this more of an active tool than a passive one.

Much like Apple’s (more capable) Spotlight in recent versions of macOS, in that regard. It’s not hard to imagine how the launcher could be extended further, to handle more than simple find-and-retrieve tasks.

We do know Canonical is keen to ‘ramp up’ AI features in Ubuntu. It released the Myna AI dictation tool in tech preview this month, and its engineers are using LLMs and agentic coding tools for various efforts, infra management, etc.

But the company has also said it won’t be bolting AI on for its own sake. Any integrations it does explore will, even in this ‘simulation’, be predicated around practical use-cases and making use of on-device AI models.

Try the demo (remember it’s a demo)

You can install the warty-prototype launcher demo from the Snap Store. It will run on most supported Ubuntu releases:

sudo snap install warty-prototype --edge

Once installed, launch it from the command-line. Click the Ubuntu icon in the top panel to reveal the launcher (and the menu of simulations to see in action).

Just keep in mind that you can’t use this to do anything. It’s a launcher mockup, not a real tool. It won’t integrate with your system, find your apps or double-up as your therapist-cum-psychosis-inducer.

  1. For those wondering why ‘warty’, that was the codename of the first Ubuntu release – so named as the first version was likely to be a bit of a unrefined one. ↩︎

title: Epic’s new vibe-coded games launcher is available on Ubuntu
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Epic Games has confirmed that Fortnite is coming to Linux, and the launcher it will arrive through is available to try in preview on Ubuntu – a vibe-coded wonder that’s been royally roasted on the internet.

The gaming company has also announced a rebuilt version of its anti-cheat tech for Linux, which will be required to run Fortnite to Linux. Easy Anti-Cheat v2‘s stricter system requirements include a signed kernel and TPM 2.0.

Easy Anti-Cheat has been available on Linux for a while, including for PC games running via Proton. Not all games developers trust or use it as it’s not considered as robust or tamper-proof as the Windows version. V2 is more stringent.

Now, the nuances of anti-cheat is not something I can dive into (as I am not a gamer). Epic has listed the system requirements its new version needs to work (and thus any games that rely on it), and rationale on why.

Playing a protected game (one that needs uses anti-cheat) will require running a Linux kernel ‘signed with a well-known key’ (which Canonical’s Ubuntu Linux kernel is). Kernel modules added in, like NVIDIA GPU drivers, mist also be signed by a reputable outfit.

Those aren’t the only hurdles.

A Linux gaming rig must have Secure Boot turned on and IOMMU support enabled in its BIOS; a TPM 2.0 must be present; the kernel BPF LSM kernel modules have to be loaded, and kexec must be disabled. Plus… Well, a fair bit that sounds effort-y.

Epic is reaching out to Linux distros and asking Linux distros to reach out to it to get them on board with EAC v2’s requirements. Notably, the Steam Deck does not support the required features right now. Epic says its working with Valve.

Clearly aware of the palaver, and perhaps the buy-in needed, Epic suggests gamers may wish to maintain their own separate bootloader entry with the mandated kernel features and security bits enabled, and boot from this to play a protected game.

Epic’s vibe-coded new launcher

Epic hasn’t said, thus far, when to expect Fortnite’s Linux release, but it’ll be available through a new version of the Epic Games Launcher, which is now in preview.

Noting that “programming is hard”, Epic chose to vibe-code its new games launcher and is quite proud of the fact. It’s even boosting about how much faster it is than Valve’s Steam client.

The initial preview is light on features, say Epic, which does say there is a shopping cart, so poking fun at Valve’s Steam client is not a fair comparison (or a well-spirited one if Fornite for Linux will run via Proton, as some suggest it will).

Reactions to Epic’s proudly vibe-coded launcher have not been kind. Some Linux users trying it have already reported a fleet of issues, including being unable to download the Unreal Engine in-app.

If you want to try it out on Ubuntu and see if the derision is earned, it’s in preview with an AppImage build for Linux.

Download the AppImage from Epic Games, mark it executable, then double-click to open. Sign in with a valid Epic account and your library and cloud saves should appear. It’s in preview, so don’t expect miracles, but do expect it to improve.

Well, maybe.

If you’re an Epic gamer (I’m sorry) running Linux I’d love to know what you think of the new launcher, and whether the roasting its received on Reddit and X to date is deserved…

title: KeePassXC 2.8 released with Qt6, support for Wayland auto-type
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
If KeePassXC is your password-management app of choice on Linux, the new 2.8.0 update is going to please.

KeePassXC 2.8.0 sees some “long-awaited new features” arrive, including a Qt6 port of the main app interface, auto-type support on Wayland via XDG Desktop Portals, fingerprint unlock and a new experimental Aarch64 AppImage.

The Qt6 port has been a long-gestating effort. There’s no dramatic change to the way that KeePassXC looks and behaves (maybe a bit sharper on HiDPI), but it also benefits from being able to access improvements in platform capabilities, security and so on.

Auto-type is what allows your saved login details to be entered into another app’s username, password, etc fields without copying and pasting. Wayland security protocols meant this wasn’t an easy-add, but it’s now present.

KeePassXC 2.8.0 adds Quick Unlock for fingerprint unlocking (via PolKit) on Linux, which saves the need to type in a master password each session. It also adds remote database support from locations such as WebDAV or SFT.

Users of the Linux AppImage benefit from various buffs, among which come TLS tweaks to reduce errors when site/provider favicons are downloaded, as well as when checking for updates.

The AppImage creates and refreshes its desktop menu entry, and uses systemd-run when available to make Wayland Auto-Type work on GNOME and KDE if using the AppImage.

Other changes of note:

  • Keyboard shortcuts are now configurable
  • App lockups on systems with <2 CPU cores solved
  • keyutils is included in the KeePassXC snap
  • Generate RSA, ECDSA, and Ed25519 keys
  • Proton Pass import now supports Wi-Fi & SSH keys

Plus, further work, fixes and security patches. The official changelog on GitHub provides a detailed list of everything that’s changed in this update.

Install KeePassXC on Ubuntu

KeePassXC is free, open-source software. It can be downloaded from the official website page for all major OSes. Ubuntu users can also use the KeePassXC PPA or install it from Flathub, both methods being fully supported.

While there is an official KeePassXC snap maintained by the team, it is not fully supported and the team would prefer users looking for a sandboxed format to run the Flatpak instead.

title: Still Roaring: Bluefin Classic and LTS
author: Juan Resendiz
summary: I want to start this by clearing the air: the Bluefin you know and love is going nowhere! It's still here, just with a new look and a few new raptor wranglers at the helm. Let me start by introducing myself. I'm Juan Resendiz, I'm from Florida and I do nerd stuff over at Concept To Cloud during the day. I heard Jorge's call and he had me sold at dinosaurs. Linux was the cherry on top.
content:
I want to start this by clearing the air: the Bluefin you know and love is going nowhere! It's still here, just with a new look and a few new raptor wranglers at the helm. Let me start by introducing myself. I'm Juan Resendiz, I'm from Florida and I do nerd stuff over at Concept To Cloud during the day. I heard Jorge's call and he had me sold at dinosaurs. Linux was the cherry on top.

When I decided to step up I had no idea what I was getting myself into. Heck, I still don't! But what I do know is I believe in Jorge's vision for operating systems, and my mission is to continue the hard work he and the team before me started. Now I'm not saying they've gone anywhere: they've been awesome with the transition and I can honestly say I feel very comfortable already thanks to the mentorship and guidance of everyone involved.

But now to why we are all here. The original and classic Bluefin you all know is now Bluefin Classic. And Bluefin LTS is still LTS... it isn't going anywhere either. For those who are just here to know if it will continue to get supported and don't really care for the tech talk, rest assured: your friends, parents and grandparents will still be good to go. For the rest of my tech folks, read on.

What's changing​

Bluefin Classic will still be under Universal Blue. The only thing that will be changing is we will pull directly from Fedora now. We are currently testing with the F44 and F45 beta versions of the swap. F45 is on track for October. You do not have to do anything except for the normal updates as they come. You are good to go and still supported. We are going nowhere.

So what does "pull directly from Fedora" actually mean? Today Classic is built on top of a Universal Blue base image, which sits on top of Fedora Silverblue. With the new setup Classic builds straight on Fedora's own Silverblue image instead. One less layer in the middle, and updates come right from Fedora. Same Bluefin on top, same apps, same ujust, same everything you're used to.

We're also testing more than ever. Classic now passes the Project Bluefin testsuite's common checks, so every image gets booted and poked at, not just built. And the weekly updates keep rolling like always: stable still lands every Tuesday (recent ones brought kernel 7.2). Oh, and Classic got its own look too: a shiny new Bluefin Classic wordmark from the awesome Delphic Melody.

LTS, the honest part. It had a rough summer, which is why :lts hasn't updated since July. Builds are green again on x86 and ARM, the boot hang is fixed, and Project Bluefin LTS ships daily. Getting :lts updated is next. But it will be getting a bit of a bigger change. It's moving its home to Project Bluefin, but you don't need to do anything today. Also: we're working on DX for LTS so nobody gets left behind, and we'll post before anyone moves.

If the move isn't ready, it doesn't happen. Simple as that.

What you need to do​

Nothing! Seriously. Whether you're on Classic or LTS, keep updating like you always have. If anything ever changes for you, you'll hear about it here first.

What about Dakota and Utah?​

I've seen this one a lot, so let's clear it up. Dakota is its own thing, built a totally different way, and moving to it means a fresh install. Utah is the new one built on Fedora Hummingbird. Neither one is replacing Classic. If you're happy on Classic, stay on Classic. As Jorge put it: "you would just stay on what you have."

For the curious though: I've been testing switching from Classic to Utah in VMs, from both F44 and F45. It boots, your files and SSH keys come along for the ride, and you can roll right back to Classic if you change your mind. When that's ready for everyone it'll be an opt-in ujust command. Nobody gets moved without asking.

How you can help​

Run Classic or LTS? You're already helping! If something breaks, tell us: open an issue on GitHub or drop it in #dev-classic. Want to go further? Test the images and PRs. murphym18's builder and the testsuite make that a lot less painful than it used to be.

Thank you​

None of this is a one person job. Huge thanks to Jorge for the ZFS fix and for keeping the merges moving, murphym18 for jumping into reviews, testing images on his own machine and building a tool that makes testing every Classic image way less painful, James (hanthor) for the ARM fix and for getting us the access we needed, Robin for the LTS reviews and merges, bsherman for keeping the CentOS builds around so the move has room to breathe, and Danathar and Kyle Rankin for the testsuite reviews. You all made a new guy feel right at home.

Also a big shout out to Delphic Melody for the Classic and LTS wordmarks, and to JF and inffy for jumping in to answer questions and point us in the right direction.

Where to find us​

Got questions, found a bug, or just want to say hi? Come find us in #dev-classic on the Project Bluefin Discord, or drop a comment on the Classic and LTS discussion on GitHub. I'll be around.

Here's the discussion: Handing off ublue-os/bluefin and bluefin-lts to the next generation. And keep an eye out, the November wallpaper fix is on its way.

Classic and LTS are still roaring, and we plan on keeping it that way. 🦖

title: Ubuntu rolls out php2shell, eMudhra certificate fixes
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Ubuntu has released security updates for the php2shell PHP flaw that’s led to websites being taken offline, and a key compromise at the eMudhra certificate authority.

Desktop Ubuntu isn’t directly affected by php2shell, since PHP isn’t installed by default. The certificate issue is more of a browser-based concern, though Google, Apple, Mozilla et al blocked the bad certificates on 17 October.

Ubuntu’s ca-certificates package update removes two root certificates from the list Ubuntu trusts, both of whom had vouched for eMudhra. This will help protect tools like curl and wget that don’t use their own lists.

Open Software Updater to check for any updates available on your setup1, and install them

You may have already heard about the security vulnerabilities since both have received mainstream media coverage over the past few days, php2shell in particular.

php2shell is the name given to two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which affect the PHP interpreter. A bug could enable an attacker with network access to run code through any PHP application without logging in.

PHP is used by around 70% of websites, including WordPress-based ones like this one, so the scale of the exploit is potentially huge. Many legacy websites tick over year-on-year with minimal maintenance, running on outdated versions of PHP…

On the CVSS 4.0 severity scale, php2shell score 9.2 – critical. Cloudflare has already seen attack traffic aimed at the bugs, but it hasn’t said whether any succeeded.

The eMudhra security key compromise, if exploited, would allow attackers to create fake security certificates for websites and impersonate legitimate servers.

Just update, innit

If you run Ubuntu on a server, cloud or somewhere else you think PHP may be involved, it’s best to make the effort the go and update (or check your host provider for details on when they will) to be sure.

All Ubuntu versions with php5 or newer are affected2, but only Ubuntu versions still supported by Canonical (14.04 LTS through 26.04 LTS, and 26.103) will receive the fix – which can be applied along any other updates:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

On servers, upgrading everything isn’t always viable, so the package can be upgraded singularly. Canonical say any app or service that uses the PHP interpreter should be also be restarted manually if a full system reboot isn’t possible.

Say safe!

  1. If PHP isn’t installed, you won’t get the PHP fix – you don’t need it – but ca-certificates is preinstalled ↩︎
  2. While PHP only supports v8.1 and newer, Canonical backports critical fixes for supported Ubuntu releases, so as far php5 on Ubuntu 14.04 LTS is patched. ↩︎
  3. Ubuntu 14.04, 16.04 and 18.04 LTS only get the update if Ubuntu Pro is enabled. ↩︎

title: PS5 Linux hack now supports (some) newer firmware versions
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
You may recall hearing the PS5 can now run Linux. The catch was that it needed a console running much older firmware, long before Sony nixed the exploits used.

Well, the jailbreak door is ajar again (‘get a better metaphor, Joey’ – the world).

The new pLinux5-NG project adapts the old PS5 Linux bootloader to use a different set of exploits: Relapse jailbreak and Byepervisor-Reborn, the latter to circumvent the console’s hypervisor protections.

It allows booting Linux on PS5 consoles with newer firmware versions than previously required, as recent as July 2026’s v13.60. But – catch time – this particular effort only supports firmware 13.20.

Sony’s newest 14.x firmware also block the exploits used by this. As PSN access requires the latest system software, casual gamers with piqued interest in jailbreaking may find they’re more interested in using it as intended.

Rewarding benchmarks show promise

Now, most PS5 owners aren’t hankering to run GIMP or browse the web in Firefox on their console. The main aspiration is to use Sony’s gaming hardware as a regular Linux gaming PC and run Steam titles, etc.

Tests on older firmware did show some interesting results. GTA V Enhanced reportedly ran at close to 60fps at 1440p. While those kind of results don’t map to the new bootloader on more recent firmware, it shows merit in the undertaking.

A PS5 will never be a practical Linux gaming PC. It’s far less hassle (and expense, for those needing to buy an un-updated console) to build, buy or upgrade a traditional PC.

But hackporting efforts like this aren’t really so much about ‘why’ as ‘why not.

Every firmware revision that can be made to run Linux – whatever the leaps and hurdles involved – brings the whole idea of running PC games on a PS5 a little closer to reality.

(via notebookcheck)

title: Firefox 158.0.1 brings eMudhra certificate security fixes
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Mozilla Firefox 158.0.1 is rolling out with some important security fixes.

Now, I don’t tend to cover Firefox point releases as mainly ship minor fixes for things the majority of users won’t have noticed were wrong in the first place. The Firefox 158.0.1 update is more ‘meaty’ than usual fare.

Among the security advisories this update covers are eight intermediate certificates belonging to the eMudhra certificate authority, whose private keys were compromised.

Anyone holding those keys could issue certificates that browsers accept as genuine for any website. If they can also intercept a user’s connection, they could impersonate the site and read or alter the traffic.

Most Firefox users were already protected as Mozilla revoked the certificates on 17 October (within hours of being notified) using OneCRL, which works in the background.

Even so, Firefox 158.0.1 bundles the revocation into this update. Users whose network policies or other settings disable OneCRL updates get covered when upgrading to this release.

Bug fixes in this build resolve the usual grab-bag of issues, including:

  • Websites jumping to the top of the page during text selection
  • Built-in VPN unable to activate for some users
  • Firefox windows on the wrong monitor on Linux multi-monitor setups
  • Some JPEG XL format showing semi-transparent areas too dark

The update is already live. If you use Firefox on Windows or macOS, or run the Linux binary builds, you’ll get the update in-app next time you run it. If Firefox is installed from a repo or alternative store, you’ll need to install it manually.

Ubuntu users running the Firefox Snap will receive this update automatically in the background, and it will apply on the next app restart.

(via soeren-hentzschel.at)

title: Give Nautilus file manager the ‘Computer’ view it lacks
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
The Nautilus file manager is great for browsing your files and folders, but it lacks a dedicated way to see all your drives a how much space is left on each – but you can add one.

Nautilus My Computer is a third-party view for GNOME Files providing a centralised page listing drives, with storage usage bars to show which mounts, volumes, partitions, etc., have room to spare and which are getting full.

Drives can be interacted with like folders, so double-click on one to enter it or right-click to access options to open it in new tab, or window or to unmount or eject, etc., depending on the drive/mount type.

A ‘Preferred Folders’ section sits at the top of the view showing common folders and locations. This can be managed; you can pin your most-used folders here for quicker access and remove the things you don’t find useful.

The overview page can present as a big or compact view, the different being visible in the in the screenshot at the top of this article.

A customisable computer view

Right-click Computer at the top of the sidebar to open the add-on’s settings. From there, you can customise which drives are shown, including system partitions like EFI, boot and swap, and whether to show drives separated by type or merged together.

You can also change the colour of usage bars shown beneath drives if the default system accent colour isn’t your vibe. And if you want Nautilus to open in My Computer view each time you start it (rather than your Home folder), there’s a toggle for that.

Nautilus My Computer also gives you greater control over Nautilus’ sidebar, letting you hide entries like as Recent or Starred, and change sidebar icons for bookmarks and locations, which is great when adding custom folders.

Miller columns in Nautilus? Oh yes

This add-on also offers an optional (beta-grade) Column View that offers Miller-style browsing. Select a folder to see its contents in the next column, keeping the folders above in view so you can see where you are.

And yes, you can drag and drop files between columns too, which is useful.

Selecting a file (rather than folder) in column view pens a file preview column showing simple file stats. Multiple selected files are rendered as a stack, as in Finder on macOS, with a combined file size for the selection.

Install Nautilus My Computer on Ubuntu

To use this you need to add a third-party repository and install a package from outside of Ubuntu’s official, supported archives.

You can install My Computer view from a PPA maintained by the developer. It has a pre-built package for Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (resolute) with GNOME 50, but support for 26.10 (stonking) is planned:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:yannmasoch/nautilus-my-computer
sudo apt install nautilus-my-computer

Fully quit/restart Nautilus after installing this to ensure it drops into place.

Worth installing?

Nautilus had a traditional Computer view of its own in the past, but it was removed in 2012, since it duplicated entries in the sidebar. Drives could later be accessed from Other Locations, but that view got retooled in GNOME 47 as a Network section

Since mounts/drives appear in the sidebar, the Properties dialog shows free space and getting to / requires a click on the path bar and a key press, there’s arguably no need for a dedicated view.

Still, that doesn’t mean such a view isn’t convenient for some. This effort gives those who miss one, the ability to have one.

But as a third-party integration that patches itself into Nautilus (not an official GNOME feature or using an official API), you should only install this if you’re aware it may be broken by future system updates to Nautilus and may affect the file manager’s stability.

Thanks to Kinggo!

title: BleachBit 6.0.6 fixes admin cleaning on Linux
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
BleachBit, the free, open-source and cross-platform system cleaning utility has a new maintenance release out – with support for Ubuntu 26.10.

BleachBit 6.0.6 introduces cleaners for the Helium browser and Docker Desktop (including its AI assistant).

This update also boosts app startup times, and makes deep scan, file deletion and file wiping faster, the latter now wiping in 512 KiB blocks rather than 4 KiB.

A few preexisting cleaners now extend to more areas.

Stale crash reports, GPU caches and session files for Claude, VS Code-based editors and Chromium can (optionally; variously) be expunged with this update. LibreWolf cleaning now covers .deb and Flatpak versions of the browser on Linux.

For Ubuntu users, BleachBit 6.0.6 is able to detect and remove more snap revisions (you can remove revisions manually if you run low on space, which if you install Myna on Ubuntu and try out various AI models, the revision backups add up).

It also brings an official .deb installer for Ubuntu 26.10, which is welcome.

Elsewhere on Linux, issues running BleachBit as Administrator (a separate mode for cleaning system files) on RedHat were resolved by using pkexec. This is also recommended if using admin mode on Ubuntu with a .deb-installed build.

Windows users gain plenty of plenty of platform-specific fixes, and a new(ish) logo, as the familiar BleachBit icon is now placed on a square. An SVG icon is shipped for Linux and BSD too.

Work on the BleachBit macOS port continues. This update hooks up cleaners for Adobe Acrobat, Claude, Devin, GIMP, Google Earth, TeamViewer, Visual Studio Code, VLC, Zen browser and Zoom.

You can download BleachBit from the official website, which has installers and runtimes for all major operating system, including .deb and AppImage options for Ubuntu.

title: Audacious 4.6.2 fills the last gaps in its Qt Winamp mode
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
A small update to the Audacious music player is out, with its Qt Winamp interface now offering ‘feature parity’ with the GTK version.

Audacious 4.6.2 allows Winamp skin files to be dropped on the main window to install them when running in Qt mode, shows advanced skin selection in the settings window and improves X11/XWayland support for showing on all workspaces.

Other improvements in this update to the newer 4.6.x series, and the first since June 2026, include a boost to accessibility as toolbar buttons, including player controls, can be cycled through using keyboard tab and arrow keys.

Seeking in SID audio files and the MPRIS OpenUri method have also been added.

Bug fixes resolve issues running the player with Qt 6.12 on Wayland and playing short audio files under PipeWire. The StreamTuner radio plugin was fixed (and respects proxy settings), and AAC audio files show quality and channels values in the Song Info panel.

Finally, Audacious once again builds on Linux distributions lacking statx support (which are mainly older releases using older kernel versions).

For those unfamiliar with it, Audacious is a free, open-source music player that is highly configurable and modular. It can be run with GTK or Qt UIs, both of which can load a classic Winamp-style interface.

Install Audacious 4.6.2

You can download Audacious for Windows, macOS and Linux from the official project website, or fetch the source code from GitHub. 

You can also get Audacious on Flathub (unverified, and v4.6.2 isn’t present there at the time of writing). There is an unofficial Audacious snap on the Snap Store, but it’s a few releases behind the current one. Not advised.

title: NordVPN 6.0 for Linux is coming – with ‘breaking’ changes
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
NordVPN are updating their Linux app to offer a “cleaner, simpler way to manage VPN connections” from the command line.

The NordVPN 6.0 update, which is coming soon (so not out yet), “cuts down” the number of commands that “overlap”. The company say this will make it easier for users to enable and configure VPN settings.

Among the changes, NordVPN 6.0 combines protocol and technology settings in a nordvpn set protocol command, while obfuscation is now handled by NordWhisper, rather than a separate setting.

And now that standard servers support P2P traffic, there’s no longer any need to create a dedicated P2P server group and then connect to it.

As part of the cleanup, some commands have been removed, including virtual server selection (as it’s now handled automatically).

Some commands have been renamed, with whitelist changed to allowlist, and the overly wordy threatprotectionlite shortened to just protection.

More details on the upcoming changes are available on the NordVPN blog.

Changes aren’t backward compatible

NordVPN say some of the ‘breaking changes’ will affect scripts, cron jobs, systemd units, etc. that interface with its CLI. They’re therefore signposting all of this in advance, so users have time to update any affected configurations before it lands.

As NordVPN 6.0 stores its settings differently, once users have upgraded to v6.0, they won’t be able to downgrade to an earlier version and retain their settings, as the new format isn’t backward compatible.

Doesn’t affect GUI users

If you use the NordVPN Linux GUI introduced last year, these changes won’t materially alter how you use the app or configure its features, though some server and obfuscation settings are presented a little differently.

Additionally, NordVPN lets users download WireGuard setup files for their servers. These aren’t new, but make it easier to set up VPN connections manually on routers, Linux devices, NAS, etc. that support WireGuard.

No release date for NordVPN 6.0 is given (that I can see), but expect it to arrive sooner rather than later.

Get NordVPN Linux app on the Snap Store

title: Tiling Shell now supports mouse button layout activation
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
A new version of the Tiling Shell GNOME extension is out, adding support for GNOME 51 and a faster way to tile app windows using nothing but your mouse.

Tiling Shell v18.0 lets you use your right mouse button for tiling system activation. It’s feature fans of Tiling Shell had requested, many accustomed to it from Windows’ PowerToys’ FancyZones.

You click your left button to grab and drag the window then, with it held, hold the right mouse button to trigger the on-screen tiling layout. Release the left button over a zone and the window snaps to it – no keys needed.

It sounds more laborious than it feels in use, here’s a quick video demo:

The “right mouse button” tiling option is not enabled by default, so if you want to try this out, you’ll need to open the extension’s settings dialog and enable it.

It adds to Tiling Shell’s compliment of ways to manage windows. That include drag-and-drop zones, keyboard shortcuts and the ability to right-click GTK windows and choose a position from the context menu – pick and choose the ones that work for you.

Tiling Shell v18’s other changes

This update also resolves issue with scaling. If you found the snap assistant, menu, layout editor and other UI elements looked excessively large on your desktop when fractional scaling was enabled, things should look normal again now.

You can now set a shortcut to un-tile all windows from a tiling layout at once, which is nifty, and decide if changing the active layout on one workspace, changes it for all workspaces.

And there’s an additional (still optional) “raise together” behaviour to limit this behaviour to the current display, so tiled windows on other monitors aren’t raised with it.

Installing the extension

If you want to try it out, this update is available on the GNOME Extensions website, where it works with GNOME 45 through 51 (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or later and you’re good).

While Ubuntu 26.10 has its own layout picker to drop windows on to, Tiling Shell lets you create, edit and switch between your own custom layouts.

Existing users get this update automatically, though it will only apply after logging out and back in – if you’ve not done so for a few days, a reminder to.

When using Tiling Shell on Ubuntu, turn off the built-in Tiling Assistant extension. This will avoid conflicts between two competing approaches. Go to Settings > Ubuntu Desktop > Enhanced Tiling and slide the toggle off.

Get Tiling Shell on GNOME Extensions

title: Linux 7.3 is out, speeds up ext4 and low-VRAM AMD GPUs
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Linus Torvalds has announced the release of Linux 7.3, a new mainline kernel – the one Ubuntu 26.10 is running on.

Linux 7.3 is another big update, improving gaming performance for AMD GPUs with low VRAM, boosting ext4 I/O and reworking how the kernel splits CPU time between groups of apps to improve efficiency.

It’s expected to become the new Long Term Support version.

Writing on the Linux kernel mailing list, Torvalds said: “It’s Sunday afternoon, and this week I somehow kept my wits together long enough to keep track of the day of the week, so the release isn’t randomly delayed. Will wonders never cease?”.

They might, sadly – so must this article’s intro. On to the recap.

Linux 7.3 features

Better AMD performance with low VRAM

If your AMD graphics card has a limited amount of video memory (VRAM), Linux 7.3 handles tight memory situations better thanks to a new approach to resource allocation.

Previously, if VRAM filled up while running multiple apps, the kernel allocated space on a first-come, first-served basis. If you opened, say, a game late, it could be forced off the card’s faster VRAM and into system RAM (GTT).

In Linux 7.3, the kernel can ‘evict’ other apps’ unprotected background data out of VRAM to make room for tasks with higher priority, like a game requesting protected memory.

Valve’s Natalie Vock did the work. In tests with Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, the change allowed the game to run well on an 8GB GPU even when the settings were adjusted to push memory needs towards 9GB of VRAM.

It’s only part of the work; further VRAM management changes are on the way in future kernel releases.

Older AMD GPU and CPU fixes

The past few kernels have delivered fixes and tune-ups for older graphics cards, and that trend isn’t letting up yet.

DRM format modifiers (labels, in effect, that describe how an image buffer looks) are now available on AMD Radeon GPUs from the HD 7000 series (GCN 1.0), boosting performance in some cases and improving support for Vulkan-based Wayland compositors.

Meanwhile, old AMD Athlon XP (as well as some Intel Pentium III/Celeron) CPUs can use the SFENCE instruction for memory-write ordering without needing SSE2, resolving an incorrect requirement in earlier kernels.

There is, of course, more AMD (and Intel) work in this release, but it’s for hardware that isn’t out yet (and won’t be for a while). I prefer to focus on improvements for things you use, rather than report that an upcoming GPU barely works a bit better now.

Faster cgroup CPU scheduling

Linux 7.3 rejigs how the kernel shares CPU time between apps and services, aiming to keep systems responsive when background tasks are competing for resources.

The scheduler now allocates CPU time between groups of processes that run mainly on the CP and moves cgroups to a single run queue to reduce latency. A new concur mode has been made default, albeit with the option to restore the old behaviour.

The cover note said the new default was chosen in the hope that it “serves more people than it hurts“. Cgroup scheduling has been a focal point of gripes about tardiness, so changes in this area will be welcomed.

Tests by scheduler maintainer Peter Zijlstra earlier in the year showed promising results, with one game’s minimum frame rate raised from 3.8fps to 20.6fps with 8 heavy background processes, and its average frame rate bumped from 48fps to 57.2fps.

Faster ext4 reads and writes

Ext4, Ubuntu’s default filesystem, sees a set of welcome performance boosts. Parallel direct I/O writes (which skip the page cache) are faster, as is fallocate(), and a buffered-write regression was fixed.

Ext4 (and XFS) also speed up small, direct reads from disks.

Tests by a ByteDance engineer, using a PCIe Gen5 NVMe SSD, saw 4K random-read performance leap from 1.92 million to 2.19 million operations per second. Gains were higher when using io_uring to handle more reads at once.

The ntfs3 driver has basic support for alternate data streams, a Windows feature that lets files store extra data alongside their contents. The newer ntfs driver (optional since Linux 7.1) adds read-only support for Windows overlay filter (WOF) compression.

Steam Controller, MSI Claw & more hardware support

The 2026 Steam Controller bags an initial driver in Linux 7.3, and a new MSI Claw gamepad driver was added by Valve. The original Steam Controller driver adds support for more sensors.

The HyperX QuadCast 2 USB microphone now reports when it’s muted, and the kernel copes when the microphone of the Logitech PRO X Wireless headset is attached or detached.

The Logitech HID driver (used for mic) supports HID++ 2.0 reprogrammable buttons, which owners of the Logitech Signature M650 will be pleased to hear.

The pricey Pioneer DJ DJM-S11, a 2-channel DJ mixer, picks up USB audio support, and USB passthrough on the M-Audio Venom synthesiser was resolved, while internal mics are now detected on TUXEDO laptops based on the TongFang XxAF5xxx.

The kernel now checks USB-C cable capabilities for altmode support (e.g., DisplayPort and Thunderbolt) before it tries to use them, which should resolve issues with unsupported cables being assumed to support things they don’t.

Sensors on more ASUS motherboards, like the ProArt Z690-CREATOR WIFI and ROG CROSSHAIR X870E HERO, now report. Realtek’s 8922DE and 8922DE-VS PCI Wi-Fi adapters are newly supported too.

Apple M3 Pro, Max & Ultra support

Bring-up (very formative support) for Apple M3 Pro, Max and Ultra chips ships in this release (Linux 7.2 added initial support for the base M3). Don’t expect too much; the M3 support is early and not as immediately usable as the kernel’s M1 and M2 support.

Other Apple-related changes in Linux 7.3 see the kernel’s built-in SMB file server (ksmbd) gain optional support for Apple Time Machine. This will let Mac users use Linux-based network shares to back up their macOS systems.

And Apple’s Studio Display reliably works with AMD GPUs, as the AMDGPU DC (display core) driver copes with the monitor’s dual-stream tech better. Desktop compositors no longer see the Studio Display’s’ tiled 5K panel as two separate screens.

Other changes in Linux 7.3

Other notable improvements in this kernel:

  • sched_ext sub-schedulers let cgroups run BPF-based schedulers
  • Block devices support RWF_DONTCACHE for selective caching
  • New sandboxing technique with failfs & fchroot
  • SMB server support for Apple Time Machine
  • PID 1 and kernel threads now have separate filesystem states
  • New library APIs for common AES encryption modes
  • Up to 5x faster btrfs fsync operations (in some scenarios)
  • FUSE gains buffer pools and zero-copy I/O over io_uring
  • Nouveau adds NVDEC (needed for Vulkan Video in NVK)
  • Swap gains swap_ops structure to aid future improvements
  • Big TCP packets in UDP tunnels managed by VXLAN & GENEVE
  • Rust PowerPC support

Also added was a huge slab of LLM-assisted code to let hypervisors track virtual machine memory usage by marking page ranges as ‘no access’ to reclaim cold pages.

How to get Linux 7.3 on Ubuntu

Ubuntu 26.10 ships with Linux 7.3 out of the box, and will pick up the final release via software updates in the coming week or two. If you use Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, you’ll receive this kernel in the next HWE update, due early next year (2027).

On other Ubuntu releases, you can install Linux 7.3 at your own risk using Canonical’s mainline kernel builds. However, those are not recommended. They lack Ubuntu-specific patches and drivers. They come with zero support, get no security updates, etc.

If your system is working well, there is no reason to chase newer kernels for the sake of it.

Record breaker

Per stats from LWN, Linux 7.3 included 18,765 non-merge commits from over 3,000 developers. Of those, 807 were first-time kernel developers. That is a sizeable uptick in newbies.

The Linux 7.4 merge window will open tomorrow, when the fun starts anew. It’ll be interesting to see if it surpasses the new records set by this kernel.

title: Linux Mint’s new system monitor does more than you’d expect
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
December’s Linux Mint 27 release will include a brand new system monitor tool preinstalled.

The app is called Superlight (well, that’s the project and package name; the user-facing label is just System Monitor). It shows hardware, app and process usage, relays battery stats and has an interactive storage page to find out what files and folders are using the most space.

It’s still under active development, but I took it for a spin to see how it fares and what it offers. Keep in mind that more features may be added or changed between now and when it gets its first stable release.

Linux Mint’s Superlight is super nice

Superlight shows the Resources page each time you open it.

At the top is an “overall usage” graph. This plots CPU, GPU, RAM and Swap usage over the past 60 seconds on the same chart. Having a unified view makes it trivial to see what the machine is doing as a whole, at a glance.

It also has separate graphs tracking CPU core usage and network and storage activity, as well as ones for system temperature(s) and fan speed(s). Graphs are collapsible; when only one graph is visible, it’s larger.

There are separate views for viewing running apps and their respective process count, CPU usage and memory. Click a column header to sort items by value, or dragged to reposition them into an order you prefer.

Both the Apps and Processes pages have a search bar to filter by name. The Processes page also lets you filter by all, user, or system processes, and show them in a tree to reveal the parent–child relationships.

On laptops, Mint’s new system monitor app surfaces battery and power usage on a graph, along with estimated charging/discharging time and info, including make, model, technology, capacity, charge cycles and overall battery health.

The Storage page is something I didn’t expect to see in this app but, truth be told, it’ll be the one page I use the most as like a faster and more intuitive Disk Usage Analyser, making it easier to see what’s eating up space on a disk – local or external.

Storage also doubles up as a simple system cleaning tool. The “clear cache” button freed up 900MB of cruft on my test device’s internal 32GB eMMC (it’s a converted Chromebook).

Performance is good

In my test with the current development version, Superlight didn’t feel noticeably heavier than the out-going GNOME System Monitor in what it does1, though when the Resources page is in view with lots of graphs visible, they do spike upward.

It’s a promising start.

GNOME System Monitor is functional, but looks somewhat anachronistic among newer, modern-looking apps. Ubuntu chose to replace it with Resources, and other desktop environments have user-friendly offerings too – even COSMIC has its own.

Linux Mint’s option is promising.

Mint has plans to add viewing system logs to its new system monitor too, and there’s clearly scope to add some basic configuration options (interval times, being a main one).

One thing this app doesn’t do – yet – that other modern system monitors like Resources and Mission Center do is list component detail, e.g., CPU model, socket, instruction sets or memory timings, banks, and so on.

But as some hardware spec minutiae is surfaced in Linux Mint’s System Information tool, there’s an argument for keeping things focused here.

New terminal, archive and calendar apps coming

Superlight is not the only brand new app Linux Mint is working on. A new calendar and clock utility, ebook reader and archive manager are in the mix. And Velocitty is Linux Mint’s new terminal emulator, inspired by Ghostty and Pytxis2.

All of Mint’s new software is developed as part of the XApp Project. Other apps, like Pix, Thingy and Library are part of this. The aim is to develop a set of software that works well across any Linux desktop environment, not just Cinnamon.

  1. One modest irony to running any system monitor app that it uses system resources to report system resources. All that real-time probing, tracking and graph rendering doesn’t happen by magic. ↩︎
  2. But Mint doesn’t plan to add support for terminal profiles, containers or links like the latter app ↩︎

title: Now Playing Card shows media info for multiple apps at a time
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Now Playing Card is a GNOME Shell extension that shows track info and playback controls for every audio app and media tab open, all in one place – the panel or the Quick Settings menu.

GNOME’s default media controller (and the many now playing applets and add-ons I’ve written about in the past) is fine for what you’re playing at the time, but less good if you juggle multiple audio apps during your day.

With Now Playing Card, pausing one thing to start playing another doesn’t mean it vanishes. So the podcast and Spotify track you paused mid-way through to check out a YouTube video in your browser? They stick around, ready to resume.

Now Playing Card uses ‘cards’ for each player, with album art (size can be changed), player icon and a functional progress bar you can click on to seek (if the player supports it). Plus, playback controls, including loop and shuffle (where available).

Since multiple players being on pause could take up a lot of room in the applet, the extension uses an ‘accordion’ effect to make best use of space. Only one player card is enlarged at a time, the rest being compact until clicked.

It can also show the actively-plating track name, artist and control buttons on the panel too, which is the main use-case for these things (“what’s this track” – look up and see). You can choose the position, size, behaviour, etc of those via the extension’s settings.

Adding a bit of visual flourish to the label is an animated sound wave icon or, if you want to dial up the bling, a spectrum analyser with bars reacting to audio in real time. Mercifully, you can opt for no animated tic at all, if you’d rather.

A slew of visual customisation and behavioural settings are offered. Now Playing Card hides GNOME’s stock media controller in the notification/calendar pop-over (never sure what most people call it) when active.

I do find that applet text scaling is a little “off” compared to other applets I open, but perhaps accommodate multiple players – it can show up to 10 at a time – it kind of has to be smaller than standard to fit ’em in.

Not everything that plays audio and reports over MPRIS is something you might care about (browser auto-play videos, looking at you) so there is “ignore” list in settings to help you keep your card list from getting too noisy.

Want to try it? Now Playing Card is compatible with GNOME 45 to 51, which means if you’r reading from Ubuntu 24.04 LTS through to 26.10 you’re good to go.

Get Now Playing Card on GNOME Extensions

title: What’s new in the Ubuntu 26.10 flavours?
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Alongside the main edition, Ubuntu 26.10 brought new releases of community flavours, including Kubuntu, Xubuntu and a welcome return of Ubuntu MATE.

All of Ubuntu’s official flavours share the same foundations as the main release, with the Linux 7.3 kernel, Mesa 26.2 graphics drivers, updated tooling and support for installing snap packages from the Snap Store.

Read on for an overview of the key changes in some of the most popular Ubuntu flavours, and downloads links to grab an ISO if you feel like sampling one them first-hand.

Ubuntu 26.10 Flavour Recap

Xubuntu 26.10

Xubuntu 26.10 ships with Xfce 4.20, which gets bug fixes to improve stability and the burgeoning Wayland support (“for those adventurous enough to use it”, quip the team).

The Ristretto image viewer gains an option to shuffle images, improves printing and can open images from from web links. Xfce Terminal lowers its CPU usage and adds an option to turn off URL highlighting.

Screenshooter, the stock screenshot tool, can now take region and fullscreen screenshots on Wayland and removes its Imgur upload option. Catfish searches now start in the active folder. App updates loop in GIMP 3.2.6 for graphics work.

More details on the changes in the official Xubuntu 26.10 release notes.

Download Xubuntu 26.10

Ubuntu Kylin 26.10

Ubuntu Kylin 26.10 is largely a bug fix and package bump release, with no major user-facing changes. The Windows 7-style UKUI desktop environment is the same version included in the April release of 26.04.

There is, however, an eye-catching (AI generated) desktop wallpaper. It reworks Ubuntu’s official release mascot artwork1 (a stingray) in a fluid ‘glassmorphism’ style with iridescent pastel colour gradients.

Ubuntu Kylin 26.04’s background reinterpreted the mascot art (memorably, a photograph of a raccoon-shaped island surrounded by sea with upside-down seagulls flying over it), so I’m hoping this becomes a new tradition.

Download Ubuntu Kylin 26.10

Lubuntu 26.10

Lubuntu 26.10 ships with the LXQt 2.4.0 desktop, described upstream as “mostly bugfixes and code cleanup”, but with minor improvements, like a horizontal layout for the sound applet and transient notifications no long linger.

X11 is still the default desktop session in Lubuntu 26.10 but a Wayland session is included and available to select the login screen, based on Miriway.

Download Lubuntu 26.10

Ubuntu Unity 26.10

Ubuntu Unity 26.10 is a maintenance release that continues using Unity 7.7, albeit with a fresh set of bug fixes and code cleanups to move away from unmaintained packages.

The aim is keep the standard Unity desktop ticking over while the team works on a the long-awaited shift to Lomiri. On that front, Ubuntu Unity 26.10 ships with the Lomiri Calculator, Files and Terminal apps preinstalled.

Download Ubuntu Unity 26.10

Kubuntu 26.10

The Kubuntu 26.10 release announcement says it offers “the latest KDE Plasma2“. It actually comes with Plasma 6.7 not the newly-launched Plasma 6.8, but it’s still one version newer than what’s on the Kubuntu 26.04 release.

Multi-monitor users can now assigned virtual desktops to specific displays, and switch between them more easily with new keyboard shortcuts.

Other changes include theme and dark mode switching bugs, a glide effect on desktop notifications, timezone offset labels show in the Digital Clock widget and an option to enable type-ahead searching on the desktop.

As in its 26.04 release, a Plasma X11 desktop session not included, but can be installed manually. It will be the final release where that’s possible as Plasma 6.8 has dropped the plasma-session-x11 entirely.

Download Kubuntu 26.10

Ubuntu MATE 26.10

Ubuntu MATE is back with its 26.10 release, the first to be put out under its new maintainers. Not every MATE package has been updated to its newest upstream version, but what ones are included are said to be stable and offer bug fixes.

The flavour skipped the 26.04 LTS earlier this year. The release notes say this is the first release to incorporate Ubuntu’s switch to Dracut. It also drops gdei and sees ifupdown replaced with netplan.

Getting the flavour back on its feet under a new team was never going to be an overnight thing. While a fair number of ‘known issues’ are listed in this release (broken RedShift, missing icons, VM quirks), it’s good to see it back.

Download Ubuntu MATE 26.10

Ubuntu Studio

Ubuntu Studio 26.10 continues to cater to creatives of all types, but musicians will find more audio apps available to them, including Sonic Pi live-coding environment and SuperCollider for ‘algorithmic’ compositions.

A command-line white-noise generator, jnoise, is also available. Many other audio tools have been updated, as have a slew of other software, including newer versions of OBS Studio, GIMP, Ardour, Krita and Kdenlive.

The Ubuntu Studio installer now allows individual packages to be picked from meta packages, and the UI of the flavour’s audio configuration wizard has been streamlined.

Download Ubuntu Studio 26.10

Other flavours available too

Edubuntu 26.10 lets administrators pick individual packages from age-group software sets at install time and updates its Paperboy news reader for media literacy lessons in secondary and tertiary education.

Ubuntu Budgie 26.10 adds a new widget for finding and playing internet radio stations and supports automatic day/night wallpapers, while Ubuntu Cinnamon 26.10 updates its desktop to Cinnamon 6.6.9.

title: Microsoft Defender is now available on Linux desktops
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Microsoft Defender is now available for Linux desktops.

Shocked? In 2026, you shouldn’t be. Microsoft’s down with the penguins these days: there’s a Linux kernel in Windows, it owns GitHub and makes Edge for Linux (not that too many people use it).

Why not some rootin’-tootin’, threat-detectin’ n’ virus-protectin’ software on top, eh?

This article is in our Explainer format. An imaginary chat through the why, what and, often, whatever of some Linux news with zero obligation to sound excited about it. Expect snark.

Name: Microsoft Defender for Linux.

Age: Public preview, so, pass?

Appearance: A line item on an E5 invoice.

What is it? Microsoft’s security suite, now available for Linux desktops (albeit in a public preview).

Microsoft’s security suite. On Linux…. Where have you been? Defender has been available for Linux servers since 2020. Desktops were inevitable.

Why now? Microsoft says as “more developers begin to use Linux desktops” (begin?!) their devices become a target for attackers – but easy for company IT bods to overlook. Hence their pitch to “close that visibility gap”.

Fair enough. Does it run on Ubuntu? LTS releases only: Ubuntu 16.04 LTS through 26.04 LTS on Intel/AMD desktops, and 20.04 to 26.04 on Arm64.

—16.04? Any Linux server and kernel combo Defender already supports is on the desktop guest list. Debian, Fedora, RHEL, SLES, Rocky and, yes, ye olde Ubuntu LTS’ – doing their thing, hanging on via Ubuntu Pro’s ever-extending support periods.

How do I install it? You don’t. Your employer does. Rather, can. A standalone Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, or Microsoft 365 E5 or E7 is needed to use this. If reading that sentence left you looking blank, hurrah: proof this news won’t be fuel for the EEE truthers.

Let’s say I wanted this, can I buy it for my own laptop? Er, you’d need to talk to a Microsoft salesperson to find out more, I guess. This isn’t a shrink-wrapped product for home users.

How does my employer get it? It’s a preview, so they might not want to. If they are brave, they can – *puts on reading glasses, adopts LinkedIn voice* – “onboard eligible Linux workstations using any of the existing deployment methods”.

Is there an actual app? Not really, no. Desktops devices appear in the company’s admin portal alongside their Linux machines, be it a sever, a data centre stack or a battered, bruised and heavily stickered ThinkPad on an engineer’s desk

Thing is, I heard Linux doesn’t need antivirus. Is that true? Oh boy, here we go…

Do say: “Linux desktops are important enough to make an enterprise security roadmap!”

Don’t say: “Is it available as a snap yet?”

title: Ubuntu 26.10 is out with GNOME 51, Linux 7.3 & new tiling trick
author: OMG! Ubuntu!
content:
Ubuntu 26.10 has been released, with a faster way to tile windows, passkey sign-in at the login screen and a full set of Rust-based core utilities.

The newest interim release, supported for the next 9 months, ships GNOME 51, Mesa 26.2 and the Linux 7.3 kernel. Plus, a more capable App Center, new desktop ISOs for RISC-V hardware and expanded TPM-backed full-disk encryption.

Keen to know more? Here’s a rundown of what’s new, and what’s worth knowing before you install or upgrade to 26.10.

Ubuntu 26.10: What’s New?

Window tiling gets a drag-up layout picker

Ubuntu 26.10 debuts a newer, faster way to tile windows mid-drag.

When you start moving a window a layout picker peeks in from the top of the screen. Drag a window up towards it to expose the layout picker. Move a window over a zone to see a ghost preview of where the window will land. If happy, release to snap it in place.

Nifty? Sure, but also potentially annoying. Ubuntu doesn’t surface an easy way to turn it off out-of-the-box, but if you find the layout picker flitting in and out distracting on every window drag, this command disables the pop-up:

gsettings set org.gnome.shell.extensions.tiling-assistant enable-layout-picker false

To turn it back on, run the same command again, but put  true in place of false.

See if your PC is Ubuntu Certified (it probably isn’t)

Checking whether your laptop or PC is Ubuntu Certified is easier in 26.10: open Settings > System and find out.

Status checks go through the Ubuntu Hardware API via the hwctl client, which became a snap package in this release.

If your computer matches a certified device, the new Ubuntu Certified page says so. If it doesn’t, it says that too. And if it’s a close but not exact match, it tells you that as well and gives a link to a device listing page on the Ubuntu website to learn more.

Don’t fret if your device isn’t certified: most aren’t. The label is only given to devices whose OEM paid Canonical to test and maintain support for a specific version of Ubuntu.

Sign PDFs with your real signature

Document Viewer (aka Papers) lets you add handwritten signatures to PDFs and save them for future use. Draw one with your mouse, stylus/graphics tablet or touchscreen via the new canvas, or import a photo of your signature and let the app remove the background.

Signatures are stored so you can quickly apply them again, and they work like other annotations so you can reposition and resize them on the page.

Other changes include more descriptive names for paper sizes in document properties and free text annotations added to documents are now printed out by default.

Keyboard control for screenshots & new shutter sound

Screenshot selections can be adjusted from the keyboard.

Draw an area out, then press a keyboard arrow key to pick a side of the selection – keep tapping to make it bigger or smaller, or hold Shift to move in larger steps or Ctrl in smaller ones. Hold Alt with your arrow to move the entire selection area.

If you lose track of what you’re doing, tap R to reset and start over.

A new sound plays when taking screenshots. GNOME chose to replace the “inappropriate” camera shutter sound issue and save the blushes of those netting weird stares when screen-snapping in public.

Nautilus gets a drag counter and tab overview

Nautilus now shows a file count as you drag multiple files to a new folder or drive. This makes it easier to be know you absolutely did rubber-band select the right number of files from a folder.

Backend changes also mean files in large folders load faster during refreshes. At small widths a new tab overview button appears to make it easier to see and switch between tabs – useful in tiled setups.

Desktop icons ported to GTK4

DING, the desktop icons GNOME Shell extension Ubuntu preinstalled by default, moved to GTK4 earlier this year. That change buffs the visual style of context menus and dialogs so they match the rest of the desktop.

You’ll also find the desktop right-click menu opens a fraction faster. There used to be a slight pause in appearing while DING checked the system clipboard for any content to paste. Clipboard checks now run asynchronously to speed things up.

Desktop icon stacks can be opened and closed from the keyboard now too, and the Open With dialog no longer shows an option to ‘Find new apps’ for the associated file since it tried to open GNOME Software and, well, Ubuntu doesn’t use that…

Sign in with a passkey or Entra ID

The GDM login and lock screens now let you sign in with FIDO2 passkeys or web-based sign-in flows (smart cards were already supported).

It will mainly benefits users on corporate and managed devices, and a unified authentication framework will allow more sign-in methods to be added in future.

Additionally, if your workplace or school uses Microsoft Entra ID, you can sign in to Ubuntu using your Entra password and approve the MFA prompt with Microsoft Authenticator or a one-time code. It works on desktop, terminal and SSH.

App Center now offers driver management

App Center gains an Add-ons section with new pages: Additional Drivers, to enable or switch drivers (only appears on devices with hardware needing them, e.g., NVIDIA GPUs); Media Support to install codecs needed by some music and video formats.

Ubuntu’s default GUI software tool is also now better at matching the Snap and Debian versions of the same app.

For apps available in both formats, a unified details page shows download size, publisher, permissions and version number, so you can pick the one you want.

Updating software via App Center has been made more reliable, with apps no longer lingering in the update queue immediately after being updated. And if you install third-party Debs, it finally lets you install newer builds of apps you previously installed.

Separate amd64v3 installer for newer CPUs

Ubuntu 26.10 is available in download in more ways than before, with a separate amd64v3 ISO newly spun up for this release, albeit only available to download from the cdimage server, which houses ‘alternative’ downloads, and not the Ubuntu website.

The amd64v3 image installs Ubuntu with packages optimised for CPUs supporting x86-64-v3 feature level. Most Intel and AMD chips from 2015 onwards do, but some budget and embedded processors lack the required features so can’t boot from a -v3 image.

Benchmarks show modest performance gains (~1%), most noticeable in software that makes use of the newer CPU instructions the amd64-v3 ISO is optimised for, thinks like scientific computing or heavy video processing.

Settings gains a set of new toggles

Settings has more options, toggles and switches to poke around with.

In Mouse & Touchpad, a toggle lets you choose to disable the touchpad if a mouse is plugged in, while system details on the About page are now listed as a single page with reordered information (and a link to view the GNOME release notes).

On a touchscreen? Displays has a toggle to control auto-rotation …Which, is self-explanatory. When arranging the position of multiple monitors, the display squares now snap at centre alignment with the main monitor when you move them around.

The Network pane gains DNS domain search settings, but support for WEP wireless security is gone from Wi-Fi configuration because of how outdated and insecure it is.

And the Reduce Motion setting in Accessibility now does what it says and dials down animations, albeit not everywhere: the app picker and overview zoom are unaffected when it’s enabled.

Memory killer tries to keep your desktop alive

When memory runs out, Ubuntu 26.10 now tries to kill apps before any services that hold the session together. This means that a rogue browser tab or background process running out of control is less likely to cause a desktop crash, and you being punted back to the login screen.

GNOME remembers each monitor’s brightness

GNOME Shell now remembers each of your monitor’s brightness level, along with any colour mode setting (e.g., HDR) and restores them between reboots. ‘How is that a change?’, you wonder.

Previously, the kernel was relied on to remember display brightness. But power-saving modes can adjust that, so a dimmed value might reapply on the next boot. GNOME now remembers brightness for each monitor, and tells them apart by their EDID.

APT help is now genuinely helpful

Ubuntu 26.10 ships with APT 3.3.3, a modest update with a major benefit: --help  is now specific to the command you ran (the release notes call this “interactive” help).

In earlier versions, adding --help to a subcommand would tell you… little. For example, apt install --help got you the same output as running apt --help. If you wanted to know which flags install accepted, you’d have to open the man page.

In 26.10, the help flag is now specific to the subcommand so apt install --help now lists the options that apply to install. Other subcommands work the same way (not all, so keep that in mind). It should reduce visits to Google to find an option or syntax construction.

TPM disk encryption reaches more machines

Ubuntu 26.10 can be installed with TPM-backed full disk encryption (FDE) on devices that lack a hardware root of trust (hardware that lets the OS verify firmware hasn’t been meddled with).

The catch is you’ll need to set a PIN or passphrase during installation, but PCs made since 2021 have one and unlock automatically, so no PIN will be needed.

Resources tracks NPU usage

Resources, the system monitor Ubuntu adopted in 26.04, can report NPU activity for AMD Ryzen 7040, 8040 and Ryzen AI 300/400-series chips, including real-time power and performance stats.

Usage numbers now appear over the graphs in the sidebar instead of beneath them, and a tap of F9 will show or hide the sidebar (saves clicking the button to do it). Also, the app is better at tracing and reporting Steam games and Snap apps too.

First official RISC-V desktop image

An official, but entirely experimental, desktop image for modern RISC-V boards is available for the first time.

The RISC-V desktop images come in GNOME and minimal Xubuntu flavours, aimed at the SpacemiT K3 and QEMU, respectively. No official support is provided (updates do arrive, ofc) and the GNOME ISO lacks a few desktop snaps, including App Center.

Linux 7.3 included (as a release candidate)

Ubuntu 26.10 ships with Linux 7.3 but—dramatic piano stab—it’s not a stable kernel version.

Linux 7.3 is still in development, on course for release at the end of October. The kernel baked in to the ISO is a release candidate build. Users of 26.10 will be updated to the stable kernel via software updates.

Among Linux 7.3 highlights is early support for Snapdragon X2 Elite machines, including the Asus Zenbook A14, as well as more bits of hardware working on X Elite models, including webcams.

EXT4 gets a streamlined multi-block allocator to make file space pre-allocations faster during large downloads, while FUSE with io_uring also gets zero-copy support, so a FUSE server can read client data directly.

There’s also a KSM fix to reduce UI micro-stutters under heavy memory loads while VRAM management is notably improved on lower-end graphics cards with under 8GB of video memory, delivering an appreciable uptick in gaming performance.

Mesa 26.2 & NVIDIA 615 land

Graphics get a bump. Mesa 26.2 delivers mesh shader support to NVK, the open-source NVIDIA Vulkan driver, and low-latency Vulkan Video encode and decode for AMD GPUs.

NVIDIA’s 615 driver series replaces 595 and 610 series, and now only ships the open kernel modules, which cover Turing and newer GPUs. Older cards will need the 580 series.

Core utilities finish the move to Rust

Ubuntu’s move to Rust-based core utilities is now complete, with cp, mv and rm coming from uutils. Rust-based OpenPGP tooling (Sequoia) is preinstalled but not default (Canonical plans to make it the default in 27.04).

dbus-daemon ditched after 22 years

Further down the stack, dbus-broker replaces dbus-daemon as the system’s message bus, improving the reliability and security of how desktop apps and services talk to each other. There’s little change to notice, though it should mean fewer desktop features misbehave under heavy load.

Package updates & other changes in 26.10

On the package side, Ubuntu 26.10 make sure of the following out of the box:

  • systemd 261.3
  • PipeWire 1.6.8
  • BlueZ 5.87
  • GStreamer 1.28.7
  • OpenSSL 4.0.3

Among others, while notable software bumps in the 26.10 repos (some may see minor updates in the coming months, so what’s listed are the versions available at the time of release) include:

  • LibreOffice 26.8
  • Audacity 3.7.8
  • Blender 5.0.1
  • GIMP 3.2.6
  • VLC 3.0.24
  • FFmpeg 8.1
  • Krita 6.0.3

Developer toolchains available or preinstalled include OpenJDK 25 (with OpenJDK 27 also available to install), .NET 10, Python 3.14.7, LLVM 22.1.8 and Rust 1.97.

If an app you regularly install from the Ubuntu repos has issued an update since April, there’s a good chance it is packaged and present in the stonking repos!

Getting Ubuntu 26.10

Where do I download Ubuntu 26.10?

You can download Ubuntu 26.10 desktop for Intel/AMD devices from the Ubuntu website, or from the Ubuntu release server (which is where the official website fetches ISOs from), from today, 15 October 2026.

For the x86-64-v3, RISC-V, Raspberry Pi or WSL images, head to the cdimage sever to download those.

Ubuntu 26.10 runs on most modern 64-bit Intel/AMD computers, as well as Arm64 devices like Raspberry Pi and Snapdragon laptops, and on RVA23 RISC-V developer boards like the SpacemiT K3 and SiFive BigSky platform.

How long is Ubuntu 26.10 support?

Ubuntu 26.10 was released Thursday, 15 October, 2026 and is supported with ongoing updates for 9 months (so until July 2027). Upgrades to the next release, Ubuntu 27.04, will be available in April.

Can I upgrade to Ubuntu 26.10?

Most devices that run Ubuntu 26.04 LTS can upgrade to 26.10. The ‌upgrade is in place, keeping your files, apps and settings.

But as LTS releases are configured to only upgrade to new LTS releases by default, you’ll need to opt in to be notified of non-LTS upgrades:

sudo sed -i 's/^Prompt=lts$/Prompt=normal/' /etc/update-manager/release-upgrades

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS systems using TPM-backed FDE can not upgrade to Ubuntu 26.10. It is a temporary restriction; Canonical says it will enable upgrades at some point during the support window for this release.

If you use Ubuntu 25.10, 24.04 LTS or any other version, you cannot upgrade to 26.10 directly. Instead, you must first upgrade to the next in-series release, then the next, and so on, until you end up on 26.10. In those instances, it is easier to do a fresh install.

Which of these changes will you notice first? Tell me in the comments!
